--[p308]-- 4.3.3.1.1.2 Radicals generated by hydrogen abstraction
Abstraction of hydrogen by excited-state molecules makes possible the generation of radicals from molecules with low excitation energies, which effectively extends photoionization that can initiate photopolymerization of reactive monomers into the visible part of the spectrum. Examples of hydrogen-abstraction reactions include those by the excited triplet states of ketones such as anthraquinone (XXX).

--[p126]-- 2.7.3 Solubility switching approaches to realizing contrast between exposed and unexposed regions of the resist during development
There are quite a number of approaches to realizing contrast between the exposed and unexposed regions of the resist film, based on exposure-induced solubility or polarity switching of the film, all of which are described in detail in

--[p128]-- For positive-tone aqueous development of, for example, polar and charged chemical amplification resists, ionic interactions driven by highly polar polymer–polymer, hydration, and hydrogen bonding interactions decrease and breakdown the polymer–polymer interactions, making it easier for the water molecules of the developer to displace these interactions and solvate the charged polymeric units, ultimately dissolving them in the developer.
--[p127]-- 2.18): (a) crosslink formation, (b) chain scissioning, and (c) functional group transformation, including deprotection, rearrangement, etc. A good example of crosslinking resist is the classical cyclized polyisoprene resists, which are readily crosslinked upon exposure via azide groups, making them insoluble in most suitable nonpolar solvents. These nonpolar solvents will dissolve the unexposed linear polymer, producing a negative-tone image.
--[p127]-- Krysak, “Solvent development processing of chemically amplified resists: Chemistry, physics, and polymer science considerations,” Proc. SPIE 7972, 792905 (2011).
For resists based on exposure-induced functional group transformation such as in chemical amplification resists, depending on their polarity and the polarity of the developer solvent, different types of interactions mediate the dissolution of the part that is dissolved in the developer.
--[p128]-- In contrast, in negative-tone development in nonpolar solvent of the above polar and charged chemical amplification resists, the strong ionic polymer–polymer interactions, driven by polar hydrogen bonds of the exposed part of the film, make it much more difficult for solvent molecules to displace these interactions. Therefore, while the unexposed regions are readily developed away, the exposed polar region will exclude solvent penetration, leading to high-contrast unswollen patterns.
--[p127]-- Under normal circumstances, a resist with extensive chemical crosslink formation should have sufficient elastic resistance to inhibit large dimensional change during development.
Exposure-induced chain scissioning that leads to reduction of resist polymer molecular weight is another approach to effecting polarity switching and, hence, contrast between the exposed and unexposed region of the film during solvent development.
--[p127]-- However, given that the polarity of the polymer chain undergoes little change upon crosslinking, the solvent can still strongly solvate the exposed polymer chains, invariably leading to significant swelling of the negative-tone image. In fact, the large degree of swelling associated with this resist is suggestive of a low-level crosslinking.

===== [p295-297] Theory of Photochemical and Radiochemical Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 4.3.2.2.4 Esterification imaging mechanism (5块) =====
--[p295]-- 4.3.2.2.4 Esterification imaging mechanism
The esterification reaction of carboxylic acids and anhydrides has been exploited in the design of aqueous-base-developable negative resists because such reactions change the polarity of the resins from soluble to insoluble. A significant number of negative resists designed for ArF lithography are based on this principle.
--[p295]-- It should be pointed out that the presence of unreacted carboxylic acid units in the exposed regions of the film causes penetration of water into the film, resulting in swelling-induced distortion.<sup>223</sup>

--[p295]-- Examples of such resists are based on the intramolecular esterification of resins bearing g-hydroxy acid moieties and prepared from the cyclopolymerization of dienes of norbornene and maleic anhydride in a reaction in which the anhydride is converted to g-hydroxy acid using NaBH , with a simultaneous formation of g-lactone (Scheme 4.26a).<sup>222</sup> The g-hydroxy acid moiety (in Schemes 4.26a and 4.26b) undergoes acid-catalyzed intramolecular esterification (known as ring closure) to form g-lactone, effectively a polarity switch for negative-tone imaging with aqueous base developer.

--[p81]-- 2.6.4 Image formation in the resist
In order to highlight the subtleties of the influence of the vector nature of light on the formation of an image in the resist (especially at high numerical apertures, where that influence depends greatly on the polarization state of light and the angles of various discrete diffraction orders that pass through the lens and add to form the image), we will consider two plane waves transiting a mask with an array of simple lines and spaces.
--[p82]-- If the two electric fields do not interfere with each other, the total intensity is the sum of the individual intensities (i.e., it is a constant) and given by
$$
I = | E _ { 1 } | ^ { 2 } + | E _ { 2 } | ^ { 2 } .\tag{2.52}
$$
If, however, there is a complete interference between the two electric fields, the total intensity is given by
$$
I = | E _ { 1 } + E _ { 2 } | ^ { 2 } .\tag{2.53}
$$
--[p82]-- For instance, the amount of the electric field vector $E _ { 2 }$ that points in the same direction as $E _ { 1 }$ is the geometric projection $E _ { 2 }$ cos (2u). It thus follows that the intensity for this case is given by the coherent (electric field) sum of the parts that overlap plus the incoherent (intensity) sum of the parts that do not overlap:
$$
I = | E _ { 1 } + E _ { 2 } \cos ( 2 \Theta ) | ^ { 2 } + | E _ { 2 } \sin ( 2 \Theta ) | ^ { 2 } .\tag{2.54}
$$
--[p82]-- We must note that for $\theta \ : = \ : 0$ , Eq. (2.54) reduces to the perfectly coherent (interfering) sum of Eq. (2.53). If $\theta \ = \ 4 5$ deg, the two electric fields are perpendicular to each other, and Eq. (2.54) transforms into the perfectly incoherent (noninterfering) sum of Eq. (2.52).

===== [p430-430] Chapter 5 Theory of Block Copolymer Self-assembly Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 5.2.3.2 Synthesis of representative diblock copolymers by cationic polymerization (2块) =====
--[p430]-- To efficiently produce living polymers with well-defined molecular weight properties, including low polydispersity, the crossover reaction from the polymerization of one block to the other must be efficient. Efficient crossover reaction occurs when the monomers have almost equal reactivities or when the more reactive monomer is polymerized first, followed by the addition of the less reactive monomer. Monomer reactivity is efficiently estimated with the nucleophilicity parameter $N .
^ { 1 8 9 }$ Next, we briefly review some representative BCPs synthesized with this technique.
--[p430]-- 5.2.3.2 Synthesis of representative diblock copolymers by cationic polymerization
Cationic polymerization synthesis of BCPs is accomplished by sequentially adding the monomers to the reaction vessel containing the appropriate solvent, Lewis acid initiators, and maintaining an appropriately low temperature.

===== [p255-255] Theory of Photochemical and Radiochemical Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 4.3 Negative-Resist Imaging Mechanisms (5块) =====
--[p255]-- 4.3 Negative-Resist Imaging Mechanisms
As stated earlier, when the exposed part of the negative resist film is developed in an appropriate solvent, the polymers (as in crosslinking resists) and monomers (as in photo- and radiation-initiated polymerization resists) in the areas that have not been exposed retain their original linear (or branched) solvency and are removed by the developer solution.
--[p255]-- Because the dissolution rate of a polymer decreases as the molecular weight increases, common approaches used in the design of negative resists include crosslinking of high-molecularweight linear polymers, radiation-induced polarity changes in the functional groups of linear polymers, and polymerization of multifunctional monomers. These techniques have been fairly well reviewed.<sup>96</sup>
--[p255]-- In this way, a negative image is formed by the selective solvency of the exposed and unexposed areas in the developer.<sup>94</sup>
In addition to having the ability to be crosslinked and resisting the action of the developer in the exposed areas, negative resist resins must be adherent to wafer substrate surfaces and capable of thoroughly wetting them. Wetting occurs when the polymer molecules have a stronger attraction for the substrate surface than they have between themselves.
--[p255]-- The polymers and monomers as the case may be in the exposed areas, on the other hand, having been crosslinked (as with crosslinking resists) and polymerized (as with photoand radiation-initiated polymerization resists), respectively, and having had their molecular weight and sizes significantly increased, are able to resist the developer action and are therefore not removed.
--[p255]-- Poor wetting occurs when the polymer molecules have stronger attractive forces between themselves than the substrate surface, which reduces their attraction for the latter. Adhesion is therefore the result of an attraction between sites on the substrate surface and the polymer molecule.<sup>95</sup>
Figure 4.1 shows the three main classes of reactions used to generate images in negative working resist systems.

===== [p45-45] MOLECULAR THEORY OF LITHOGRAPHY > 1.3.6 Molecular self-assembly lithography (5块) =====
--[p45]-- mathrm { e t c . } ] ^ { 6 4 }$ are well-known precursor materials for SAMs on gold, the most extensively studied substrate. Organosilanes are often used to form SAMs on Si surfaces through Si-O-substrate siloxane bonds; an alkyl group is responsible for the ordered nature of the film.<sup>65</sup>
--[p45]-- Resists based on SAMs have also been successfully deposited on metals such as gold, aluminum, titanium, zirconium, silver, copper, and platinum as well as $\mathrm { S i O } _ { 2 } .$ GaAs, and other surfaces,<sup>62</sup> inspired no doubt by the first demonstration of the formation of long-chain v-substituted dialkyldisulfides on gold in 1983.<sup>63</sup> Alkane-thiols and dialkydisulfides (lipid-like organic molecules having the general formula: $\mathrm { H S - } ( \mathrm { C H } _ { 2 } ) _ { n } { - } X$ and $X \mathrm { - } ( \mathrm { C H } _ { 2 } ) \mathrm { - } \mathrm { S S } \mathrm { - } ( \mathrm { C H } _ { 2 } ) _ { m } \mathrm { - } Y ,$ respectively, where n and m indicate alkyl chain length and X, Y, the end groups $[ \mathrm { - C H } _ { 3 } ,$ -azobenzene, -OH, $\
--[p45]-- These SAM films can be molecularly engineered to be patternable with various types of energetic radiations, including DUV, soft x rays, ion beams, and low-energy electrons.<sup>60</sup> Device features smaller than 20 nm have been successfully patterned on SAMs with scanning tunneling microscopes (STMs) and conventional EBL systems. 61
--[p45]-- In one form of this technique, self-assembling precursor molecules from solutions or vapor phase react at interfaces to produce layers of monomolecular thickness that are chemically bonded to solid surfaces through thermodynamically favorable bond formation involving chemisorption. Such layers belong to a class of materials called self-assembled monolayers (SAMs) and make good ultrathin-film resist candidates.
--[p45]-- 1.3.6 Molecular self-assembly lithography
Lithography based on molecular self-assembly, a chemical process in which molecules spontaneously organize to form larger ordered structures, represents one of the newest emerging lithographic techniques.

===== [p452-453] Chapter 5 Theory of Block Copolymer Self-assembly Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 5.4.4 Solvent annealing (6块) =====
--[p452]-- Empirical evidence indicates that polymer diffusion increases with the addition of solvent, even as $T _ { \mathrm { g } }$ decreases.<sup>279,280,281</sup> Given the enhanced mobility of polymer under solvent annealing conditions, strongly segregating block pairs such as poly(styrene-b-ethylene oxide) (PS-b-PEO, $\chi \ : = \ : 0 . 0 8 )$ are capable of low defect densities after exposure to solvent vapor.
--[p453]-- Very slow solvent evaporation rates (0.2 nL/s) induced inplane formation of cylinders, intermediate evaporation (5 nL/s) induced vertical orientation of cylinders, while fast evaporation (200 nL/s) induced vertical microphase separated structures with poor long-range order.

--[p452]-- 5.4.4 Solvent annealing
For long-range order, sufficient mobility must be achieved in both blocks of the BCP. --[p452]-- For instance, $5 \ \mathrm { \textmu m } ^ { 2 }$ single grains of vertically oriented cylinders have been achieved with PS-b-PEO exposed to an atmosphere of benzene and water for two days.<sup>282</sup>
Given that evaporation from a thin film is a highly directional process, usually in the direction normal to the substrate, an appreciable degree of orientation control can be achieved with solvent annealing.
--[p453]-- As the solvent evaporates from the top of the film in a decreasing manner towards the bottom, domains tend to orient in the same direction, inducing alignment of anisotropic domains normal to the direction of solvent evaporation. Kim and Libera<sup>283</sup> have shown that the evaporation rate of the solvent-infused film has a strong effect on the orientation of the BCP cylinders in a poly(styrene-bbutadiene-styrene) (PS-b-PB-b-PS) triblock copolymer.

===== [p124-126] Chapter 2 Theory of the Lithographic Process > 2.7.2 The nature of the development process (16块) =====
--[p125]-- In this way, high contrast between the exposed and unexposed parts of the resist film is maintained in chemical amplification resists.
It should be mentioned that it is possible to develop the above-described chemical amplification resist in a negative tone, simply by developing it in a nonpolar solvent.
--[p125]-- In the specific case of positive-tone aqueous development of a chemical amplification resist based on polar deprotected polymeric acid, the carboxylic acid functional group of the latter is quickly ionized in the 0.26 N TMAH developer into its carboxylate anion and proton, creating a polyelectrolyte that is easily dissolved.
--[p124]-- If the polymer–solvent interactions are stronger than the polymer–polymer attractive forces, the chain segments will start to absorb solvent molecules, increasing the volume of the polymer matrix, and will eventually become fully solvated (completely surrounded by solvent molecules), unfolding and loosening out from the coiled shape [Fig. 2.16(b)]. This constitutes the first stage of the dissolution process.
--[p126]-- Here, strong hydrogen bonding interaction and hydrophobic interactions between the molecules of the exposed and charged polymeric acid film, which tend to sequester polar molecules from nonpolar molecules, lead to effective resistance to dissolution of this part in the nonpolar developer solvent.
--[p126]-- Here, ionic interactions and polyelectrolyte effects are absent. Instead, the solvent molecules, having similar solubility parameters as the polymers of the nonexposed part, displace the polymer–polymer van der Waals interactions in the unexposed part of the film, using similarly weak van der Waals bonds, and thus leading to dissolution.
--[p124]-- It should be pointed out, however, that if a highly crosslinked polymer is involved, where the polymer–polymer interactions are much stronger than the polymer–solvent interactions, the dissolution process stops at this first stage, giving rise to a swollen polymer gel.
--[p125]-- If the polymers have functional units that can react with the solvent molecules, reactions such as, for example, acid–base neutralization reactions will take place, giving rise to chemical development of the resist. If there are no functional reactive units on the polymers, no reaction will occur, and the development will proceed in a purely physical fashion.
--[p124]-- If on the other hand, the polymer–solvent interactions are still strong enough relative to the polymer–polymer interactions, the solvation–unfolding–swelling process will continue until all of the polymer segments are solvated, following which the fully unfolded and loosened coil of the polymer will diffuse out of the swollen gel layer, dispersing into the developer solution.
--[p126]-- The nonpolar and unexposed part of the resist film, having a similar solubility parameter as the nonpolar solvent, readily dissolves in the latter, thus affording contrast between the exposed and unexposed part of the resist films.
The negative-tone development of nonpolar and uncharged resist polymeric films in nonpolar solvents proceeds in a somewhat similar but slightly different manner compared to that described above for development in polar solvents.
--[p124]-- When a polymer is added to the developer solution, attractive as well as dispersion forces start to act between the polymer segments, according to their polarity, chemical properties, and solubility parameter (see below).
--[p124]-- Now fully solvated, with solvent molecules filling the empty space between the loosened polymer segments, the dispersed polymer coils adopt a spheroidal or ellipsoidal form [Fig. 2.16(c)], occupying a volume referred to as the hydrodynamic volume.
211. ibid.
212. J. M. Shaw and M. Hatzakis, “Developer temperature effects on e-beam and optically exposed positive photoresist,” J. Electrochem. Soc. 126(11), 2026–2031 (1979).
--[p125]-- So, in a nutshell, the solubility of the resist polymer in the developer medium depends on the ability of the developer molecules to solvate the polymer molecule and to displace or break down polymer–polymer interactions, as shown in Fig. 2.17.
--[p124]-- 2.7.2 The nature of the development process
Resist resins are predominantly comprised of fairly high-molecular-weight polymers with long chains having a large number of segments, forming tightly folded coils that are further entangled with each other and held together by cohesive attractive intra- and intermolecular forces, including dispersion, dipole–dipole interaction, induction, and hydrogen bonding [see Fig. 2.16(a)].
--[p125]-- The negative charges present on this polymeric acid polyelectrolyte solvates water molecules through hydration interactions (discussed in Chapter 3), leading to the breakdown of the polymer–polymer interaction. Equally important, the negative charges on the polymeric acid polyelectrolyte molecules through electrostatic repulsion cause the expansion of the polymer coil [Fig. 3.16(b)], providing an elastic force that aids dissolution.
--[p124]-- As such, their dissolution in the developer solvent can be noticeably slower than those of lower-molecular-weight molecules. There appear to be two main stages associated with resist polymer dissolution in nonpolar solvents: the first is the swelling step, which is followed by the actual dissolution step.
--[p125]-- While the exposed and deprotected part of the resist film dissolves in the developer, mediated by the above ionic interactions, the unexposed and nonpolar part of the resist film does not dissolve in the developer, in part, due to a lack of these ionic interactions. In addition, the strong hydrogen bonding of the developer water molecules with each other leads to effective resistance of this nonpolar part of the resist film to dissolve in the polar aqueous developer.

===== [p467-468] Chapter 6 Theory of Imprint Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 6.3.1 Thermal imprint lithographic imaging mechanism (13块) =====
--[p467]-- TIL resists can be formulated with polymers that crosslink and form thermosets during the imprinting process, instead of flowing like their thermoplastic counterparts.
--[p468]-- The process begins with heating the wafer and master to $T _ { 2 } ,$ , which is, for example, 80–100°C above the $T _ { \mathrm { g } }$ of the imprint resist polymer, as already stated. Pressure of 100–1000 kPa is then applied to press the master against the softened polymer. The polymer will flow at this point and will fill the cavities in the master, forming an inverse replica of the master.

--[p468]-- As not all polymers melt and flow, those that do not will decompose before the flow transition point and, as such, are not useful as imprint resist polymers. Embossing/imprinting can, in principle, be performed at $T _ { \mathrm { g } }$ but would take place too slowly to be economical in a production environment.
The thermal imprint process can be visualized in the pressure–temperature diagram of Fig. 6.2. Figure 6.3 shows a schematic for the TIL process.
--[p467]-- The flow is induced by pressing a template/ master/stamp containing the features to be printed against the viscoelastic, rubbery, glassy polymer fluid, such that the flowed polymer fills the cavities in the master, forming an inverse replica of the master once the polymer melt is solidified by cooling below the $T _ { \mathrm { g } } .$ .
--[p468]-- 6.1 is the glass transition temperature, where the polymer makes the transition from a solid amorphous material to a viscous, rubbery, glassy fluid. The second transition is the flow transition, where the polymer melts. This is the regime where embossing/imprinting is easily and quickly performed, and, as such, is the imprint processing regime.
--[p467]-- 6.3.1 Thermal imprint lithographic imaging mechanism
The thermal imprint lithographic imaging mechanism is based on pressuredriven flow of thermoplastic resist polymer at a higher temperature than its glass transition temperature $T _ { \mathrm { g } } .$ .
--[p467]-- The imprinting or embossing temperature is typically 80–100 °C higher than the $T _ { \mathrm { g } }$ of the polymer.<sup>28</sup> The imprint force is on the order of 100–1000 kPa, and hold time is on the order of minutes. Demolding or de-embossing takes place after cooling below the $T _ { \mathrm { g } }$ of the polymer. In principle, the imprinted features are true replicas of the master/ template/stamp, and any-sized pattern can be made.

===== [p68-70] Chapter 2 Theory of the Lithographic Process > 2.4 Soft Bake (5块) =====
--[p68]-- 2.4 Soft Bake
Following the spin-coating of the resist on the wafer, the next processing step is the soft bake (also called prebake or post-apply bake). The purpose of this bake is to densify the film and drive off residual solvent.
--[p70]-- Figure 2.6(c) shows the impact of baking time on solvent diffusivity, which rises during the initial few seconds, reaching a maximum at about 2 s, before decreasing and reaching a steady state at around 8 s. Figure 2.6(d) shows a typical change in resist thickness during baking, which decreases as the resist density increases.
Typical soft-bake temperatures are 90–120 °C for 60 s on a hot plate, followed by a cooling step on a chill plate to achieve consistent wafer temperature control.
The boiling points of most resist solvents are on the order of 140 °C, far higher than the soft-bake temperatures of resists.
--[p69]-- SPIE 2195, 584–595 (1994).
Figures 2.6(a)–(d) show the mechanisms of different physical processes taking place during the first 10 s of soft baking a typical resist on a vacuum hot plate.<sup>53</sup> Figure 2.6(a) shows that the temperature of the wafer increases with an initial rapid rise during the first seconds of baking, before leveling off after 3 s. Figure 2.6(b) shows the solvent loss during this time, which continues to decrease well out to 10 s and beyond.
--[p68]-- Other consequences of soft baking include a reduction of free volume and polymer relaxation, which have been suggested to be useful in improving resist process performance.<sup>51</sup> The soft bake also improves adhesion of the resist to the substrate, promotes resist uniformity on the wafer, and aids in better linewidth control during etching.
52. C. A. Mack D. P. DeWitt, B. K. Tsai, and G. Yetter, “Modeling of solvent evaporation effects for hot plate baking of photoresist,” Proc.
--[p70]-- Temperature control is important for soft-baking processes and becomes increasingly critical as the IC industry shifts the bulk of production to chemical amplification resists.<sup>54</sup> To achieve the stringent temperature uniformity specifications necessary for the tight critical dimension (CD) control specifications for advanced semiconductor lithography, careful consideration of the vacuum hot plate design, including uniform wafer-tohot-plate contact, airflow, thermal management, and contamination control, are mandated.<sup>55</sup>

===== [p63-63] Chapter 2 Theory of the Lithographic Process > 2.3.3 Instabilities in UTR films (1块) =====
--[p63]-- 2.3.3 Instabilities in UTR films
Instabilities in UTR polymer films are manifested in two main ways: (1) defects resulting from the coating process, substrate nonuniformities, and conjoining pressure, and (2) discontinuities in the thermophysical properties of the films due to interfacial effects and polymer cooperative and surface dynamics.

--[p154]-- 3.4.1 General van der Waals interactions operating during resist film PEB and development in the developer solution medium
Van der Waals forces are the collective name of a set of forces characterized by the same power dependence on distance.
--[p154]-- Three main components constitute the overall van der Waals forces: orientation, induction, and dispersion forces. We briefly review the components of van der Waals forces below.
The importance of van der Waals forces derives from the fact that they are always involved in the interaction between bodies, unlike other kinds of forces that require a particular feature, for example, an electric charge or a layer of adsorbed macromolelcules, etc.

--[p239]-- Consequently, the photoreaction occurs exclusively from the triplet state and may proceed by a different route from the singlet state reaction.<sup>52</sup>
To achieve spectral sensitization by singlet energy transfer with a sensitizer that absorbs at a longer wavelength than the reactant would require endothermic energy transfer, which under normal circumstances is not a practical solution.
--[p239]-- 4.2.5.1.1 Triplet sensitization
Triplet sensitization is associated with exothermic energy transfer from the triplet excited state of the sensitizer to the ground state of the reactant. The majority of sensitization processes in organic resist systems is based on this reaction:
$$
S _ { 0 } ( r e a c t a n t ) + T ^ { * } ( s e n s i t i z e r )  T ^ { * } ( r e a c t a n t ) + S _ { 0 } ( s e n s i t i z e r ) .\tag{[4.3]}
$$
--[p241]-- long triplet lifetime to increase the probability of energy transfer between sensitizer and reactant;
4. the ability to strongly absorb the available radiation in a spectral region where the reactant does not absorb; and
5. solubility in the reaction medium (solvent or polymer matrix).
--[p240]-- As shown in Fig. 4.8, there are two pathways for sensitizing the naphthalene reactant by acetophenone. In the first pathway, upon absorption of the exposure energy, the ground-state $S _ { 0 }$ electrons of the sensitizer are promoted to their excited singlet state $S _ { 1 }$ , whose energy level lies above that of the first triplet state $T _ { 1 }$ . The $S _ { 1 }$ electrons of the sensitizer can radiatively transfer their energy via ISC and decay down to $T _ { 1 }$ of the sensitizer.
--[p241]-- As a general rule, these conditions are satisfied in the aromatic ketones, where the $n \pi ^ { * }$ character of the excited states (triplets and singlet) favors ISC, high values of $\Phi _ { \mathrm { T } }$ , and a small singlet–triplet splitting. This explains why the majority of common sensitizers are either ketones or contain the carbonyl group somewhere in their structure.<sup>57</sup> Table 4.3 shows a list of common sensitizers.
--[p241]-- And because the $S _ { 1 }$ state of acetophenone lies at a much higher energy level than its $T _ { 1 }$ state, the electrons can radiatively decay from the former to the latter via ISC. Additionally, because the $T _ { 1 }$ state of acetophenone is at much higher energy level than the $T _ { 1 }$ state of naphthalene, the electrons of the former can radiatively transfer their energy and decay to the $T _ { 1 }$ state of naphthalene, thereby sensitizing it.
--[p239]-- However, it is possible to accomplish the same situation with a sensitizer whose singlet excited state lies below that of the reactant, but whose triplet level lies above the triplet level of the reactant,<sup>54</sup> as schematically illustrated in Fig. 4.8 for the pair naphthalene (reactant)–acetophenone (sensitizer).<sup>55</sup>

--[p202]-- 3.6.1.2 Enthalpy of mixing developer solvent and resist polymeric solute

===== [p185-185] Chapter 3 Theory of Molecular Interactions in Lithography > 3.4.5 Steric interactions (3块) =====
--[p185]-- This interaction typically leads to a repulsive osmotic force due to the unfavorable entropy associated with confining the particle and the chains of the polymers of the resist film surface, or confining them between the polymer in the developer and the resist film surface. This repulsion is referred to as steric or overlap repulsion, and it plays a very important role in the stabilization of colloidal particles that would normally coagulate in a solvent.
--[p185]-- For this reason, a small amount of polymer may be intentionally added to colloidal dispersions of nanoparticle resists to stabilize them. Such polymer additives are referred to as being protective against coagulation.
--[p185]-- 3.4.5 Steric interactions
When a colloidal particle or a polymer in the developer solution approaches the polymeric resist film surface, it experiences a force once its outer segment and that of the polymer begin to overlap—that is, once the separation between them is below a few radii of gyration of the polymer.

===== [p208-210] Chapter 3 Theory of Molecular Interactions in Lithography > 3.7.2 Ambipolar diffusion of photoacid ions (22块) =====
--[p208]-- 3.7.2 Ambipolar diffusion of photoacid ions
The exposure process of photoresists, especially those that are chemically amplified, comprising essentially dielectric polymeric films and PAGs, creates a solid electrolyte solution with nonuniform photoacid distribution. By baking the exposed resist film, a uniform distribution of the acid throughout the film is achieved over a given time interval.
--[p209]-- Because of their much smaller size and larger diffusion coefficient, the acids tend to escape faster to the boundaries than their counterions, resulting in a local charge separation. Due to this charge separation, an electric field builds up between the acid space charges and their counterion space charges. This electric field tends to retard the acids and accelerate the counterions to diffuse toward the boundaries.

===== [p416-418] Chapter 5 Theory of Block Copolymer Self-assembly Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 5.2.1.3.2.1 Synthesis of linear symmetric triblock copolymers containing two different monomers (ABA triblocks) (12块) =====
--[p416]-- There are inherent advantages to using this technique: most importantly, an exact symmetric triblock copolymer is formed. Additionally, only two steps are required instead of three as is the case in the sequential monomer addition procedure. As excess living anions are used to ensure complete reaction of both groups of the coupling agent, an additional fractionation step is employed to separate the ABA triblock from the excess AB diblock.
--[p418]-- Preparation of a symmetric ABA triblock copolymer with the use of a difunctional initiator—an organometallic compound with two anionic sites that are able to initiate polymerization—involves a two-step process in which the monomers of the middle B block are first polymerized to completion, followed by the addition and polymerization of the A block monomers.
--[p416]-- In the coupling of living AB chains, a living diblock copolymer, having the same composition but half the molecular weight of the final triblock copolymer, is synthesized by sequential addition of monomers. Next, an appropriate coupling agent, such as a compound with functional groups that are able to react with the active anions at the chain ends and form covalent bonds, is used to connect two AB chains, resulting in the desired symmetric triblock copolymer.
--[p417]-- Here, a poly(styrene-b-isoprene) diblock copolymer is first formed such that the length of the poly(isoprene) block is half of that in the final triblock copolymer. Next, the living diblocks are coupled using $\mathrm { ( C H } _ { 3 } ) _ { 2 } \mathrm { S i C l } _ { 2 }$ as the coupling agent. A small excess of the living diblock is used to ensure complete coupling, necessitating solvent/nonsolvent fractionation of the final product to isolate the pure triblock copolymer.
--[p418]-- Many difunctional initiators soluble in polar and/or nonpolar solvents have been reported to be efficient in anionic polymerization of relevant monomers.<sup>158,159,160,161,162</sup> Well-defined poly(styrene-b-1,4-butadiene-b-styerene) triblock copolymers with dienic middle block and styrenic outer blocks are synthesized in hydrocarbon solvents using a difunctional initiator derived from 1,3-bis(1-phenylethenyl)benzene (PEB), after the methods of Lo,<sup>163</sup> Quirk<sup>164</sup> and Cunningham,<sup>165</sup> as shown in Scheme 5.12.

===== [p235-235] Theory of Photochemical and Radiochemical Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 4.2.3.2 Exchange transfer (5块) =====
--[p235]-- 4.2.3.2 Exchange transfer
The exchange transfer mechanism is based on electron exchange between a donor–acceptor pair of molecules. According to Dexter,<sup>30</sup> the distance dependence for this process is given by
$$
k _ { \mathrm { E T } } ( e x c h a n g e ) = K J \exp \biggl ( - \frac { 2 R _ { \mathrm { D A } } } { L } \biggr ) ,\tag{4.28}
$$
--[p235]-- where K is a constant for a given donor–acceptor pair, J is a fully normalized spectral overlap integral that is equivalent to $\begin{array} { r } { \int f _ { \mathrm { D } } ( \nu ) \mathfrak { E } _ { \mathrm { A } } ( \nu ) \frac { d \nu } { \nu ^ { 4 } } } \end{array}$ of Eq. (4.26), and L is the sum of the van der Waals radii of the donor and acceptor.
--[p235]-- Reiser observes that the rate of exchange transfer falls off even more rapidly with increasing molecular separation than the rate of dipole resonance transfer.<sup>31</sup>
By necessity, the exchange mechanism requires orbital overlap between donor and acceptor molecules, which means that it operates only over “collisional” distances on the order of 10 Å.
--[p235]-- Furthermore, exchange transfer is also less sensitive to changes in spin multiplicity than dipole resonance transfer. It is the mechanism responsible for the triplet-to-singlet energy transfer in the spectral sensitization processes of organic photochemistry.<sup>33</sup>
30. D. L. Dexter, “A theory of sensitized luminescence in solids,” J. Chem. Phys. 21, 836–850 (1953).
31. A. Reiser, Photoreactive Polymers: The Science and Technology of Resists, John Wiley & Sons, New York, p. 74 (1989).
32.
ibid.
--[p235]-- While the exchange transfer mechanism also depends on spectral overlap, it does not depend on the intensities of the radiative transitions and is therefore a more general energy transfer mechanism. Also, this type of energy transfer is rather nonspecific and occurs on almost every encounter, provided the process is exothermic (i.e., $\{ E _ { \mathrm { D ^ { * } } } - E _ { \mathrm { A ^ { * } } } \} < 0 )$ 32

--[p169]-- We note that this charged surface will induce a given distribution in surrounding ions, that is, a dependence of the ion density on the distance from the surface. The concentration of ions whose charge is opposite to that of the surface (counterions) increases with respect to the bulk value close to the surface, leading to what is called an electric double layer, and decreases as the distance from the surface increases.
--[p169]-- Ultimately, this negatively charged resist surface is balanced by an equal but oppositely charged region of counterions. Some of these counterions will be bound, usually transiently, to the surface within the so-called Stern or Helmholtz layer, while others will form an atmosphere of ions in rapid thermal motion close to the surface, known as the diffuse electric double layer (see Fig. 3.7).
--[p168]-- Polymeric resist film surfaces immersed in 0.26 N TMAH developer solvent, a high-dielectric-constant solvent given that it is predominantly water, can acquire a charge basically through two different mechanisms that include ionization of suitable polar functional groups and specific adsorption of ions.<sup>37</sup> The first mechanism involves the dissociation of dissociable groups such as carboxyl, hydroxyl, sulfate, amino etc., that are present on the resist surface, where they are intentionally introduced or inadvertently produced, for example, from surface oxidation. The second mechanism arises from the adsorption of charged molecules onto the resist film surface.
--[p169]-- Our system has two phases: the liquid phase 1 of the developer solution and the solid phase 2 of the resist film.

We choose as the model for the polymer a long-chain molecule consisting of x chain segments, each of which is of the same size (i.e., volume) as a solvent molecule.

--[p123]-- 2.7.1 Resist development methods
Since the invention of photolithography in 1826, resists have been developed by methods ranging from immersion to spray to puddle processes, either in batch mode or in continuous mode. Resist development in the 1970s and early 1980s typically involved immersion development, in which batches of wafers were immersed in tanks of developers for a given length of time.
--[p124]-- 30–75 s, following which the developer is rinsed off with deionized water. Additional puddles may sometimes be applied to the wafer in order to reduce defects.<sup>211</sup> The tubes carrying the developer to the wafer are jacketed, and their temperature is actively controlled to within $\pm 0 .
--[p124]-- This can cause variations in the concentration of the developer and temperature of the resist film because of evaporative cooling, leading to variations in development rates and ultimately to poor CD uniformity.
--[p123]-- The single-wafer puddle process, operating in an automatic continuous mode in a track system, is now the most commonly used method for resist development. It involves an initial dispense of the developer on each wafer, forming a puddle that covers the entire wafer surface for a period of typically

===== [p236-238] Theory of Photochemical and Radiochemical Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 4.2.4 Energy migration in resist polymers (13块) =====
--[p237]-- Furthermore, interrupting the sequence of naphthalene units, e.g., by copolymerization with methyl methacrylate, results in diminution of the delayed fluorescence, which is observed only as long as significant blocks of naphthyl groups still remain.<sup>44</sup> It is for similar reasons that delayed fluorescence, e.g., in poly(2-vinylnaphthalene) is dependent on molecular weight, i.e., on chain length.<sup>45</sup>
--[p237]-- In contrast, when 1% poly(1-vinylnaphthalene) is blended with 99% of polystyrene, the result is mainly polystyrene phosphorescence. These results lend themselves to the conclusion that energy migration must occur intramolecularly via the manifold of phenyl groups attached to the polyvinyl backbone.<sup>42</sup> The same conclusion was also reached from the observation of delayed fluorescence in highly dilute solid solutions of poly(1-vinylnaphthalene) in organic glasses at 77 K.
--[p237]-- The delayed fluorescence in this system is attributed to the encounter of two triplet excited states, which, in turn, provides evidence for triplet migration along the chain. On encounter, the two triplet states are believed to disproportionately form an excited state (which emits fluorescence) and a singlet ground state, as shown in the following reaction:<sup>43</sup>
$$
T _ { 1 } ^ { * } + T _ { 1 } ^ { * } {  } S _ { 1 } ^ { * } + S _ { 0 } .\tag{[4.2]}

--[p236]-- A few years later, Kallman and co-workers<sup>37</sup> reported observing long-range energy migration in polystyrene (a common resist polymer platform in DUV lithography) and in some other polymers.
The thought then was that in these systems the exciton traveled along the phenyl groups in the side chains of the polymer in a process termed down-chain migration.
--[p236]-- 4.2.4 Energy migration in resist polymers
Other than energy transfer, the other process for transporting energy from one resist component to the other is energy migration. While energy transfer in resist systems is mediated via coulombic or dipolar interactions and electron exchange or orbital interactions, energy migration is mediated via excitons.
--[p236]-- Reiser, Photoreactive Polymers: The Science and Technology of Resists, John Wiley & Sons, New York, p. 75 (1989).
35. ibid.
36. A. S. Davydov, Theory of Molecular Excitons, McGraw-Hill, New York (1962).
37. F. H. Brown, M. Furst, and H. Kallmann, “Light and high energy induced energy transfer in liquid and rigid organic scintillators,” Discuss. Faraday Soc. 27, 43 (1959).
--[p238]-- The range of energy migration in some of these materials has been reported to be on the order of angstroms.<sup>46</sup>
It should be mentioned that side-chain interaction in polystyrene and in similar polymers not only promotes energy migration, but also promotes the formation of excimers that occur in solution mainly as a result of conformational transitions, which bring neighboring fluorophores into juxtaposition.
--[p236]-- Energy migration in resist polymer matrices plays a very important role by chanelling energy to reactive sites, be they scissioning or crosslinking points on the polymer backbone or deprotection sites on the pendant groups of the polymer.<sup>35</sup> It was Frenkel who introduced the term exciton for the energy quantum mobile in an ensemble of identical molecules.
--[p238]-- This is the reason that polystyrene films, for example, exclusively emit excimer fluorescence, although the concentration of the excimer sites is low, on the order of 1 mol%.<sup>48</sup> In these systems, the excimer sites are supplied with excitation energy by exciton migration. Of particular interest is the fact that the concentration of excimer sites tends to limit the exciton migration range in these systems.<sup>49</sup>
--[p236]-- This view was later confirmed by Fox et al.<sup>38</sup> and David et al.,<sup>39</sup> who studied the fluorescence behavior of copolymers and of polymer blends, and also by Cozzens and Fox,<sup>40</sup> who observed that in copolymers of styrene and 1-vinylnaphthalene (I) containing only 1% napthalene and 99% of benzene units, napthalene phosphorescence was observed almost exclusively.<sup>41</sup>
33. ibid.
34. A.
--[p236]-- In 1935 Davydow described the spectral characteristics of such systems in more detail, illuminating in the attempt a number of unexplained phenomena in solid state physics.<sup>36</sup> Both Frenkel and Davydow predicted the possibility of energy migration not only in crystals but also in partially ordered arrays and even in amorphous systems, of which resist polymers are a part.
--[p238]-- Down-chain energy migration has since been widely experimentally investigated and confirmed, and is now known to be a common phenomenon that plays a significant role in the degradation and stabilization of polymers, including those used in resist applications. The polymer chain in these systems acts as an “antenna” that conducts energy either to a reactive site or away from the point of incidence to a quencher where it can be harmlessly dissipated.
--[p238]-- In bulk polymers, excimer emission is much more pronounced, given that energy migration also occurs between chains. Reiser asserts that excimer emission occurs in bulk polymers from monomer pairs that have the required conformation already in the ground state.<sup>47</sup>
Another characteristic of excimers in polymers is that they have lower excitation energy than the isolated monomer, implying that excimer sites in a polymer matrix can act as exciton traps.

--[p16]-- In addition, the book will provide the theoretical basis for the main unit operations of the advanced lithographic process, as well as for advanced lithographic imaging mechanisms, including photochemical and radiochemical, imprint, and directed selfassembly imaging mechanisms.
The book is intended for students and professionals whose knowledge of lithography extends to the chemistry and physics underlying its various unit operations, and the imaging mechanisms of its various forms.
--[p16]-- This book is intended to fill this need. It attempts to systematically explain with physical-chemical theories the molecular-level interactions that underlie the essential aspects of lithographic imaging phenomena. The effects of such molecular-level interactions become all the more heightened in the regime of single-digit to a few tens of nanometer-patterned feature length scales, a regime that overlaps the radius of gyration of the resist polymers used in the patterning.
--[p16]-- Preface
The science and technology of lithography, especially advanced semiconductor lithography, have now reached such an advanced stage of development and promise such numerous applications (as evidenced by the numerous technologies that the field is now enabling—from electronics to photonics, catalysis to medicine, energy transduction and storage to sensing) that there is a need for a single, reasonably complete, unified exposition of the molecular theory that underlies lithographic imaging.

When a transition occurs between states of different multiplicity, it is termed an intersystem crossing (ISC). Intersystem crossings are spin-forbidden transitions that are due to the intervention (in aromatic systems) of out-ofplane vibrations or by the state-mixing effects of heavy atoms.
--[p226]-- Fluorescence is a spin-allowed radiative transition between states of the same multiplicity $( \mathrm { e } . \mathrm { g } . , S _ { 1 }  S _ { 0 } )$ . --[p224]-- The general laws of photochemistry stipulate that only the light absorbed by a system is effective in producing a photochemical change. Each photon or quantum absorbed activates at most one molecule in the primary excitation step of a photochemical sequence; i.e., each photon or quantum absorbed by a molecule has a certain probability of populating either the lowest excited state $S _ { 1 } ,$ or the lowest triplet state $T _ { 1 }$ .
--[p226]-- For reactions in condensed phases such as solid resist films, the lowest excited singlet state $( S _ { 1 } )$ is a state from which photochemical reactions occur. Formation of a triplet state by direct photon absorption by a ground state molecule is spin forbidden. The very fast rate of IC from upper singlet states $( S _ { 2 } , S _ { 3 } , \ldots )$ to the lowest excited singlet $( S _ { 1 } )$ makes photochemical reactions unlikely from upper states.

===== [p138-139] Chapter 2 Theory of the Lithographic Process > 2.8.2 UV radiation curing (10块) =====
--[p139]-- The process requires careful balancing of curing of the skin of the pattern (to ensure that it is uniform), while ensuring that the bulk of the resist is prevented from flowing when the hot plate is ramped close to the $T _ { \mathrm { g } }$ of the resist. The surface of the resist pattern is given a harder cure (it receives UV + bake) than the bulk (which receives only thermal cure).
--[p139]-- This problem highlights one of the main drawbacks of UV radiation curing.<sup>276</sup>
273. ibid.
274. ibid.
275. J. C. Mathews and J. I. Wilmott, Jr., “Stabilization of single layer and multilayer resist patterns to aluminum etching environments,” Proc. SPIE 470, 194–202 (1984); J. C. Matthews, “Hardening of photoresist,” U.S. Patent No. 4,548,688 (1985).
--[p139]-- Although the novolac DUV curing chemistry readily takes place in the presence of oxygen, it can also take place in a nitrogen atmosphere, in which case the novolac acts as a self-oxidizer.<sup>274</sup> For resist systems based on acrylate-, alicyclic and hybrid acrylate/alicyclic polymers used in DUV 193-nm lithography as well as 157-nm lithography, which are generally very transparent at DUV wavelengths, they can be cured at the vacuum UV (VUV) wavelength of 172 nm.
--[p138]-- UV radiation curing of resists has been commonly used to harden the outer shell of the resist, thereby allowing higher postbake temperatures to be attained without destroying the patterned image. The high optical absorbance of resins such as novolac at wavelengths below 300 nm (absorbance $\gg 1 ~ \mu \mathrm { m } ^ { - 1 } )$ prevents crosslinking to substantial depths.<sup>268</sup> Although the efficiency is quite low, novolac resins can be made to crosslink at DUV wavelengths (240–260 nm).
--[p138]-- Carrying out this process at high temperature facilitates the curing.<sup>269</sup> Subjecting patterned resist features to DUV exposure at temperatures above $1 5 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ results in a thermally stabilized surface crust.
--[p138]-- The process is outlined in Scheme 2.6.<sup>270</sup> In particular, the scheme shows that DUV irradiation induces radical chain reactions in novolac that crosslink the outer resist layer only, given the high absorbance of novolac at 250 nm.<sup>271</sup> Multifunctional DNQs can also undergo DUV curing by crosslinking via novolac ester formation, involving primarily radical reactions and oxidation induced in the novolac.<sup>272</sup>
A low-pressure mercury arc lamp is normally used as a source of shortwavelength UV radiation curing of phenolic resin-based resists.
--[p138]-- 2.8.2 UV radiation curing
To improve the thermal properties of resists and prevent thermal deformation of resist pattern profiles during the dry etching process, where the temperature of the wafer often exceeds the deformation temperature of untreated resist, UV radiation curing that results in crosslinking is sometimes used.<sup>267</sup> DNQ/novolac, poly(hydroxystyrene), acrylate, alicyclic, and a whole host of other resist platforms used in advanced lithography are amenable to UV curing.
--[p139]-- A technique involving the combination of UV radiation curing with hotplate (ramped) baking of the patterned resist, which allows for a more efficient process, has been reported.<sup>275</sup> In this technique a fast cure is obtained by encapsulating the bulk of the resist (which is being cured by the hot plate) with the UV-cured surface film. The bulk resist temperature is ramped from a lower temperature and is kept below the $T _ { \mathrm { g } }$ of the surface-cured film.
--[p139]-- It should be pointed out that although the harder cured surface layer may hold together patterned features, it may also encapsulate some of the volatiles and solvents, which, when subjected later to temperatures higher than the postbake temperature (for example, plasma etching or ion implantation), can cause trapped solvent evolution that can wrinkle or crack the brittle surface layer of the resist in a process called reticulation.
--[p138]-- Elevating the temperature of the DUV cure process leads to oxidation of the bulk of the resist feature and results in resist features that can withstand thermal processes up to $2 1 0 \mathrm { ~  ~ { ~ \circ ~ } ~ } _ { C }$ without significant resist flow.

--[p187]-- 3.5 Overall Developer–Resist Interaction Potential and the Dissolution Process
The main contributors to the overall developer–resist interactions that lead to resist dissolution are electrostatic, van der Waals, hydrophobic, and hydration interactions.
--[p188]-- In addition, these charges on the polymer also have the effect of expanding the polymer coil through electrostatic repulsion, which, in turn, provides an elastic force that aids the dissolution process. Once the polymer is dissolved in the developer solution, additional interactions including hydrogen bonding and acid–base interactions start to play significant roles, especially in terms of transporting ions and maintaining the stability of the dissolved ions within the developer solution.
--[p189]-- However, when the developer solvent is nonpolar, the resist described above can be processed as a negative resist, as the solvent can remove the unexposed part of the film. This is possible here because the nonpolar solvent molecules can break up the polymer–polymer van der Waals interactions and form van der Waals bonds between themselves and the molecules of the nonpolar polymer, leading to the dissolution of the nonpolar polymer in the nonpolar developer solvent.

--[p70]-- The entire operation that ensures proper overlay<sup>56</sup> between layers of the IC device is called alignment and is carried out with specialized equipment that is part of the exposure tool.<sup>57</sup> Specifically, alignment can be defined as the process of determining the position, orientation, and distortion of select patterns already on the wafer and then placing them in correct relation to the image projected from the reticle.
--[p70]-- As ICs are fabricated in a series of process steps, including lithography, etch, ion implantation, film deposition, planarization, etc., the alignment step ensures that each new pattern is placed at the proper location on top of the preceding layers.
--[p70]-- Alignment should be fast, repeatable, accurate, and precise. The outcome of the alignment process, or how accurately each successive pattern is matched to the previous layer, is known as overlay<sup>58</sup> and is a very critical factor in determining if the final device will function properly or not. Specifically, overlay is “a vector quantity defined at every point on the wafer.

--[p70]-- 2.5 Alignment
Once the resist-coated wafer has been soft baked in the track system, it is cooled and sent into the wafer stage of the exposure tool. Resist processing equipment is commonly interfaced directly with an exposure tool, in which case the wafer transfer is automatic. Once inside the exposure tool, the wafer is aligned to patterns on the reticle so as to ensure that the pattern can be transferred to the proper location on the resist-coated wafer surface.

===== [p28-28] MOLECULAR THEORY OF LITHOGRAPHY > 1.3.1.1.3 Dry ArF (193 nm) lithography (1块) =====
--[p28]-- 1.3.1.1.3 Dry ArF (193 nm) lithography
At the heart of dry ArF lithography lies an exposure tool equipped with an ArF exciplex laser source (emitting 193-nm-wavelength photons) and used to pattern chemical amplification resists based on acrylate, cycloolefin, and cycloolefin/maleic anhydride (COMA) polymer platforms. This exposure tool is used for device generations spanning the 90-nm and 65-nm technology nodes.

===== [p273-275] Theory of Photochemical and Radiochemical Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 4.3.1.2.2.2 Condensation/intermolecular dehydration with acid-sensitive electrophile (crosslinking agent) imaging mechanism (13块) =====
--[p275]-- Schepsis, “Negative-tone resist system using vinyl cyclic acetal crosslinker,” Proc. SPIE 2724, 315–322 (1996).

--[p273]-- 4.3.1.2.2.2 Condensation/intermolecular dehydration with acid-sensitive electrophile (crosslinking agent) imaging mechanism
--[p273]-- The N-carbonium ion undergoes electrophilic substitution onto the electron-rich benzene ring of the novolac resin, regenerating a proton (Scheme 4.10). Crosslinking results because the melamine compound is multifunctional and can link up three different novolac polymer chains at each melamine molecule.
--[p273]-- Acid-catalyzed condensation reaction mechanisms have been exploited in the design of aqueous-base-developable negative-resist systems.<sup>148</sup> The condensation resists typically are composed of three components including a base soluble binder resin bearing reaction sites for crosslinking (typically phenolic resins), a radiation-sensitive acid generator, and an acid-sensitive latent electrophile that serves as the crosslinking agent.<sup>149</sup> The very first acid-catalyzed condensation resist system comprised a novolac/DNQ photoresist and an Nmethoxymethylated melamine crosslinker. When exposed to near-UV photons, DNQ photolyzes to produce indene carboxylic acid, which reacts with the melamine crosslinker to generate an N-carbonium ion, along with methanol.
--[p275]-- Both the C-alkylation and O-alkylation lead to crosslinking and the destruction of the base-solubilizing phenolic OH groups in the exposed areas of the resist. This results in negativetone imaging. These condensation negative resists have found widespread application in DUV 248-nm, electron beam, and x-ray lithographies, where they have provided excellent lithographic performance.<sup>158</sup>
152. J. W. Thackeray, G. W. Orsula, J. F. Bohland, and A. W.
--[p275]-- McCullough, “Approaches to deep ultraviolet photolithography utilizing acide hardened resin photoresist systems,” J. Vac. Sci. Technol. B 7, 1620–1623 (1989); A. K. Berry, K. A. ===== [p292-295] Theory of Photochemical and Radiochemical Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 4.3.2.2.3 Condensation imaging mechanism (12块) =====
--[p293]-- The second set of variations on the condensation reaction concept involves the acid-catalyzed methylolation of phenols by aldehydes, with the aldehyde functioning as a latent electrophile (Scheme 4.22). Because the methylolated phenolic resin dissolves much more slowly in aqueous base than its precursor resin, this concept is utilized in negative-tone imaging.<sup>214</sup> In addition, methylolated phenol can undergo further crosslinking, which further lowers the dissolution rate.<sup>215</sup>
--[p292]-- Calixerenes and dendrimers have also been used as matrix resins for negative-tone imaging through condensation.<sup>212</sup> Variations on the condensation reaction concept that do not involve crosslinking have also been employed in the design of negative resists.
--[p294]-- All of these condensation reactions are contributory to crosslinking and therefore to negative-tone aqueous base development.<sup>218</sup>
Self-condensation of silanol compounds in phenolic matrix resins has also been adapted for use in water-developable negative-tone resist applications (Scheme 4.25).<sup>219</sup>
These resists function on the basis of polarity change instead of crosslinking.
--[p293]-- The third set of variations on the aqueous-base-developable condensation resist design concept involves self-condensation systems, typified by polymeric furan derivatives. A typical example is based on the copolymer poly[4- hydroxystyrene-co-4-(3-furyl-3-hydroxypropyl)styrene] (Scheme 4.23), which is prepared by radical copolymerization of the acetyl-protected furan monomer with BOCST, followed by base hydrolysis.
--[p292]-- The first set of these variations on the condensation reaction concept include the attachment of bulky substituent to the phenolic group through C- or O-alkylation, which significantly decreases the dissolution rate of the phenolic resin in aqueous base (Scheme 4.21).
--[p293]-- In the presence of a photogenerated acid, the furan methanol residue, which is highly reactive toward electrophiles, attacks the ring carbons. This step, facilitated by a mesomeric electron release from oxygen, results in a stable carbocation, which undergoes electrophilic substitution reactions onto the furfuryl ring, effectively crosslinking the chains and reducing the solubility of the exposed areas of the resin in aqueous base developer relative to the precursor (unexposed) resin.
--[p294]-- Another example of a self-condensation negative-resist system comprises poly(4-(1-hydroxyethyl)styrene with a secondary alcohol pendant group, which crosslinks through acid-catalyzed interchain dehydration, forming ether linkages. Development with alcohol produces negative-tone images.
--[p292]-- Specific examples include N-hydroxy- and acetoxymethylimides, which, although are monofunctional latent electrophiles, do undergo acid-catalyzed condensation reaction with phenolic resins, reducing their dissolution rate in the exposed areas and providing negative imaging upon aqueous base development.<sup>213</sup>
--[p294]-- The aqueous-basedevelopable version of this resist is produced by copolymerizing styrenic secondary alcohol monomer with 4-acetoxystyrene, followed by base hydrolysis (Scheme 4.24).<sup>217</sup> Upon exposure, the photogenerated acid catalyzes intermolecular dehydration of the resin, resulting in self-condensation to di(a-methylbenzene)ether, O-alkylation to a-methylbenzyl phenyl ether, and C-alkylation to o-(a-methylbenzyl)phenol.
--[p295]-- When formulated with phenolic resins, base-soluble silanol compounds such as phenylsilanediol function as dissolution promoters of the former; however, upon exposure and PEB, these silanol compounds are converted to polysiloxanes through acid-catalyzed condensation, which, during aqueous base development, form a hydrophobic barrier surrounding the phenolic OH groups and lead to negative-tone imaging of the phenolic resins.<sup>220</sup> Silesquioxanes have also been employed in a similar manner in negative-resist applications.<sup>221</sup>
--[p293]-- This results in a negative-tone image. In this way, the pendant furfuryl groups serve as both the latent electrophile and the nucleophile.<sup>216</sup>

===== [p470-471] Chapter 6 Theory of Imprint Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 6.3.3 Comparison of PIL and TIL (5块) =====
--[p471]-- To be able to use imprinted polymer for pattern transfer to underlying layers, the polymer left in the indented areas, the so-called residual layer (Fig. 6.3), must be removed. This is typically accomplished with ${ \bf O } _ { 2 }$ plasma etch, as long as the resist does not contain silicon since ${ \bf O } _ { 2 }$ is not an effective etchant for silicon. This residual layer originates due to the fact that the flow of the polymer is not without resistance.<sup>34</sup>
--[p470]-- 6.3.3 Comparison of PIL and TIL
PIL offers some inherent advantages over TIL. The first advantage relates to the fact that PIL is a room-temperature process, without the time-consuming heating and cooling cycles of TIL. The second advantage of PIL over TIL is related to the first advantage, in the sense that the room-temperature processing of PIL prevents the registration problem arising from the different coefficients of thermal expansion of the substrate and the template, which plagues TIL.
--[p470]-- Viheriälä, T. Niemi, J. Kontio, and M. Pessa, “Nanoimprint Lithography: Next Generation Nanopatterning Methods for Nanophotonics Fabrication,” in Recent Optical and Photonic Technologies, K. Y. Kim, Ed., InTech, Rijeka, Croatia (2010). 32. ibid.
PIL is not without drawbacks. The imprinted resist film suffers from significant shrinkage (both vertical and lateral) that can distort the sharpness of the printed feature. Shrinking is not a major issue in TIL.
--[p470]-- The third advantage relates to the fact that fluids having low viscosity (2–50 mPa-s) can be used with PIL, thus making it possible to use low imprint pressures and shorter imprint cycles, and, consequently, ensuring faster throughput than TIL systems.<sup>33</sup> The throughput of TIL is rather low because the imprint resist polymer and the master/stamp are heated by conduction, and heating is an integral part of the process that is not easily decoupled from other process parameters.
31. J.
--[p471]-- Both PIL and TIL suffer from some peculiar issues. The first issue relates to the difficulty of filling the structures in the mold in a uniform and conformal manner. The second issue relates to the difficulty of reproducing the features with a high degree of fidelity. The third issue relates to releasing the master after imprinting without damaging the imprinted features. Sometimes, the master remains stuck on the printed features.

--[p119]-- 2.6.6.2 Stochastic treatment of photon absorption and exposure
The object here is to determine the probability that a molecule of lightsensitive material in the resist (PAG or sensitizer) will react to form an acid (in other words, become exposed), subject to the molecule absorbing a photon.
--[p120]-- In the case where the reaction volume is extremely large, and the exposure dose is reasonably large, the number of photogenerated acid molecules is large, and the statistical uncertainty in the acid concentration is thus small. On the other hand, for small reaction volumes or extremely low doses, a small number of photogenerated acid molecules results in a large uncertainty in the actual number within the reaction volume. The second term on the right hand side of Eq.
(2.167) is the contribution from photon shot noise.<sup>194</sup>

===== [p63-64] Chapter 2 Theory of the Lithographic Process > 2.3.3.1 Spin coating and instabilities in UTR films (8块) =====
--[p63]-- 2.3.3.1 Spin coating and instabilities in UTR films
Consider the spin-coating process, in which centrifugal forces cause the spreading of fluids against viscous resistance. There are at least three definable stages in the process of flow and coating of substrates: movement of the liquid contact line across the substrate, thinning of the film in the liquid state, and curing of the final film.
--[p64]-- Conjoining forces overwhelm the tendency for surface tension to level the film, thus driving the growth of surface modulation until they reach the substrate to nucleate a hole.
--[p63]-- Van der Waals forces dominate in determining the film stability<sup>29</sup> of ultrathin films spin-coated on nonwetting substrates (nonwetting in the sense that a drop of the solution makes a finite contact angle upon being placed on the substrate<sup>30</sup>). Such films can become unstable, and dewetting can occur.
--[p63]-- Complete dewetting occurs when all holes have coalesced, forming polygons composed of isolated droplets of materials.

--[p63]-- Experimental and theoretical studies suggest that dewetting begins with a nucleation event leading to the formation of a dry patch.<sup>31</sup> The hole grows by transport of material away from the nucleation site to a retreating rim surrounding the hole. --[p283]-- 4.3.1.4 Quantifying crosslinking during resist exposure
It is well known that when a polymer resist undergoes radiation crosslinking, initially the weight-average molecular weight and the intrinsic viscosity increase proportionately with radiation dose, until they reach extremely large values.
--[p283]-- In the preceding sections we have presented the chemical mechanisms by which this takes place; here, we concentrate on the physical consequences of the chemical process, following the approach of Reiser.<sup>179</sup>
Many theories that attempt to explain the experimental behavior of crosslinked polymers have been proposed, and some of them are briefly reviewed here.
--[p284]-- As a result, the largest molecule in the ensemble rapidly crosslinks with other nearby molecules, forming a many-branched supermolecule that permeates the whole irradiated area. This produces a continuous three-dimensional network that the solvent may penetrate, but which it can no longer dissolve. This insoluble residue or gel in a solid matrix constitutes the image in negative-tone resist imaging.

===== [p428-428] Chapter 5 Theory of Block Copolymer Self-assembly Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 5.2.3.1.1 Initiation (2块) =====
--[p428]-- 5.2.3.1.1 Initiation
Initiation involves two sequential steps: (1) the generation of a proton either via ionization (for strong protonic acids in nonaqueuos media) or via the interaction of the Lewis acids with the cocatalyst to form a proton donor; and (2) the addition of the proton to the monomer.
--[p428]-- The addition of the catalyst ion pair across the double bond is such that the proton adds to the carbon that bears the greatest electron density, thereby forming the most stable carbonium ion, as illustrated in Scheme 5.19.

--[p38]-- 1.3.5 Imprint lithography
Imprint lithography, invented by Chou and co-workers,<sup>38</sup> is a 1 printing technique based on the principle of mechanical deformation of a thin thermoplastic polymeric film (in the case of thermal imprint lithography) or photocurable resist liquid film, comprising monomers, oligomers, additives, initiators (in the case of photoimprint lithography).
--[p38]-- Melngailis, “Applications of ion microbeams lithography and direct processing,” in Handbook of VLSI Microlithography: Principles, Technology and Applications, J. N. Helbert, Ed., William Andrew Inc. Norwich, New York, pp. 790–855 (2001).
38. S. Y. Chou, P. R. Krauss, and P. J. Renstrom, “Imprint of sub 25 nm vias and trenches in polymers,” Appl. Phys. Lett. 67, 3114–3116 (1995).
39. ibid.
--[p38]-- It involves directly pressing the resist with a template/mold/stamp containing a negative of the pattern of the features to be printed, such that the resist flows and fills the open areas of the mold, replicating the desired pattern. As its imaging mechanism is not mediated by photons or charged beam particles such as electrons or ions, which suffer from diffraction or beam scattering, it can achieve resolutions beyond the limitations set by diffraction.
--[p38]-- One significant advantage of imprint lithography over standard photolithography is its ability to pattern three-dimensional topographies in a single step, thus reducing the cost of fabricating such a device. Such topographies are critical for connecting different layers on an integrated circuit. 39
--[p38]-- Its resolution depends mainly on the minimum template feature size that can often be fabricated with EBL. Among its many attractive attributes are high resolution, low cost of ownership, and its ability to pattern large-area structures in both planar and roll-to-roll formats, to mention but a few.

===== [p52-52] Chapter 2 Theory of the Lithographic Process > 2.1 Introduction (4块) =====
--[p52]-- Following baking, if necessary, the resist film is at this point developed in an appropriate developer, with the standard being 0.26 N (2.38 wt%) tetramethyl ammonium hydroxide aqueous solution. The molecular interactions between the molecules of the exposed, unexposed, and baked resist film with the developer medium (discussed in Chapter 3) are responsible for the contrast between the exposed and unexposed areas of the film.
--[p52]-- Absent these interactions, it would not be possible to discriminate between the exposed and unexposed part of the resist, which, in turn, would make it impossible to transfer the mask patterns of the integrated circuit to the semiconductor wafer substrate.
The steps in the semiconductor lithographic process are outlined in Fig. 2.1 (and illustrated in Fig. 1.1 of Chapter 1) for a negative and a positive resist.
--[p52]-- The chemical and physical principles underlying each step are discussed at length in the following sections. Where appropriate, lithographic models involving most of these steps are also provided, with a view to providing a framework for predicting lithographic outcomes given a defined set of input resist materials and process variables, as well as exposure conditions.
--[p52]-- 2.1 Introduction
The object of semiconductor lithography is to transfer patterns of integrated circuits drawn on the mask or reticle to the semiconductor wafer substrate. The transfer is carried out by projecting the image of the reticle with the aid of appropriate optical elements of an exposure tool onto a radiation-sensitive resist material coated on the semiconductor wafer, typically made of silicon, then stepping or scanning the imaging field across the entire wafer to complete a layer.

--[p121]-- Next came poly(4-tert-butylcarbonyloxy styrene) resists, which were used until the 130-nm technology node. In recent times, poly(acrylate) and poly(cycloolefin) resists have been the workhorses and have been used from 90-nm technology down to the leading-edge 14-nm technology node.

--[p121]-- From the very first resist ever used in photolithography—bitumen of Judea—to those currently used, resists have always been developed in either an organic solvent or an aqueous base solvent. Bitumen of Judea is a photocrosslinkable polymer, which the inventor of photolithography, Nicéphore Niépce in 1826 photocrosslinked with sunlight, with the aid of a pinhole camera, affording a negative-tone image, albeit a coarse one, of his courtyard.
--[p122]-- Both classes of developers are typically formulated with additives such as surfactants to improve wetting.<sup>202</sup> The buffered systems can be used at a lower pH for the same normality and thus offer better discrimination, dark erosion, and contrast.<sup>203</sup> Although alkali bases such as NaOH and KOH were used as developers in earlier times for device fabrication, today they are no longer in use for this application because alkali metals such as sodium and potassium have been implicated in gate oxide degradation.<sup>204</sup>

201. For a general discussion on the constitution of developers, see for example, U.
--[p121]-- He developed the image in a nonpolar organic solvent of lavender oil. While organic solvents have been used primarily to develop negative-tone resists, aqueous base developers have been used to develop positive resists.
--[p123]-- For instance, supercritical $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ has no dipole moment, but it does have a quadrupole moment, which makes it appropriate for use as a developer for fluorinated and silicone-containing resists, as well as for resists containing ester and carbonate functional groups. With their low surface energies, silicone fluids offer opportunities for mitigating pattern collapse, especially in very small geometries.
--[p123]-- Environmentally friendly developers based on nonpolar solvents such as supercritical $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 } ,$ hydrofluoroethers, and silicone fluids have been demonstrated to develop resists primarily in the negative tone.<sup>209</sup> With very unusual properties, they offer unique advantages beyond being environmentally friendly.

--[p121]-- The primary goal of resist development is to render a highly nonlinear response to the latent image generated during the PEB step, which in effect is the transferred aerial image of the mask in the resist. In its essence, the development step completes the imaging process, which effectively results in the transformation of the two-dimensional image of the mask into a threedimensional relief image of the mask on the resist film.
--[p122]-- The standard liquid chemical developers<sup>201</sup> that have been in use in the IC industry are basic, aqueous solutions. The main two classes are the buffered metal-ion containing (e.g., sodium metasilicate) developers and the metal-ionfree (MIF) developers [e.g., aqueous solutions of tetramethylammonium hydroxide (TMAH)].
--[p123]-- TMAH developers show slower development speed than those of NaOH and KOH solutions at the same normality.<sup>206</sup> Remarkably, when TMAH and metal-ion-containing developers are mixed, even at parts-per-million level, a substantial decrease of the dissolution rate well below that of TMAH solution is observed.<sup>207</sup> One other remarkable effect is that metal-ion-containing NaOH and MIF TMAH developers also differ substantially in the influence of temperature on the resist dissolution rate. While the development rate decreases with developer temperature for TMAH developers, the trend is the opposite for metal-ion-containing developers such as NaOH and KOH.<sup>208</sup>
--[p121]-- 2.7 Development
Following the PEB for both conventional and chemical amplification resists, the resist film is developed in a liquid chemical developer to dissolve the soluble regions of the resist film. For negative resists, the soluble region of resist film is the unexposed part, while, for the positive resists, it is the exposed part.

===== [p230-230] Theory of Photochemical and Radiochemical Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 4.2.2.1 Excimers (6块) =====
--[p230]-- A good example of application of excimers is in lithographic exposure sources such as F<sub>2</sub>-excimer lasers.
14. A. Reiser, Photoreactive Polymers: The Science and Technology of Resists, John Wiley & Sons, New York, pp. 67–68 (1989).
--[p230]-- Its origin is in the change of orbital symmetry that accompanies excitation and leads to cooperative (positive) orbital overlap and hence to bonding between the two systems.<sup>14</sup> Examples in resist systems can be found in aromatic and hetero-aromatic molecules used in photoactive compounds (PACs).
Figure 4.7 is a potential energy diagram of an excimer-forming pair of molecules.
--[p230]-- Worthy of note is the red shift and the loss of vibrational structure in this figure, which can be understood from the shape of the potential energy surfaces of the two molecules as they approach each other. In the ground state, as the two molecules come within the distance of their van der Waals radii, they repel each other, indicated in the graph by the rise in the potential energy.
--[p230]-- However, in the excited state, the attractive force of the positive orbital overlap creates a potential energy well that defines the excimer. The depth of this well is the excimer-binding energy B, which equals the amount of energy by which the excimer is stabilized relative to the energy of the excited state of an isolated (monomeric) molecule. Through fluorescence emission, the paired molecule is returned to the shoulder of the repulsive branch of the potential energy curve.
--[p230]-- 4.2.2.1 Excimers
Excimers<sup>13</sup> (excited dimers) are formed by pairs of molecules or atoms that do not significantly interact in the ground state, but are weakly bonded in the excited state. The bonding in the excimer takes place between an excited molecule and a ground-state molecule of the same species.
--[p230]-- The change in energy corresponding to the fluorescence transition from the excimer $\Delta E _ { \mathrm { F D } }$ (excitation energy of the excimer) is smaller than the change in energy in the fluorescence of the monomer $\Delta E _ { \mathrm { F M } }$ (excitation energy of the monomer), hence the red shift in the emission. Furthermore, this energy change covers a continuous range of values and does not contain any vibrational fine structure of the molecular skeleton.<sup>15</sup>
13.
