===== [p289-290] Theory of Photochemical and Radiochemical Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 4.3.2.2.1 Pinacol rearrangement imaging mechanism (5块) =====
--[p290]-- Aqueous-base-developable two- and three-component negative resists based on the principle of pinacol rearrangement have also been reported.<sup>206</sup> The pinacol rearrangement principle has also been extended to aqueous-basedevelopable negative-tone resists designed for 193-nm lithography.
--[p290]-- The system comprises a copolymer of 5-(2-trifluoromethyl-1,1,1-trifluoro-2-hydroxpropyl)-2- norbornene (NBHFA) and norbornene bearing a pendant vic-diol (Scheme 4.19).<sup>207</sup> Exposing a resist film comprising this resin and PAG to 193-nm photons results in the generation of photoacid, which, in turn, can convert the diol groups in the exposed part of the film to ketones, forming hydrogen bonding with the surrounding NBHFA hydroxyl groups, thus inhibiting the dissolution of the copolymer in an aqueous base, and resulting in negative-tone images.<sup>208</sup>
--[p289]-- 4.3.2.2.1 Pinacol rearrangement imaging mechanism
A pinacol–pinacolone rearrangement reaction involving a polarity switch of a polar to a nonpolar functional group in a resist polymer has been exploited in chemically amplified lithographic imaging.<sup>203</sup> The pinacol rearrangement involves conversion of vic-diols to ketones or aldehydes with the aid of an acid catalyst (see Scheme 4.18).
--[p289]-- A dry film of this polymer is readily converted to a nonconjugated ketone by reaction with a photochemically generated acid.<sup>204</sup> Developing the exposed film in an alcoholic solvent such as isopropanol dissolves the unexposed polar diol polymer, without dissolving the less polar ketone polymer in the exposed regions, creating a negative-tone image. The diol polymer is thermally stable to 225 °C in the absence of acid.<sup>205</sup>
--[p289]-- A good example of a negative imaging polymeric resist based on this principle comprises poly[3-methyl-2-(4-vinylphenyl)-2,3-butanediol], which is prepared by radical polymerization of the styrenic diol monomer.

===== [p185-185] Chapter 3 Theory of Molecular Interactions in Lithography > 3.4.6 Hydration interactions (5块) =====
--[p185]-- 3.4.6 Hydration interactions
Hydration interactions are interactions associated with the molecular ordering of the developer water molecules around a hydrophilic resist polymeric acid film surface or dissolved resist polymeric acid molecules or other ionic species, resulting in a zone extending a few molecular diameters, wherein the properties of the developer water (e.g., density, positional and orientational order, and mobility) are significantly different from the corresponding bulk values.
--[p185]-- This interaction has some important consequences. First, it affects the local dielectric constant of the developer since the water molecules within the hydration zone can no longer respond to an electric field as they would in the bulk. The restricted mobility of the developer water molecules around the polymeric acid surface or small ions might indicate that the effective dielectric constant should be lower in this hydration zone than in the developer solution bulk.
--[p185]-- Second, when the hydration zones of two solvated molecules or surfaces overlap, a short-range force is established between them.
The short-range hydration interaction is a repulsive force that decays exponentially with distance as follows:<sup>65</sup>
$$
w ( r ) = + w _ { 0 } e ^ { - r / D _ { \mathrm { h y d r a t } } } ,\tag{3.109}
$$
--[p185]-- where r is the distance separating the two surfaces, $D _ { \mathrm { h y d r a t } }$ is the hydration decay length (2–10 Å; for 1:1 electrolytes), and $w _ { 0 }$ is the initial hydration energy of the surface $( 1 - 5 \times 1 0 ^ { - 2 0 }$ J on a per-molecule basis).<sup>66</sup>

--[p243]-- In essence, photochemistry deals with the chemistry of electronically excited molecules, and it ceases at around 90–100 nm; the region below this belongs to the province of radiation chemistry, i.e., the chemistry induced by the absorption of a, b, g, or x rays.<sup>60</sup>

Although radiation chemistry and photochemistry are clearly distinct, the boundary between them can be rather confusing at times. In resist photochemistry, radiation quanta applied to the resist as part of the exposure process are absorbed by specific chromophores in the resist molecules and compounds, which as a result get promoted into well-defined excited states.
--[p244]-- If the energy of the delivered quanta exceeds some of the bond energies in the resist molecules and compounds, as in DUV and VUV lithographies, photochemistry leads to fragmentation and occasionally to ionization. The main characteristic feature of radiation chemistry of resists is that energy absorption is not associated with a particular chromophore, but occurs at random in the resist material. Often, radiation chemistry does not involve the species that absorbs the photon.
--[p243]-- In lithographic technologies utilizing charged particles such as electrons, ion beams, and high-energy ionizing radiations like x rays, including EUV photons (otherwise called soft x rays), resist imaging exploits the chemical effects of these charged particles and radiations.

--[p243]-- A major characteristic of these charged particles and ionizing radiations is that the energy of the individual quantum is much higher than the energy of the chemical bonds in the resist material and larger than the ionizing potentials of its constituent atoms. As a result, the primary result of the interaction between the highenergy radiation and charged particles with the material is ionization. A whole sequence of steps typically follows, ultimately leading to a variety of products.
--[p243]-- 4.2.6 Radiation chemistry versus photochemistry of resists
Table 4.4 summarizes the lithographic exposure wavelengths and energies used in exposing resist materials. Generally speaking, conventional photochemistry deals with valence or outer-shell electronic excitation associated with radiation lying in the approximate wavelength range of 190–700 nm. Below about 150 nm, higher energy processes including photoionization become progressively more dominant.
--[p244]-- In concrete terms, radiation chemistry can be defined as being concerned with quantal energies in excess of the ionization energy of common atoms and molecules—greater than 30 eV (700 kcal/mol),<sup>62</sup> corresponding to a wavelength of roughly 41 nm.

===== [p232-233] Theory of Photochemical and Radiochemical Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 4.2.3 Energy transfer (3块) =====
--[p233]-- The two distinct coupling mechanisms that have been recognized to mediate the transfer process include coulombic or dipolar interaction (proposed by Förster<sup>22</sup>) and electron exchange or orbital interaction (proposed by Dexter<sup>23</sup>).
--[p232]-- 4.2.3 Energy transfer
Exposure-induced energy transfer in a resist matrix occurs not only between different states of one radiation-sensitive resist molecule or component, it can also occur between such molecules or components when they are in close proximity to each other. It is customary to designate the molecule that carries the excitation energy as the donor D and the molecule that accepts the energy as the acceptor A; the governing reaction is represented by
$$
--[p232]-- D ^ { * } + A  D + A ^ { * } .\tag{[4.1]}
$$
18. ibid.
Energy transfer between molecules in resists is an electronic process that is essentially adiabatic. Such a transfer will occur with reasonable probability only if the excitation energy of $D ^ { * }$ equals or is greater than that of $A ^ { * } \colon ^ { 2 0 } E _ { \mathrm { D } ^ { * } } \geq E _ { \mathrm { A } ^ { * } }$
At the point of transfer, donor and acceptor molecules are coupled and do form a single quantum mechanical entity.

--[p433]-- 5.3 Physics of Micro- and Nanophase Separation in Block Copolymer Systems
The self-assembly of BCPs into spatially periodic patterns commonly referred to as microphases or nanophases, depending on length scale, is governed by a delicate balance between the interaction energy and the chain stretching between the blocks that make up the copolymer.
--[p436]-- For typical dissimilar monomer pairs with no strong specific interactions such as hydrogen bonding, charges, etc., $\chi _ { \mathrm { A B } }$ is positive and small compared with unity. For instance, $\chi _ { \mathrm { S I } }$ between styrene and isoprene is of the order of 0.1. Furthermore, $\chi _ { \mathrm { A B } }$ usually varies inversely with temperature, so that mixing is promoted as the temperature increases.
--[p437]-- A major difficulty in theoretical treatment of phase separation in BCPs is to accurately sum up the competing free-energy contributions of interaction energy and elastic energy within the unit cell of a periodic micro- or nanophase structure. By minimizing the free energy for a particular geometry (relative to all other candidate geometries), one can determine the most likely configuration and scale lengths for a copolymer of a given composition and molecular weight.
--[p436]-- Equation (5.23) forms the basis of all theories of micro- and nanophase separation in BCP systems and, thus, underlies the mechanism of BCP selfassembly lithography.
Without the covalent bond connecting the two blocks of the BCP, the thermodynamic forces described above would lead to a macrophase separation—a state of coexistence of bulk phases, similar to that seen when oil and vinegar separate into macroscopically sized droplets in a salad dressing.
--[p434]-- A noteworthy illustrative, albeit extreme, example of this fact relates to mixtures of isotopes of the same polymer such as, for example, polystyrene and deuterated polystyrene, which have been demonstrated to be immiscible at sufficiently high molecular weight.
--[p435]-- Polymer surface tension prevents the formation of a discrete terrace step. Instead, a graded interface in which the film thickness changes over the span of several microdomains is formed. At these transitions, where the local film thickness differs from integer multiples of the lattice constant, differences in size, or even morphology of the microdomain compared to the bulk may occur.

199. S. F. Hahn, “An improved method for the diimide hydrogenation of butadiene and isoprene containing polymers,” J. Polym. Sci. Part A: Polym. Chem. 30, 397–408 (1992).
BCP systems self-assemble into many complex structures.
--[p437]-- Because there are fewer configurations available to extended polymer chains than to those in their native randomly coiled state, an entropic restoring force is generated that serves to limit the phase separation between A and B blocks to mesoscopic dimensions.
--[p437]-- The form of this entropic force law is approximately Hookian, and the law forms the basis for understanding the elasticity of rubberlike materials.<sup>213</sup> For a chain or block of N monomers extended to a distance R, the elastic free energy that leads to the entropic force is given by
$$
F _ { \mathrm { e } } = { \frac { 3 k _ { \mathrm { B } } T R ^ { 2 } } { 2 N a ^ { 2 } } } ,\tag{5.24}
$$
where a is a monomer size scale that depends on the local structure of the polymer chain.
--[p435]-- As an example, terraces of height $L _ { 0 }$ will form on top of a foundation film of height $n L _ { 0 }$ (with n being an integer). Also referred to as “islands” and “holes,” these are primarily found in spherical and parallel lamellar morphologies.<sup>209,210,211</sup> A high energy cost is associated with the formation of islands and holes due to the resulting increase in contact area between the polymer film and air.
--[p435]-- This morphology develops due to the surface and substrate boundary conditions that demand that the most energetically compatible block be expressed at each of the surfaces. In addition, these surface-parallel lamellae optimize the interfacial energetics of the system by minimizing the size of the A–B interface while maintaining $L _ { 0 }$ periodicity.

A positive $\chi _ { \mathrm { A B } }$ value is indicative of net repulsion between A and B monomers, while a negative value is indicative of an attractive interaction, a sort of free-energy drive toward mixing.

===== [p249-250] Theory of Photochemical and Radiochemical Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 4.2.9 Sensitivity and exposure radiation (13块) =====
--[p249]-- Bowden, Eds., American Chemical Society, Washington, D.C., pp. 212–213 (1994).
It is well established that the primary high-energy beam interacts with the resist material in a manner that is dependent only on the capture cross section of the atoms in the resist, and not on its molecular structure, to produce a cascade of lower-energy secondary and Auger electrons with short range travel in the resist, inducing molecular-structure-dependent reactions.
--[p250]-- In specific terms, for lithographies based on these high-energy charged particles or EUV photons, the primary charged particle or photons do not expose resists. Instead, they generate secondary electrons on account of their interaction with resist polymers and PAGs, which, in turn, expose the resist. For the specific case of EUV, the primary photons generate photoelectrons, which, in turn, generate secondary electrons.
Absent these secondary electrons, EUV lithography, x-ray lithography, electron beam and ion beam lithographies, etc., would be impossible!
--[p249]-- Simply, the resist sensitivity correlation between the different types of charged-particle beams, x rays, and EUV photons suggests that the chemical reactions responsible for the generation of differential solubility in these systems do not stem directly from interaction of the resists with the primary beam. In all the above-mentioned lithographic technologies, the energy of the primary beam greatly exceeds the bond strength and ionization potential of the components of the resist materials.
--[p250]-- Because the chemistry results from interaction of the secondary, low-energy electrons, the resist responds similarly to the source of these low-energy electrons, irrespective of the nature of the high-energy primary beam that engendered them. In other words, the secondary electrons produced by x-ray, electron beam, ion beam, or EUV photons are all alike, physically and chemically, and all look alike to the resist molecules.
--[p249]-- This is, in fact, the case; there is good correlation between electron sensitivities and x-ray sensitivities of most practical resists designed for these lithographies,<sup>74</sup> and between electron and ion sensitivities,<sup>75</sup> and between electron beam and EUV photon sensitivities. In other words, resists that are sensitive to electron beam radiation are also sensitive to x-ray radiation, ion beam radiation, and EUV photons.
--[p250]-- Thus, the chemical response to high-energy radiation is essentially the same regardless of the nature of the primary beam, and the extent of response and sensitivity depends only on the efficiency with which the primary beam interacts with the resist film to produce the secondary electrons. This efficiency, in turn, depends only on the capture cross section, which is related to the beam energy and the atomic composition of the resist.<sup>77</sup>
--[p249]-- So, here is one of the few instances in all of lithography where nature’s interest and ours are aligned.

--[p231]-- Under this scenario, the interaction between the two molecules is stronger than in conventional excimers, and the transient excited species formed as a result is termed an exciplex<sup>16</sup> (excited complex).
15. A. Reiser, Photoreactive Polymers: The Science and Technology of Resists, John-Wiley & Sons, New York, p. 68 (1989).
16. Examples of the application of exciplexes in lithography include KrF and ArF exciplex laser light sources for 248-nm and 193-nm lithographies, respectively.
Characteristically, exciplexes emit a structureless, red-shifted fluorescence, or phosphorescence, similar to that of an excimer.<sup>17</sup>
--[p232]-- It should be pointed out that exciplexes are often stages in the complete transfer of an electron from one molecule to another, leading to the formation of radical ion pairs and, finally, of separated radical ions.<sup>18</sup> An illustrative example is the photoreaction of benzophenone (a common resist sensitizer) with tertiary amines (a common resist quencher), as illustrated in Scheme 4.1.<sup>19</sup>
--[p231]-- 4.2.2.2 Exciplexes
The interaction upon excitation of two similar molecules that do not have identical structures, e.g., resist sensitizers such as anthracene and tetracene, can lead to the formation of hetero-excimers. If the two molecules differ significantly in their electron affinities such that one is an electron donor and the other an electron acceptor, the bonding process may be accompanied by a partial transfer of charge.

--[p446]-- 5.4.2 Chemical patterning or chemo-epitaxy
Here, top-down lithography is used to pattern substrates with chemicals, offering means of directing phase separation and assembly in thin BCP films. Through the use of such substrates, local domain orientation, film surface morphology, and long-range order can be affected and sometimes controlled. In particular, when the period of the substrate pattern approaches molecular dimensions, a surface-perpendicular orientation of the block domains is induced.

--[p304]-- A. Peroxides
A good example of peroxides is benzoyl peroxide (BPO) (XXII), which, on excitation, fragments into two benzoyl radicals (Scheme 4.29).<sup>249</sup> The excitation energy of this radical is roughly 100 kcal/mole, much higher than the energy of the —O—O— bond (30 kcal/mole).

===== [p75-75] Chapter 2 Theory of the Lithographic Process > 2.6.2 Aerial image formation (2块) =====
--[p75]-- 2.6.2 Aerial image formation
An aerial image is the intensity of the exposure radiation in the plane of the wafer. The extended source method or Hopkins’ method<sup>72</sup> is often used to predict the aerial image of a partially coherent, diffractionlimited, low-NA aberrated projection system based on scalar diffraction theory. For very high NA, vector calculations involving the complete solution of Maxwell’s equations are used. The illumination may be of a single wavelength or broadband.
--[p75]-- The illumination source may be a conventional disk shape or other more complicated shapes, as in off-axis illumination.<sup>73</sup>

===== [p36-38] MOLECULAR THEORY OF LITHOGRAPHY > 1.3.4 Ion beam lithography (9块) =====
--[p37]-- The large effective mass of an ion and its greater cross section of interaction with atoms of the resist when compared with that of an electron result in energy being deposited in a much smaller volume in ion beam lithography than in EBL.
--[p36]-- It is this flexibility and effectiveness of ions in modifying the properties of the resist (a direct consequence of the fact that they can deliver both mass and energy to the latter) that underlies the premise for which they are used in ion beam lithography.<sup>32</sup>
29. ibid.
30. ibid, pp. 112–113.
31. ibid., p. 110.
32. T. M. Hall, A. Wagner, and L. F. Thompson, “Ion beam exposure characteristics of resists,” J. Vac. Sci. Technol. B 6(6), 1889–1892 (1979).
--[p36]-- 1.3.4 Ion beam lithography
An energetic ion incident on a solid resist-coated substrate can interact with the latter in a variety of phenomena that include sputtering of neutral atoms, emission of electrons, lattice damage, heat generation, and ion implantation, as shown in Fig. 1.10. In addition, the beam can produce secondary electrons, which participate in the chemical transformations of the resist such as bond breaking, of the kind that that can expose the resist.
--[p38]-- Additionally, the energy spread of the ion beam (particularly metallic sources) is significantly greater than that of electrons such that chromatic aberrations play a dominant role in limiting performance in ion beam lithography compared to EBL.<sup>36</sup> And lastly, since energetic ions carry enough energy to displace crystal lattice atoms, they can also cause considerable damage to the substrate when subjected to very thin resists.<sup>37</sup>
--[p37]-- The ion beam lithographic exposure tool is similar to that of electron beam exposure systems, the major differences being in the source and deflection lenses. The key advantages of ion beam lithography are high resolution and the fact that they can be used with resists having poor sensitivities. These advantages derive from the negligible scattering of ions, which stands in stark contrast to what occurs in EBL, where scattering constitutes a primary factor limiting resolution.
--[p37]-- As a result, energy penetration is more limited and takes place over a well-defined range in ion beam lithography.<sup>33</sup> This implies that minimum energy is delivered to the substrate, in contrast to the high-energy electrons used in EBL, which penetrate relatively deep into the substrate and lose only a small fraction of their energy in exposing the resist.
--[p38]-- Ion beam lithography is not without its drawbacks, especially when compared to EBL. Shot noise is a major issue for ion beam lithography, just as in electron beam lithography.
--[p37]-- Thus, resolution in ion beam lithography is primarily limited by the range of the secondary electrons produced as the ion loses energy in the resist; in contrast, in EBL, resolution is primarily limited by scattering of the much more energetic primary electrons.<sup>34</sup>
34. ibid.
33. M. J. Bowden, “The Lithographic Process: The Physics,” in Introduction to Microlithography, L. F. Thompson, C. G. Willson, and M. J. Bowden, Eds., American Chemical Society, Washington, D.C., p. 132 (1994).
--[p38]-- Ion current densities are significantly lower than electron current densities, a limitation that is somewhat offset by the fact that each ion deposits more energy into the resist compared to an electron, which implies that lower doses are needed to produce the same exposure effect when using ions relative to when using electrons.<sup>35</sup>

===== [p402-402] Chapter 5 Theory of Block Copolymer Self-assembly Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 5.2.1.1.2 Propagation (1块) =====
--[p402]-- 5.2.1.1.2 Propagation
Chain growth or propagation proceeds via nucleophilic attack on the initiator by the carbanionic site on the monomer, leading to the formation of a covalent bond between the monomer and the metallic center of the initiator and reformation of the first anionic active center. Chain growth will continue until all of the monomer has been consumed, or until the reaction is terminated.

--[p76]-- 2.6.3 Standing wave models
The light inside the resist film consists of incident and reflected components. The light intensity within the resist varies in the vertical direction because of absorption and interference effects associated with standing waves. Standing waves are rapidly varying light distribution within the depth of the resist. They result from the interference between the incident and reflected light within the resist.

--[p23]-- The exposure process involves directing a beam of radiation (typically ultraviolet light from a mercury arc lamp, or deep-ultraviolet (DUV) light from exciplex and excimer lasers, or extreme ultraviolet photons, or electrons or even ions) to a mask, creating a transmitted or reflected image, which then is made to pass through a set of lenses or mirrors, as the case may be, which in turn focuses the image into the resist on the surface of a resist-coated semiconductor substrate such as a silicon wafer.<sup>5</sup>

--[p25]-- Equation (1.1) demonstrates that improvements in resolution can be achieved by decreasing wavelength and/or by increasing NA. Equation (1.2), which describes the DOF of a feature of size R, shows that smaller features have less DOF.
Photoresists and radiation-sensitive resists function by radiation-induced alteration of the solubility of the materials. There are two basic classes of resist materials: negative-tone and positive-tone resists (see Fig. 1.1).
--[p25]-- Negative resists become less soluble upon exposure to radiation; that is, the unexposed areas can be selectively removed by treatment with an appropriate developer solution; positive resists selectively undergo an increase in solubility upon exposure, enabling the exposed regions to be selectively removed in the developer. Both types of resists are formulated from polymers designed to have physical and chemical properties consistent with semiconductor processing.
--[p24]-- There is an inherent gain mechanism in such resists in which one photoacid catalyzes one chemical transformation event of the resist resin before it is regenerated, and then goes on to catalyze more similar chemical transformation events.
--[p25]-- Negative resists that undergo radiation-induced crosslinking often suffer from solvent-induced swelling, which imposes a limit on their resolution. Positive resists do not usually suffer from swelling and have thus dominated the fabrication of leading-edge devices.
--[p23]-- The semiconductor lithographic<sup>3</sup> process involves transferring a circuit pattern —as might, for example, be contained in a mask—into a radiation-sensitive film (resist) and subsequently replicating that pattern in an underlying thin conductor or dielectric film of the semiconductor substrate.<sup>4</sup> The process comprises two parts: the preparation of the mask (a one-time event that can be slow and expensive) and the transfer of the mask pattern to the semiconductor substrate (a multiply repeated event that should be fast and inexpensive).
--[p25]-- Details of these processes are described by Moreau<sup>8</sup> and Thompson et al.<sup>9</sup> In the following section, we briefly review the various semiconductor lithographic techniques that are either currently being used to manufacture IC devices or are under development for potential future lithographic applications, along with the imaging mechanisms on which they depend.

Following exposure, the exposed resist film may be baked again, causing the catalytic photoacid<sup>6</sup> generated from the photoactive compound or photoacid generator contained in the photoresist to act on the polymers. Next, the exposed resist film is developed in a solvent to produce a three-dimensional relief replica of the mask pattern.

--[p391]-- 5.2.1 Block copolymers via anionic polymerization
Anionic polymerization, an addition polymerization in which the growing chain ends bear a negative charge,<sup>52</sup> is a well-established method for the synthesis of self-assembling BCPs, including those used in lithography.

--[p397]-- This polymerization method is also tolerant of a fairly large selection of monomers. Due to these advantages, anionic polymerization is the typical method used in the synthesis of polymers for self-assembly, including those used in lithography.
--[p397]-- The fact that this polymerization method is able to form well-defined polymers derives directly from its absence of termination and chain transfer reactions under normal conditions,<sup>88,89</sup> so much so that the growing chain end can remain active for a considerable length of time without deactivation, in a “living” polymerization manner.<sup>90,91,92</sup> In the presence of the “living” chain end of the first block, the sequential introduction of a second-, third-, fourth- or even higher-order monomer types into the polymerization mixture can lead to the formation of corresponding BCPs. When two different monomers A and B are involved in the polymerization, the result is a linear AB diblock copolymer.

--[p397]-- When three different monomers A, B, and C are sequentially polymerized, the result is a triblock copolymer of ABC. When two different monomers A and B are sequentially polymerized and followed by a third monomer that is chemically similar to and has a molecular weight similar to that of the first monomer A, or a molecular weight that differs from the first monomer A, the results are linear triblock copolymers of the form ABA and ABA<sup>0</sup>, respectively.
--[p397]-- Monomers for anionic polymerization are typically a-olefins substituted with an electron-withdrawing group (see structures I through V).<sup>93,94</sup> Several substituted a-olefin monomers can be polymerized via anionic polymerization except those with functional groups bearing acidic protons (or other electrophiles) because electrophiles react with carbanions and thus either quench the initiator or terminate anionic propagation.
--[p391]-- Ziegler and Schlenk invented the technique in early 1910 when they used sodium metal as initiator to polymerize diene.<sup>53</sup> In 1956, Swarc used sodium naphthalenide as an initiator for the polymerization of styrene in tetrahydrofuran (THF) and observed that upon contact with styrene the green color of the radical anions immediately turns into red, indicating the formation of styryl anions, which led him to suggest that initiation occurs via electron transfer from the sodium naphthalenide to the styrene monomer. He also noticed that after the incorporation of all of the monomers, the red color of the reaction mixture persisted, indicating that the chain ends remained intact

--[p397]-- and active for further propagation, which led him to term the polymerization scheme as “living” polymerization.<sup>86,87</sup> Following the elucidation of its mechanism by Swarc in 1956, anionic polymerization has emerged as the most powerful technique for the synthesis of well-defined copolymers—i.e., polymers with narrow molecular weight distribution and well-controlled characteristics including molecular weight, composition, microstructure, and architecture—to mention but a few properties.

--[p148]-- Stated another way, if the attractive forces between the solvent and the solute molecules of A or B are similar to the solvent–solvent and solute–solute cohesive forces, then the cohesive energies of the solvent and the solute should be nearly the same, implying that the solute molecules will be readily dissolved in the developer solvent.
--[p148]-- If, on the other hand, the opposite is true, i.e., if the attractive forces between the solvent and the solute molecules are very dissimilar to the solvent–solvent and solute–solute cohesive forces, implying that the cohesive energies of the solvent and the solute molecules are significantly different from one other, and that an exchange of a solvent molecule by a corresponding molecule in the resist part in question occurs with significant change in the interaction forces that exist between the solvent or the molecules of the resist part, then the solute will not dissolve in the solvent. In a thermodynamic sense, we say that the dissolution of the resist part in question in the developer occurs with a negligibly small heat of mixing.
--[p148]-- As such, an exchange of a solvent molecule by a corresponding molecule in the resist part in question can then occur with little or no change in the interaction forces that exist between solvent or between the molecules of the resist part.
--[p149]-- Accordingly, $\mathfrak { F } ^ { 2 }$ for polymers is determined indirectly, using a method based on the idea that the degree of solubility of a polymer (or degree of swelling of a crosslinked polymer) is at a maximum when the cohesive energy densities of the solvent and the polymer are equal. The degree of solubility or swelling of a given polymer is measured in solvents with varying $\ S ^ { 2 }$ values, and a plot is made of the solubility of the polymer as a function of $\ S ^ { 2 }$ .

--[p152]-- 3.4 Molecular Interactions in Lithography
The lithographic patterning action is initiated by agents such as electromagnetic radiation, mechanical force, or chemicals, and involves baking protocols at temperatures sufficiently high (but below the glass transition temperature of the resist polymer) to effect the phase separation of block copolymers (as in directed self-assembly lithography) or diffusion of photoacid (as in radiationbased lithography).
--[p154]-- We consider as our system an acrylate chemical amplification polymeric resist film of t-butyl ester-protected poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) containing an appropriate PAG. The resist film was coated on a wafer and exposed through a mask to appropriate radiation, such that the part of the film under the open areas of the mask was transformed by the radiation, while the unexposed part of the film under the dark area of the mask was not transformed.
--[p154]-- Both parts of the film have been appropriately baked and are now immersed in a 0.26 N aqueous solution of TMAH, the standard developer used in advanced semiconductor lithography (see Fig. 3.3). We note that the aqueous solution of TMAH contains dissociated tetramethylammonium cations and hydroxyl anions.
--[p153]-- Below we will examine these interactions in separate treatments for the development and the PEB steps of conventional chemical amplification resist systems.
A qualitative description of resist dissolution during development and PEB therefore comprises contributions from repulsive electrostatic doublelayer forces and attractive van der Waals, hydrophobic, steric, hydrogen bonding, and acid–base interactions and forces.
--[p154]-- In this way, the exposed part of the resist is transformed from a lipophilic to a hydrophilic system, while the unexposed part remains firmly liphophilic, effectively establishing a contrast between the two parts of the resist film.
--[p152]-- The patterning action is fully realized at the development step and is largely governed by the interplay of intermolecular interactions between various interfaces of molecular and ionic species in the system (see Fig. 3.1).
--[p152]-- Some of these interfaces are between different parts of the resist film and its surroundings: solid resist polymer film–developer interface, immiscible exposed resist polymer film–unexposed resist polymer film interface, exposed resist polymer film–air interface, unexposed resist polymer film–air interface, etc. We will adopt the nomenclature and methods of electrostatics and adapt the approach of Israelachvili in his treatise on intermolecular and surface forces.<sup>5</sup>
--[p153]-- Favorable interactions between the polymers within the exposed or unexposed part of the resist and the developer render that part soluble in the developer. These interactions are also at play between the protons of the photoacids and their counterions, and between these two species and other components in the resist film, as these two species diffuse in a correlated manner through the resist film under the influence of thermal gradient, to affect the critical dimension of the printed feature.

===== [p327-327] Theory of Photochemical and Radiochemical Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 4.4.1.1.1.1 Physical properties of DNQs (3块) =====
--[p327]-- • With a decomposition temperature at around $1 2 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ to $1 3 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$ , they have reasonable thermal stability over typical pre- and post-bake processing temperature regimes.
--[p327]-- 4.4.1.1.1.1 Physical properties of DNQs
Diazonaphthoquinones have some physical attributes that make them ideal candidates as photoactive components for near-UV lithography. These attributes according to Reiser<sup>337</sup> include:
• Their absorption spectra has a suitable overlap with the emission spectrum of the irradiation source (usually a mercury arc lamp).

• They are compatible with the novloac base resin, enabling them to affect the dissolution rate of the resist since they form a single phase with the resin.

===== [p407-409] Chapter 5 Theory of Block Copolymer Self-assembly Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 5.2.1.3.1 Synthesis of AB diblock copolymers (15块) =====
--[p408]-- The more initiator with respect to the monomers used in the polymerization, the lower is the molecular weight obtained since the same number of monomers are spread over a larger number of chains. As chain transfer reactions such as proton abstraction do not occur at low temperatures, carrying out the polymerization at low temperatures prevents a broadening of the molecular weight distribution.<sup>117</sup>
116. N. Hadijichristidis, S. Pispas and G. A.
--[p408]-- Some restrictions exist with respect to which monomers are suitable for block copolymerization reactions that can lead to the synthesis of well-defined AB diblock copolymers. These include the following, roughly in order of importance:<sup>116</sup>
1. The carbanion formed by the second monomer must have higher or similar stability than the one derived from the first monomer.
--[p407]-- 5.2.1.3.1 Synthesis of AB diblock copolymers
The most general method for the preparation of linear AB diblock copolymers is sequential addition of monomers, whereby the first monomer is completely polymerized, following which, the second monomer is added to the reaction vessel, and the polymerization is again allowed to proceed to completion.
--[p407]-- At the end, an appropriate terminating agent is added to the reaction mixture, and the diblock copolymer is isolated, usually by precipitation in a nonsolvent or a mixture of nonsolvents.
115. R. Waack, A. Rembaum, J. D. Coombes, and M. Szwarc, “Molecular weights of ‘living’ polymers,” J. Am. Chem. Soc. 79, 2026–2027 (1957).
--[p408]-- After completion of the polymerization and exhaustion of the first monomer, the second monomer is added to the solution now containing polymers with still-active “living” chain ends of the first monomer.
--[p408]-- In principle, because of the rapidity of the initiation step, all of the chains are initiated essentially at the same instant (at the point of initiator injection), and grow at the same rate and to about the same length until the monomer is consumed; copolymers thus formed have narrow polydispersity, as shown in Eq. (5.22).
--[p409]-- Table 5.3 lists representative samples of AB diblock copolymers formed by sequential monomer addition using anionic polymerization, some of which have been used in lithographic patterning. We highlight below aspects of the polymerization procedures for representative groups of these diblock copolymers.
--[p408]-- Molecular mass and molecular weight distribution are respectively controlled by appropriately adjusting the ratio of initiator to monomer and by carrying out the reaction at temperatures that either enhance or prevent chain transfer. The amount of initiator used in the polymerization determines the chain length of the polymer.
--[p409]-- Polar monomers such as 2-vinylpyridine and methyl methacrylate are typically polymerized in polar solvents such as tetrahydrofuran and at low temperature (78 °C). Additives such as LiCl are often used to help lower the rates of termination reactions to levels insignificant in the timeframe of the reaction. The synthesis of BCPs containing polar and nonpolar blocks typically starts with the polymerization of the nonpolar monomer because of its higher reactivity.
--[p408]-- Floudas, Block Copolymers: Synthetic Strategies, Physical Properties and Applications, John Wiley & Sons, New York, p. 4 (2003).
Nonpolar hydrocarbon monomers such as styrene, isoprene, and butadiene are readily polymerized in hydrocarbon solvents such as benzene, cyclohexane, etc. The initiator is typically alkyllithiums such as secbutyllithium. Examples of nonpolar diblock copolymers are poly(styrene-bisoprene) (PS-b-PI) and poly(styrene-b-butadiene) (PS-b-PB).
--[p408]-- Put another way: the carbanion of the first monomer must be able to initiate the polymerization of the second monomer, implying that the carbanion of the first monomer must be a stronger nucleophile than that of the second one.
2. The cross-over reaction rate, i.e., the rate of initiation of the polymerization of the second monomer by the anion of the polymer of the first monomer, must be higher than the rate of the propagation reaction of monomer B.
--[p408]-- In practical terms, AB diblock copolymerization proceeds as follows. Typically, a known amount of catalyst is added into the stirred solution of the first monomer that is kept either under vacuum or under an inert atmosphere. The living nature of anionic polymerization permits the syntheses of BCPs by sequential addition of the monomers.
--[p408]-- This leads to narrow molecular weight distribution for block B and absence of homopolymer A in the final BCP that can arise from incomplete initiation.
3. The second monomer must be very pure and practically devoid of impurities. Absent this, premature termination of the living A anion chain end can take place, leading to the formation of homopolymer of A in the final product, with attendant loss of molecular weight and composition control in the desired copolymer product.
--[p409]-- The active centers of the nonpolar block are then typically capped with 1,1-diphenylethylene in order to lower their reactivity, before the addition of the polar monomer. This helps to eliminate side reactions arising from addition of the active center to electrophilic sites in the polar monomers. Examples of copolymers containing polar and nonpolar blocks include poly(styrene-b-2-vinylpyridine) (PS-b-P2VP) and poly(styreneb-methyl methacrylate) (PS-b-PMMA).
--[p408]-- Upon completion of the polymerization and exhaustion of the second monomer, the active chain ends of the second block are terminated or destroyed by addition of appropriate reagents (such as alcohol, water, or dry ice) to the reaction mixture, thereby isolating the copolymer capped with hydrogen (if water or alcohol is used in the termination) or carboxylic acid (if carbon dioxide is used in the termination) end groups.

--[p141]-- In the depth-controlled electron beam exposure, the penetration depth is restricted to a certain fraction of the film thickness, such as the top layer, such that the irradiated top layer of the film is cured, leaving the underlying film unaffected.<sup>281</sup>
--[p141]-- Operationally, electron beam processing is controlled by the following parameters: beam energy, dose, current, processing gas, and substrate temperature. The penetration depth of the electrons into the target material is determined by the energy of the electron beam according to Grun’s formula:<sup>280</sup>
$$
R _ { \mathrm { g } } = { \frac { 0 . 0 4 6 V _ { \mathrm { a } } ^ { 1 . 7 5 } } { d } } ,\tag{2.191}
$$
--[p140]-- The crosslinking processes persist with continued electron beam irradiation and will stop only when the entire bulk of the film is crosslinked.
276. W. R. Livesay, A. L. Rubiales, M. Ross, S. Woods, and S. Campbell, “Electron beam hardening of photoresists,” Proc. SPIE 1925, 426–436 (1993).

--[p140]-- Electronic collisions are inelastic and slow down the primary electrons, making them transfer their energy into excitation energy and kinetic energy of secondary electrons within the resist. These inelastic collisions of the electron beam with the resist molecules lead to the generation of secondary electrons within the resist.
--[p140]-- The inelastic collisions also slow down the primary electrons (electron beam) as they travel through the resist film, resulting in the primary electrons imparting their energies to the resist molecules and ionizing them in the process, before they are finally absorbed.
--[p141]-- where $R _ { \mathrm { g } }$ is the Grun range (penetration depth) in mm, $V _ { \mathrm { a } }$ is the accelerating voltage or energy in KeV, and d is the density of the target material in $\mathrm { g } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 3 }$
Figure 2.20 shows the three possible electron beam processing schemes: full electron beam curing, variable-energy electron beam curing, and depthcontrolled electron beam curing.
--[p140]-- While nuclear interactions or collisions (also called Rutherford scattering) are elastic and merely change the direction of the electron within the resist, they play no significant role in electron beam curing of resists. In contrast, it is the electronic interaction between the electron beam and the resist molecules that is utilized in the electron beam curing of resists.
--[p140]-- Okoroanyanwu “Selective photoresist hardening to facilitate lateral trimming,” U.S. Patent No. 6,716,571 (2004); W. R. Livesay, A. L. Rubiales, M. Ross, S. Woods, and S. Campbell, “Electron beam hardening of photoresists,” Proc. SPIE 1925, 426–436 (1993).
278. A. Chapiro, Radiation Chemistry of Polymer Systems, John Wiley & Sons, New York, p. 42 (1962).
279. F. Billmeyer, Texbook of Polymer Science, John Wiley & Sons, New York, p. 372 (1971).
--[p141]-- The effect of crosslinking resist polymer films is to make the film stable to heat such that it cannot be made to flow or melt. A fully crosslinked resist polymer film is practically insoluble in most solvents, although it can be stripped with oxygen plasma etching. Its plasma etch resistance is superior to a similar film that is not crosslinked.
--[p140]-- The secondary electrons, in turn, travel away from their point of creation at relatively slower speeds than the primary electrons, while also producing ions along the trajectory of the secondary electrons.<sup>278</sup> Within an order of a picosecond after ionization, molecular rearrangement takes place in the ions and excited molecules, accompanied by thermal deactivation or the dissociation of valence bonds within the molecules in the resist.<sup>279</sup> The radicals created by these broken bonds may recombine with each other or form new bonds and reattach themselves to neighboring polymer chains that also have broken bonds in their side groups, effectively resulting in crosslinking of the polymer.
--[p140]-- 2.8.3 Electron beam curing of resists
Electron beam curing of postdeveloped resists aims at improving the thermal and etch stability of the patterned resist feature.<sup>277</sup> An electron beam can interact with a resist polymer primarily in two ways: nuclear and electronic interaction.
--[p141]-- In full electron beam curing, the entire film can be modified by selecting an electron beam energy such that the penetration depth of the electrons equals or is larger than the film thickness, thus producing a homogenous film with properties significantly different from the starting material. In the variable-energy electron beam curing scheme, by varying the electron beam energy with time, it is possible to vary the film properties very gradually as a function of thickness.

===== [p412-412] Chapter 5 Theory of Block Copolymer Self-assembly Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 5.2.1.3.1.2 Diblock copolymers containing styrene or dienes and methacrylate blocks (7块) =====
--[p412]-- After polymerization of the diene, the polarity of the solvent is changed by addition of THF (with or without prior removal of the hydrocarbon solvent), the temperature is lowered to $- 7 8 \ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$ and diphenylethylene (DPE) and LiCl are added; these procedures are followed by slow distillation of the methacrylate monomer into the reaction flask. The rationale behind this unique set of conditions and additives is described below.
--[p412]-- The polymerization of the methacrylate monomer requires the following: (1) low temperature $( - 7 8 \ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$ to prevent chain transfer reactions and thereby enable a narrow molecular weight distribution, (2) polar solvents (usually THF),<sup>137,138</sup> and (3) relatively less active and sterically hindered initiators to prevent the reaction of the active anions with the carbonyl group of the methacrylate monomers.
--[p412]-- The use of additives such as $\mathrm { L i C i ^ { 1 3 9 } }$ in conjunction with DPELi transformation in polar solvents and low temperatures enhance the control of the polymerization of methacrylate monomers, allowing, in some cases, polymerization at higher temperatures than normal.
--[p412]-- The complexation of the LiCl to the active chain ends results in the formation of complexes with different stereochemistry and reactivity able to perform a more controllable polymerization of the methacrylate monomers.<sup>140</sup> It must also be mentioned that the polarity of the polymerization solvent has a significant influence on the microstructure of the polymer block formed from the diene monomer.
--[p412]-- 5.2.1.3.1.2 Diblock copolymers containing styrene or dienes and methacrylate blocks
It has been established that diblock copolymers containing styrene (or styrenic monomers) or dienes (isoprene, butadiene) with methacrylate monomers can be synthesized by sequential anionic polymerization. Here, the most reactive monomer (styrenic or diene) is polymerized first in benzene (using the procedure described in Scheme 5.5).
--[p412]-- Nonpolar solvents such as benzene yield dienic polymer blocks with high 1,4 microstructure content, while polar solvents such as THF yield dienic polymer blocks with low 1,4 microstructure content.<sup>141</sup>
--[p412]-- The third requirement is the reason that a more active styrenic or dienic anion is usually transformed to a less active, more sterically hindered anion by reaction with DPE, a nonhomopolymerizable monomer (as shown in Scheme 5.5). By so doing, the polymerization of the methacrylate monomer is able to proceed in a controlled manner, yielding diblock copolymers with well-defined molecular properties, including narrow polydispersity.

--[p118]-- 2.6.6.1 Photon shot noise
In examining the photon shot noise, we consider a light source that emits photons at random at an average rate of L photons per unit time into an area A of resist. $$

--[p427]-- 5.2.3 Block copolymers via cationic polymerization
Cationic polymerization is an addition polymerization technique in which the growing chain end bears a positive charge (carbocation generated by a cationic initiator and vinyl monomer).<sup>187,188</sup> As the carbocations are very reactive and unstable, they can participate in a number of side reactions such as termination, chain transfer, and carbocation rearrangement.
--[p428]-- With the monomers being nucleophilic, chain transfer to the monomer is ever present in cationic polymerization and almost impossible to completely eliminate. Several methods are used to mitigate this problem, the most widely used being the stabilization of the carbocationic intermediates using either an appropriate counterion or an appropriate Lewis base.

===== [p40-41] MOLECULAR THEORY OF LITHOGRAPHY > 1.3.5.2 Photoimprint lithography (10块) =====
--[p40]-- The drawbacks associated with PIL include the following: (1) the imprinted resist film suffers from significant thickness shrinkage resulting from the fact that the volume of the solidified, crosslinked film is smaller than its corresponding liquid form; (2) the liquid nature of the resist film makes it difficult to confine the imprinted film to the desired areas of the substrate; and (3) given the numerous reactive components in the liquid resist formulation, the storage stability of the coated films is often very poor.
--[p40]-- The template material type affects the lifespan of the mold, with hard materials providing longer lifespans and better wear characteristics than soft materials.
43. A. Fuchs, M. Bender, and U. Plachetka, “Lithography potentials of UV-nanoimprint,” Current Applied Physics 8, 669–674 (2008).
44. M. Bender, A. Fuchs, U. Plachetka, “Status and prospects of UV-nanoimprint technology,” Microelectronic Engineering 84(4–9), 827–830 (2006).
--[p40]-- Patterning with PIL can be achieved in two main modes: (1) soft PIL (also called soft lithography) using soft templates [made of poly(dimethyl siloxane), perfluoropolyether, etc.]; and (2) hard PIL using hard and rigid templates (made of any of these materials: quartz, silicon, glass, silicon nitride, diamond, nickel, etc.). Critical materials properties considered in mold selection include hardness, thermal expansion coefficients, Poisson’s ratio, roughness, Young’s modulus, etc.
--[p41]-- The soft PIL technique has shown resolution down to 12.5-nm half pitch with good fidelity.<sup>45</sup> A major concern about soft PIL is the fact that the molds swell in most organic liquids.
--[p41]-- Hard PIL using hard rigid mold suffers from one main issue: the high stickiness of the mold to imprint resist means that the demolding force is always large, with the potential of causing damage to the patterned features. As such, a release layer with extremely low surface energy must be used to cover the surface of the mold in order to effect a smooth demolding action.
--[p40]-- Photoimprint lithography (PIL) involves the application of liquid photocurable oligomers, crosslinkers, radical initiators, and other small molecules instead of a thermoplastic polymer (as in TIL) to the substrate, following which a transparent mold (often made of quartz or fused silica) is impressed upon the above mixture formulation, with enough pressure (2000 mPas maximum) at room temperature and for time duration long enough for the resist to flow and fill the cavities in the mold, following which the now imprinted liquid resist film is photocured and solidified with light of appropriate wavelength. It is also possible to use an opaque stamp in combination with a transparent substrate through which light can be used to irradiate the imprinted resist formulation from the backside.
--[p41]-- The other issue is that it is difficult to maintain conformal contact between the hard mold and the imprint resist, which in turn imposes a restriction on the usable imprint area.
PIL using soft or flexible or conformable molds is able to overcome some of the above issues of hard molds: they can support large-area patterning; they can enable conformal contact between the mold and the resist; and they require significantly reduced pressures.
--[p40]-- Because PIL is operated at room temperature under low-pressure conditions, it offers several advantages over TIL in terms of the ability to simultaneously imprint micro- and nanostructures and easier tool design.<sup>43,44</sup> It also has superior overlay alignment accuracy compared to TIL, given its transparent mold through which overlay alignment measurement protocols can be implemented, and absence of thermal expansion issues.
--[p40]-- Typical light sources include lasers, mercury arc UV lamps and light emitting diodes, with photon outputs that have wavelengths that span the UV and visible region of the electromagnetic spectrum. The mold is removed, and pattern transfer processing, including for example, reactive ion etching, is used to transfer the pattern in the resist to the underlying substrates.

--[p31]-- 1.3.2 Extreme ultraviolet lithography
EUV lithography uses photons with 13.5-nm wavelength to expose wafers. A schematic of an EUV exposure tool is shown in Fig. 1.7.
--[p31]-- The key components of an EUV lithography (EUVL) system include the following: (1) an illumination system consisting of an EUV radiation source (for generating the plasma that in turn emits EUV photons), a condenser (to collect the EUV radiation from a plasma source, directing it to the intermediate focus, which is a point in space where a number of source specifications, such as power, étendue, etc., must be met; it is also the starting point for the illumination system), and an illumination system to provide uniform EUV radiation to the reticle, as well as the required degree of partial coherence for imaging to provide the desired pupil-fill; (2) a patterned reflective mask, formed from a multilayer-coated blank to maximize its reflectivity at a wavelength of 13.5 nm;<sup>16</sup> (3) a
--[p33]-- As the requirement for complete radiation absorption afforded by a thick absorber layer conflicts with the requirement for minimization of shadowing afforded by a thin absorber layer, a tradeoff is struck between the two extremes of absorber thickness. This results in an absorber material with sufficiently high EUV absorptivity that is also sufficiently thin to minimize shadowing on any portion of the reflected beam.
This absorber is projected to be the preferred mask material option for EUV lithography in high-volume device manufacturing.
--[p32]-- In some aspects, the fabrication of EUV masks is simpler than for leading edge masks used in longer-wavelength optical lithographies such as DUV lithography because the OPC features are expected to be much fewer and less complicated.
A patterned EUV mask, such as the one illustrated in Fig. 1.8, is created by selectively removing (by reactive ion etching) the absorber layer.
--[p33]-- Unlike what occurs in optical lithography, the incident or illuminating radiation in EUV lithography is not orthogonal to the mask, but rather is incident from a direction at an angle of a few degrees, usually 6 deg, to the mask normal. As such, thick absorber features in EUV masks will necessarily cause shadowing on the reflected beam.
--[p31]-- 1.7 is a high-temperature plasma produced by applying very short current pulses across the fuel material, e.g., a xenon-filled capillary or a stream of tin droplets between two high-voltage electrodes. EUV radiation reflected from the patterned mask is imaged by a 4 -reduction projection system onto a resist-coated silicon wafer.
--[p32]-- 17 Current reflective masks for EUV lithography consist of a Ta-based absorber layer (TaBN or TaN) deposited on a Ru-capped Mo/Si multilayer-coated blank. EUV mask blanks are similar to mask blanks for conventional optical lithography in many respects, but differ from them in these respects: (1) they are coated with 40 bilayers of Mo (2.8 nm thick) and Si (4.1 nm thick) instead of a single layer of chrome; (2) the mask substrate is a low thermal expansion material (LTEM) instead of quartz.

===== [p22-22] MOLECULAR THEORY OF LITHOGRAPHY > 1.1 Introduction (6块) =====
--[p22]-- 1.1 Introduction
At the heart of lithography are chemical transformations designed to print a relief image of an object on a flat surface. The printing involves the registration of information in the imaging layer, referred to as the resist, by means of electromagnetic radiation, or molecular self-assembly, or by embossing/imprinting. It comprises both photography and a development process that penetrates deep into the subsurface of the resist and etches away the unwanted regions of the image.
--[p22]-- We will examine and show how these electrons mediate the molecular interactions that underlie the lithographic contrast between the exposed and unexposed regions of the resist. We will also examine the lithographic process, including unit operations such as substrate preparation, coating, exposure, pre- and post-exposure baking, development, and postexposure stabilization processes.
--[p22]-- We will use as a monitor for these transformations the flow of electrons between essential components in a lithographic system, while respecting the conservation of mass<sup>1</sup> and energy<sup>2</sup> laws.
--[p22]-- The object may be a mask containing patterns of integrated circuit devices; the flat surface may be a silicon wafer coated with photo- or radiation-sensitive resist, which upon exposure and development is transformed into the relief image of the mask. Underlying these transformations are distinct chemical reactions that are mediated by electrons and governed by established chemical laws that are explainable by time-tested chemical and physical theories.
--[p22]-- Finally, we will examine the imaging mechanisms, including photo- and radiochemical, imprint, and molecular self-assembly.
In a way, this book is an attempt to examine lithography through the lens of the molecular science that it truly is, and through the effort present a reasonably complete, unified exposition of the molecular theory that underlies lithographic imaging.
--[p22]-- The approach therefore calls for critically examining the molecular-level chemical transformations that underlie lithography, and systematically explaining with physical-chemical theories the essential aspects of lithographic phenomena in the many varied forms in which the field is practiced today.

De Rosa et al.<sup>291,292</sup> investigated crystallization-induced domain orientation of poly(styrene-b-ethylene) by means of a crystallizable solvent (benzoic acid).

--[p35]-- However, they do require a stable vacuum $( 1 0 ^ { - 7 }$ to $i 0 ^ { - 9 }$ torr) and are more difficult to fabricate than pure tungsten sources.<sup>28</sup>
La ${ \bf B } _ { 6 }$ has a much lower work function than either tungsten or thoriated tungsten, which makes such sources brighter than those made from either pure tungsten or thoriated tungsten.
--[p34]-- 1.3.3.1 Electron beam lithography system
Figure 1.9 shows a schematic diagram of an electron beam lithographic exposure system, which consists of three main subsystems: electron source (gun), electron column (beam forming system), and exposure stage. A computer controls the various machine subsystems and transfers pattern information to the beam deflection coils.
Electron sources used in electron beam lithographic exposure tools are similar to those used in conventional electron microscopes.
--[p36]-- Field-emission sources use a high electric field surrounding a very sharp point of tungsten to extract electrons at the tip of the source, forming a Gaussian spot only a few nanometers in diameter.
--[p36]-- The energy spread of the electrons emitted from a field emission source is less than that from a thermionic source; this enables the field emission source to have less chromatic aberration (where electrons of slightly different energies are focused at different image planes) and higher resolution than thermionic emission sources. These field emission sources are also considerably brighter than any of the thermionic emitters.
--[p35]-- They can be divided into two main groups—thermionic or field emission—depending on the way in which they emit electrons.<sup>25</sup> The sources that rely on the emission of electrons from a material that is heated to a temperature at which electrons are emitted from the surface are referred to as thermionic sources. These sources are fabricated from materials such as tungsten, thoriated tungsten, or lanthanum hexaboride $\left( \mathrm { L a B } _ { 6 } \right)$ 26
--[p36]-- The $\mathrm { L a B } _ { 6 }$ source requires a better vacuum than that required for a thoriated tungsten source and, as a result, is less stable than sources made from the latter. $\mathrm { L a B } _ { 6 }$ is preferred for illuminating shapedbeam systems because its emission uniformity can be maintained over a larger area compared with that from the other sources.<sup>29</sup>
--[p35]-- Tungsten emission sources have fairly good current stability and tolerance to variations in vacuum conditions. They can be easily fabricated and maintained.<sup>27</sup> Thoriated tungsten sources have a work function that is lower than that of pure tungsten sources; they also emit equivalent electron current at lower temperatures than pure tungsten sources. As a result, they have much longer lifetime and are more stable than pure tungsten sources.
--[p36]-- While the maximum current i that can be delivered to a unit area a of the resist-coated substrate is limited by the brightness of the source, the parameters a, i, and t (where t is dwell time) determine the maximum dose $D _ { m a x }$ in coulombs per square centimeter, given by
$$
D _ { \mathrm { m a x } } = \frac { i t } { a } .\tag{1.7}
$$
The maximum dose delivered by the exposure tool defines the resist sensitivity required to maximize the throughput of the tool.<sup>31</sup>
--[p36]-- However, they are more difficult to fabricate and must be operated in vacuums on the order of $1 0 ^ { - 8 }$ to $1 0 ^ { - 1 0 }$ torr. They are widely used in electron beam scanning lithographic exposure tools.<sup>30</sup>

The initiators are alkyl lithiums.

===== [p385-390] Chapter 5 Theory of Block Copolymer Self-assembly Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 5.1 Introduction (20块) =====
--[p389]-- A three-step reaction provides for the synthesis of (A—B—A) or (B—A—B) triblock copolymers.<sup>43</sup> Reacting “living” diblock copolymers with n-functional coupling agents can yield $( \mathbf { A } { - } \mathbf { B } ) _ { n }$ multiblocks or starblock copolymers (when $n \geq 3 )$ . (A—B—C) or other multicomponent BCP molecular architectures are formed when three or more different monomer types are used in the polymerization process.
--[p386]-- The order–disorder transition (ODT) temperature and the specific pattern motifs formed by a given BCP thin film depend on the polymer molecular weight, the segmental interactions, and the volumetric composition.<sup>9,10</sup> In particular, the BCP thin film composition strongly determines the micro- or nanophase morphology. As an example, diblock copolymers with blocks of comparable volume exhibit a lamellar motif.
--[p389]-- Surfaces can be chemically modified to control the interfacial interactions of the blocks with the interfaces, as a way of removing any preferential affinity of the blocks.<sup>37,38,39</sup> It should be mentioned, however, that balanced interfacial interactions, while necessary, are not sufficient since both orientations satisfy this boundary constraint.
--[p385]-- Block copolymers (BCPs) comprise two or more chemically distinct polymer chains (called blocks) that are covalently bonded at one end to form a larger, more complex macromolecule. If the constituent polymers are immiscible, upon heating, phase separation can be induced (without resulting in total separation because of the covalent bonding connectivity between the copolymer chains).
--[p389]-- A vast array of BCP configurations, morphologies, or architectures can be constructed using modern synthetic chemistry techniques, based largely on termination-free anionic polymerization in which monomers are sequentially added to carbanion-terminated (“living”) linear polymer chains, controlled living radical polymerization, and cationic polymerization.
--[p389]-- A consequence of the “living” nature of these polymerization reactions is that the block and overall molecular weight distributions are nearly ideal, i.e., polydispersity index $\mathrm { ( P D I ) } ~ = ~ M _ { \mathrm { w } } / M _ { \mathrm { n } } ~ \sim ~ < 1 . 1$ , where $M _ { \mathrm { w } }$ and $M _ { \mathrm { n } }$ represent the weight and number-average molecular weights, respectively.<sup>44,45,46</sup>
43.
--[p389]-- However, by slightly modifying one of the blocks, for example, by randomly placing a second unit along the chain, small changes in the surface energies, segmental interactions, and rigidity can be effected without sacrificing the overall micro- and nanophaseseparated characteristic of the BCP.<sup>42</sup> This underscores the great synthetic versatility in designing and tailoring BCPs to control morphology in thin films.
--[p385]-- Soc. London Ser. A 348, 149 (1994).
3. F. Meng, Z. Zhong, and J. Feijen, “Stimuli-responsive polymersomes for programmed drug delivery,” Biomacromolecules 10(2), 197–209 (2009).
--[p389]-- In instances where the film thickness is not commensurate with the natural period of the BCP, only an orientation of the microdomains normal to the film surface minimizes the energy of the copolymer.<sup>40,41</sup> As the inherent chemical nature of the chain determines parameters such as segmental interactions, surface energies, and rigidity of the segments—for tuning BCP thin film morphology—these parameters are not easily changed.
--[p387]-- Other parameters that play a critical role in determining the microphase morphology include segmental interactions between the components, the rigidity of each block, the surface energies of the components, and the interactions of the blocks with the underlying substrate.
--[p387]-- As a general rule, preferential interactions of one block with the substrate or a lower surface energy of one component will force a segregation of one block to either the surface or the substrate.<sup>12,13,14</sup> The connectivity of the blocks will then force the alignment of the microdomains in an orientation parallel to the substrate.
--[p389]-- The simplest and most studied BCP architecture is the linear (A—B) diblock, obtained by the two-step anionic polymerization of A and B monomers in an (A—B) diblock copolymer, and consisting of a sequence of type-A monomers covalently bonded to a chain of type-B monomers.
--[p389]-- Polymerization of just two distinct types of monomers (e.g., styrene and isoprene) leads to a class of materials referred to as (A—B) diblock copolymers. Within this class, a variety of molecular architectures can be constructed. Figure 5.1 illustrates a basic classification of these molecular architectures, based on the number of chemically distinct blocks (i.e., number of monomer types) and topology (linear versus branched sequencing).
--[p387]-- While the parallel microdomain orientation is desirable for some applications, other applications, including lithography, require that the microdomains be oriented normal to the surface. Absent any surface modification, an external field may be required to overcome these preferential interactions.
--[p390]-- Triblock copolymers of aromatics can also be prepared via Yamamoto and Suzuki coupling reaction schemes if the central block monomer has bromine functional groups at its two ends.

--[p385]-- 5.1 Introduction
Lithography based on self-assembling block copolymers exploits the phase separation of block copolymer domains into nanoscopic structures that can be used as lithographic masks—templates for patterning and synthesizing inorganic materials and printing biomaterials. But before we proceed further, it is necessary to provide a brief background on block copolymers, how they are made, the condition under which they phase separate and self-assemble, and why they do this.
--[p386]-- Increasing the degree of compositional asymmetry between the blocks results in motifs such as gyroid, cylinder, and finally, sphere phases.<sup>11</sup> These morphologies can be obtained simply by varying the ratio of the block lengths.
--[p385]-- Buoyed by new developments, block copolymers, thoroughly studied for more than 50 years, are yet again garnering renewed research interest, principally because of their potential applications in nanotechnology,<sup>7,8</sup> of which lithography is an enabler.

--[p57]-- 2.3.1 Resist spin-coating process
In the spin-coating process, a precise amount of liquid resist is dispensed onto a wafer (either statically, i.e., with the wafer at rest, or dynamically, i.e., with the wafer rotating). The wafer is then spun at high speeds until such time that the film thickness reaches a desired value (Fig. 2.3). The process uses the dynamics of centrifugal forces to disperse a fluid of polymeric resist material over the entire wafer surface.
--[p61]-- Dispense volume, dispense rate, and other factors appear to be not particularly critical in determining the final film thickness as long as the wafer is spun for a sufficiently long time. Yet, in spite of evaporative effects, the final thickness of fluid $h _ { \mathrm { f } }$ can be fairly well predicted with an inverse power law relationship, where C is a constant depending on the viscosity and contains the effects of viscous forces:
$$
h _ { \mathrm { f } } = C \omega ^ { - N } .\tag{2.19}

This lack of swelling during development is one reason that positive resists generally have higher resolution capability than their traditional negative-resist counterparts.

--[p128]-- 2.7.4.1 Chemical development in resist processing
In chemical development, the matrix resin of the resist system dissolves in the developer through a chemical reaction. Examples of resists that use chemical development include positive resists composed of novolac resins and DNQ, as well as positive chemical amplification resists based on phenolic, acrylate, and alicyclic polymers. These resists are developed with 0.26 N aqueous solution of TMAH.

===== [p61-63] Chapter 2 Theory of the Lithographic Process > 2.3.2 Characteristics of thin resist films (10块) =====
--[p62]-- Due to the considerable optical absorption of conventional resist materials, particularly at 157-nm and 13.45-nm wavelengths, UTR processes where imaging is confined to a very thin layer (≤100 nm) of the resist are promising options for implementing these lithographies. Another consideration for using UTR processes is the reduction of feature aspect ratio as a way of mitigating pattern collapse associated with high aspect ratios.
--[p61]-- 2.3.2 Characteristics of thin resist films
The comprehensive characterization of ultrathin resist $( \leq 1 0 0 \ \mathrm { n m } )$ processes in terms of defectivity,<sup>21</sup> manufacturability,<sup>22</sup> and physical properties (structure, dynamics, stability, thermodynamic behavior, $\mathrm { e t c } ) ^ { \dot { 2 } 3 }$ have been a central point of interest in semiconductor microlithography for quite some time.
--[p61]-- Despite many years of experimental and theoretical efforts along these lines, a number of basic questions still remain unanswered. One of these issues is the fundamental lower physical limit of the resist thickness, below which lithographic patterning is not viable.
--[p62]-- Because UTR films have a higher surface-to-volume ratio than their thicker counterparts for any given feature size, they are highly interfacial. Each macromolecular component of a UTR system is close to an interface, either the solid substrate or the free-surface interface. In the most extreme case, each macromolecule is confined within the solid interface and the free surface. Consequently, ultrathin film material properties may be quite different from those of the bulk.
--[p63]-- It is difficult to produce ultrathin films that are uniform, continuous, defect free, and stable to changes in shape after aging or thermal processing. These issues together determine the thickness limit of a given UTR film below which lithography is not viable.
--[p62]-- In spite of the above-mentioned advantages of UTR processes, practical considerations often impose a choice of resist and substrate that are not fully compatible, resulting in films that are unstable or metastable with finite relaxation time.
--[p62]-- The interfacial properties of such polymer/inorganic interfaces often determine their lithographic performance and, consequently, the performance of devices fabricated with them.
Establishing the lower thickness limit of UTR films as well as understanding and controlling the causes of defects associated with such films are major challenges for the near-term development of UTR process technology.
--[p62]-- This lower limit of ultrathin resist (UTR) film thickness is of great importance in microlithography, particularly as the critical dimensions required for manufacturing semiconductor devices continue to shrink toward the length scale of individual macromolecules.
--[p62]-- In particular, the glass transition temperature $T _ { \mathrm { g } }$ may be depressed or elevated by as much as $4 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ relative to the bulk values, depending on the film thickness and the chemical nature of the solid substrate upon which the film is deposited.<sup>27</sup> This may affect the viscoelastic response of the film during subsequent thermal annealing.
--[p62]-- While thick films (.300 nm) may be stable or metastable due to gravity,<sup>24</sup> for thin films (≤100 nm), intermolecular and surface forces dominate.<sup>25</sup> UTR films are susceptible to both spontaneous thin film instabilities due to London–van der Waals interactions and defects caused by substrate imperfections (topographical features such as pits or mounds).<sup>26</sup>

--[p329]-- 4.4.1.1.2 Diazo-Meldrum’s acid-based resists
Resists with diazo-Meldrum’s acid, like their DNQ counterparts, are based on the principle of transformation (or removal) of a dissolution inhibitor by a photoreaction. The photolabile inhibitor itself, diazo-Meldrum’s acid, behaves like diazoquinone in that when formulated with novolac, it can inhibit the base solubility of the latter.
--[p330]-- With an absorption peak almost exactly at 250 nm and an ability to be bleached upon irradiation, this sensitizer when formulated with suitable novolac resin makes an optically ideal resist for DUV exposure. Its reported sensitivity (approximately 50 mJ/cm<sup>2</sup>) compares favorably with the sensitivity of conventional DNQ/novolac resists (approximately 100 mJ/cm<sup>2</sup>).<sup>347</sup>

--[p365]-- 4.4.2.1 Poly(methyl methacrylate) resist system

--[p368]-- Because PMMA has excellent resolution but low sensitivity, attempts have been made to find its derivatives or copolymers that retain its good qualities and yet have high sensitivity to radiation.<sup>469</sup> The plasma etch resistance of PMMA cannot be significantly increased, but efforts to increase its sensitivity have been largely reported to be successful.

--[p430]-- 5.2.3.2.1 Synthesis of block copolymers containing styrene and isobutylene blocks
Block copolymers containing styrene and isobutylene blocks are synthesized by polymerizing either monomer first because these two monomers have similar reactivity, after the method of Faust.<sup>190</sup> The polymerization is carried out at a temperature of $- 8 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ , using $\mathrm { T i C l } _ { 4 }$ as the Lewis acid initiator.
--[p430]-- The stability of the cations dictates which monomer is polymerized first. Because the polystyrene cation is less stable than the polyisoprene cation, undergoing a slow decomposition at monomer conversions close to 100%, isoprene monomer is typically added at a styrene conversion of approximately 95%, so as to avoid partial termination of living polystyrene (Scheme 5.23).
--[p431]-- The BCP poly(a-methylstyrene-b-isobutylene) is synthesized after the method of Li and Faust.<sup>191</sup> As a-methylstyrene and isobutylene monomers have different reactivities, different Lewis acids are used to initiate the polymerization of the different monomers. The synthesis starts with the polymerization of the a-methylstyrene monomer, initiated by the comparatively weak Lewis acid $\mathrm { B C l } _ { 3 } .$ , which is inefficient in initiating the polymerization of isobutylene.
--[p431]-- Following the formation of the poly(a-methylstyrene) block, the second monomer, isobutylene, along with its initiator, the comparatively strong Lewis acid $\mathrm { T i C l } _ { 4 } .$ , are added to the reaction vessel, now containing living chains of poly(a-methylstyrene) block cation, to yield the desired product (Scheme 5.25).

--[p66]-- 2.3.3.3 Instabilities and thermophysical properties of UTR films
Instabilities in UTR films can also be manifested as discontinuities in the thermophysical properties of the films due to interfacial effects and polymer cooperative and surface dynamics. Polymer surfaces are regions of enhanced molecular mobility as compared to the bulk, given the decreased constraints on macromolecules at a free surface.
