===== [p407-407] Chapter 5 Theory of Block Copolymer Self-assembly Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 5.2.1.3 General experimental procedures (4块) =====
--[p407]-- The reactor must, of necessity, be made with materials that are vacuum compatible. In addition, the reactants must be added via break seals.
Anionic polymerization carried out under an inert gas such as nitrogen or argon is used to maintain the absence of moisture, oxygen, or carbon dioxide.
--[p407]-- In contrast to polymerization under high vacuum, anionic polymerization under inert gas requires less effort and can be effective for the synthesis of rather simple BCPs, where the purity requirement for the BCP self-assembly process is not very exacting.
--[p407]-- 5.2.1.3 General experimental procedures
Two general experimental methods used in anionic polymerization are distinguished from each other depending on whether the polymerization reaction is carried out under high vacuum or under an inert atmosphere.
--[p407]-- Anionic polymerization under high vacuum offers the advantage of higher levels of purity over longer periods of time—a requirement for producing for high-molecular-mass polymers or polymers containing coupling agents that have long reaction times (months) and must therefore be kept very clean for a long time. The drawback of anionic polymerization is the added effort and time needed to run a reaction under vacuum.

===== [p144-145] Chapter 3 Theory of Molecular Interactions in Lithography > 3.1 Introduction (13块) =====
--[p145]-- Closely related to the hydrophobic effect is the hydrophobic interaction, which refers to the unusually strong attraction between hydrophobic molecules and surfaces in water—often stronger than their attraction in free space. The interaction between the hydrophobic part of the resist and water is attractive, due to the dispersion force. However, the interaction of water with itself is much more attractive.
--[p144]-- The contrast thus results from the immiscibility of the inert, hydrophobic, nonpolar, and unexposed (for positive resists) or exposed (for negative resists)
part of the resist film with the developer solvent, which is typically aqueous based.
--[p144]-- Combinations of these agents are also used to effect patterning, as in the combination of mechanical and chemical agents in guided/directed selfassembly that use larger topographical or chemical patterns to guide the selfassembly of much smaller patterns so as to ensure that the self-assembled patterns have predetermined locations and small domain size as opposed to the random locations and large domain sizes in unguided self-assembly.
--[p145]-- Water molecules are attracted more strongly to other water molecules than to the polymer molecules of inert resist material, and inert resist polymer molecules are attracted more strongly to other inert resist polymer molecules than to water molecules. This is part of the reason that the nonpolar inert resist does not dissolve in the aqueous developer and, hence, is the basis of the lithographic contrast in these resist systems.
--[p145]-- Similarly, in negative resists developed in nonpolar solvents, the resist polymer molecules of the unexposed part are attracted more strongly to the molecules of the developer solvent (which readily dissolves them) than the developer solvent molecules are attracted to other developer solvent molecules. The attraction between the solvent molecules and other solvent molecules is far stronger than the attraction between solvent molecules and the crosslinked polymer (the exposed part).
--[p145]-- The current length scale of feature sizes printed with advanced lithographic techniques—ranging from a few tens of nanometers to singledigit nanometers, which overlaps with the radius of gyration of the resist polymers—is squarely within the regime where molecular-level interactions begin to affect process fidelity, manifesting in phenomena such as increased line edge roughness, limitations to resolution in high-activation-energy chemical amplification resist systems because of photoacid diffusion blur, etc.
The term interaction as used here encompasses all aspects and manifestations of a force, including how it determines resist matrix resin solubility in the developer solution, ambipolar diffusion of photoacids and their counterions in the resist during PEB, etc.
--[p144]-- 3.1 Introduction
At the molecular level, the purpose of lithography is to create a difference or a contrast in a physical and/or chemical property between the exposed and unexposed area of the information registration medium, called resist, such that the net interaction between the molecules of either of these parts of the resist and the development medium is either attractive so as to be miscible with it or repulsive so as to be immiscible with it.
--[p144]-- The overall result is the preferential removal of one part of the resist relative to the other during development. This differential solubility of the exposed and unexposed regions of the resist in the developer solvent thus accounts for the contrast between the two regions.
--[p145]-- While the active or hydrophilic part of the resist dissolves readily in the aqueous developer, the hydrophobic or inert part does not, according to the old well-known chemist’s rule, “like dissolves like.” Van der Waals dispersion forces<sup>1</sup> play a very significant role in the immiscibility of the hydrophobic part of the resist with aqueous developer solution; they disrupt the existing water structure and impose a new and more ordered structure around the surrounding water molecules, but away from the inert resist material. Thus this interaction is entropically unfavorable. Hydrophobic effect is the collective term used to describe the immiscibility of the hydrophobic part of the resist with water.
--[p145]-- Also, the attraction between the crosslinked polymers with each other is far greater than the attraction between them and the solvent molecules. For all of the above reasons, the crosslinked part does not dissolve in the developer solvent, while the unexposed part readily does.
--[p145]-- We will adopt certain semiquantitative combining relations to describe these molecular forces. A thermodynamic measure of these interactions is the chemical potential. We will explore in this chapter the thermodynamics of these interactions for specific lithographic systems. Beyond this chapter, in the remainder of this book, we will explore how these interactions underlie lithographic patterning in the most significant forms it is practiced today.
1.
The origin of this name has to do with their relation to the dispersion of light in the visible and UV regions of the spectrum.
--[p144]-- The ultimate effect of the above agents is to engender molecular interactions, including van der Waals, electrostatic, hydrophobic, hydrogen bonding, acid– base, and steric interactions—to mention but the most significant ones—that act in concert during the aqueous or solvent development of the resist to determine which part of the resist will be dissolved or not, and in so doing give rise to the contrast between the exposed and unexposed areas of the resist.
--[p144]-- Agents for creating this contrast include electromagnetic radiation (as in optical, x-ray, and EUV lithography), charged particle (as in electron beam and ion beam lithography), mechanical force (as in imprint lithography), interfacial forces (as in self-assembly lithography and fine art lithography).

===== [p305-305] Theory of Photochemical and Radiochemical Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > B. Azo compounds (3块) =====

--[p305]-- B. Azo compounds
The compound 2,20-azobis(butyrolnitrile) (AIBN) (XXIII) is a good example of an azo compound that upon absorption of light can fragment to yield the 2-cyanoisopropyl radical (Scheme 4.30). This is a much more reactive radical than the benzoyl radical and therefore is more effective in initiating polymerization than the latter.
--[p305]-- In addition, the fragmentation yield of AIBN is high because a molecule of nitrogen is eliminated in the photolytic process, and the two active radicals are formed at a distance of 3 Å from each other, which increases their chances of escape from the primary cage.<sup>251</sup> This radical is not thermally stable, hence, its popularity as a thermal initiator.

Oxygen readily reacts with most initiating radicals by forming peroxy radicals that do not effectively initiate polymerization, so much so that in the early stages irradiation, this reaction channel removes the photogenerated primary radicals:
$$
R ^ { \bullet } + O _ { 2 } { \longrightarrow } R O O ^ { \bullet } .\tag{[4.42]}
$$
It is only when most of the oxygen has been consumed that the primary radicals become available for initiation.<sup>288</sup>
--[p313]-- 4.3.3.1.3 The initiation step
Once the radicals have been generated, the next step is for them to initiate polymerization. Some of them will be successful in this regard, while others will not.
--[p314]-- Other approaches employed for removing oxygen from the system include chemical means, the most popular being the reaction with (tertiary) amines, which are often used as hydrogen donors in initiation and do form radicals that react with oxygen and are transformed thereby into peroxy radicals.<sup>291</sup>
--[p313]-- The initiation step competes with the quenching (scavenging) of primary radicals by various additives (Ad) (such as stabilizers and antioxidants) and by oxygen, as shown in Reactions [4.39] through [4.41]:

--[p466]-- The imprint template is often coated with low-surface-energy materials, also called the release layer, to ensure that once the imprint process is completed, the template can be easily removed without distorting the patterned features. These materials include fluorinated SAMs (formed from fluoroalkyltricholorosilane precursor<sup>22</sup>), Teflon<sup>®</sup>, etc.
--[p465]-- The main limitation is the inhibition caused by the presence of molecular oxygen, which readily forms stable peroxy radicals during polymerization,<sup>15</sup> leading to a distinct induction period at the onset of irradiation and, ultimately, preventing the polymerization of imprint monomers at the periphery of the template.<sup>16,17</sup>
--[p463]-- 6.2 Imprint Resist Materials
The components of a given imprint resist are chosen consistent with the type of imprint process for which the resist in question will be used. TIL resist comprises basically the thermoplastic resin that is chosen to have a glass transition temperature that is within the desired operating temperature, sufficient adhesion to the substrate, and sufficient mechanical strength to withstand post-imprint processes such as reactive ion etching.
--[p463]-- The four main components of PIL resist consist of a (1) bulk polymerizable monomer, which makes up a large portion of the resist composition; (2) a photoinitiator, which initiates the polymerization process; (3) a silicon- or siloxane-containing monomer, which provides the oxygen etch resistance required to transfer the final pattern onto the underlying substrate, but that can pose stamp contamination risk because of the difficulty of cleaning it off the stamp after imprinting; and (4) a difunctional crosslinker, which crosslinks the formed polymer, enhancing the mechanical stability of the final patterned feature.<sup>3</sup> The factors that must be considered in the formulation of PIL resists include the following:
1.
--[p466]-- The net result is a cured material with improved mechanical and thermal properties and with minimal shrinkage.<sup>20</sup> A notable drawback of the POSS material is associated with its high silicon content, which, if residual silicon materials are embedded within the template features, can be extremely difficult, if not impossible, to clean off without damaging the template.<sup>21</sup>
--[p465]-- Acrylates such as t-butyl acrylates are commonly used in PIL due to the following characteristics: their low-viscosity prepolymer solutions can be easily dispensed while maintaining low volatility; they can be rapidly polymerized via photoinitiated radical polymerization; and the formed polymer can be crosslinked with ethylene glycol diacrylate. It must be noted, however, that the use of acrylates in PIL is hampered by limitations arising from the radical nature of their photopolymerization.
--[p466]-- The result of this inhibition is an extended exposure time, which, in turn, leads to a decrease in process wafer throughput when hard or rigid stamps are used. Flexible stamps based on, for example, poly(dimethyl siloxane) (PDMS), do not suffer from this problem because of their low permeability to oxygen. For this and other reasons, PDMS is now commonly used in PIL.
--[p464]-- • The prepolymer formulation must have sufficiently low viscosity so as to be easily spin coated on a substrate or automatically dispensed without its composition changing significantly due to evaporation.
• The prepolymer must be able to photopolymerize rapidly in order to ensure high throughput of the process.
• The polymerization process must occur with minimal shrinkage.
--[p464]-- • The imprinted polymer pattern must adhere very well to the substrate and yet be easily released from the imprint template at the end of the process, without being damaged or collapsing.
• The formed polymer must be mechanically and thermally stable to withstand later processes such as reactive ion etching used in transferring the patterns to underlying substrates.<sup>4</sup>

Typical monomers for PIL resists include acrylates,<sup>5,6,7,8,9,10</sup> vinyl ethers,<sup>11,12,13</sup> epoxies, and functionalized polyhedral oligomeric silsequioxanes (POSSs).<sup>14</sup> Table 6.1 shows representative components of PIL resist materials.

The functionalized POSS materials used in PIL typically incorporate methacrylate functionalities and benzocylcobutane groups. Upon exposure, the methacrylate groups undergo free-radical polymerization, and upon heating the benzocyclobutane groups are cured.

===== [p346-348] Theory of Photochemical and Radiochemical Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > A. Ester-protected poly(hydroxy styrene)-based resist systems (10块) =====
--[p346]-- A. Ester-protected poly(hydroxy styrene)-based resist systems
Ester-protected carboxylic acid functional groups in resist resins can undergo photoinduced acid-catalyzed thermolysis in a chemical amplification scheme, in the same manner as carbonates, to form aqueous-base-soluble resins, and resulting in a polarity change from a nonpolar to polar state.
--[p346]-- The dissolution rate of this resist resin is tuned simply by changing the deprotectection ratio (i.e., the ratio of the deprotected to the protected repeating units in the copolymer). The higher the deprotection ratio, the greater is the dissolution rate of the resist copolymer in aqueous base developer.
Scheme 4.55 Acid-catalyzed deprotection of poly(4-hydroxystyrene-co-4-polyhydroxystyrene-tert-butyl ester).
--[p347]-- Other ester-protected PHOST copolymers that have been employed in DUV resist applications include those protected with tert-butoxycarbonylmethyl<sup>416</sup> and tert-butyl<sup>417</sup> groups. Poly(4-vinyl benzoate)<sup>418</sup> and poly(methyl methacrylate)<sup>419</sup> are converted to poly(4-vinylbenzoic acid) and poly(methacrylic acid), respectively, by reactions with a photochemically generated acid.
--[p346]-- The ester groups in these polymers are selected to generate upon heterolysis of the C─O bond, stable carbocations that undergo spontaneous b-elimination to form olefins. The thermal and acidolytic stability can be tuned by changing the structure of the ester group.<sup>415</sup>
--[p347]-- By so doing, the neutralization reactions between the photoacids and bases in the resist matrix (otherwise known as poisoning) are prevented. This allows the photoacids to participate in deprotection reactions that define the imaging mechanism of the system. The result is that this resist is extremely resistant to airborne contamination, in contrast to the early chemical amplification resists.
--[p346]-- The synthetic route to copolymer (LII) can be through direct copolymerization of 4-hydroxystyrene with TBEST or via polymerization of TBEST, followed by partial deprotection to afford a copolymer with repeating units having about 20–30% protecting groups, with the rest being deprotected (i.e., phenolic) units. Partial protection of copolymer (LII) may also be accomplished by starting with the poly(hydroxystyrene) homopolymer and selectively protecting a fraction of the phenolic OH group.
--[p347]-- One of the most important ester-protected polyhydroxystyrene-based resist copolymers is an environmentally stable chemical amplification photoresist (therefore called ESCAP copolymer) that was developed at IBM and is based on the random copolymerization of 4-hydroxystyrene with tert-butyl acrylate (LIII).<sup>420</sup> Upon exposure, this resist copolymer is converted to a copolymer of 4-hydroxystyrene with acrylic acid through photoinduced acid-catalyzed deprotection of the tert-butyl group (see Scheme 4.56). Annealing this resist system at temperatures near its glass transition temperature fills the free volumes (voids in the resist matrix), thereby preventing out-diffusion of photoacids from the matrix and in-diffusion of airborne bases into the resist.
--[p348]-- In contrast to the partially protected PHOST copolymer, the ESCAP copolymers do not undergo thermal deprotection below $\mathrm { \bar { 1 8 0 } ^ { \circ } C }$ Furthermore, the photoacid-catalyzed conversion of the tert-butyl ester to carboxylic acid accelerates the dissolution rate in the exposed area relative to the unexposed area, effectively increasing the developer selectivity. ESCAP-type resists are by far the most widely used resists for DUV 248-nm lithography.
Some have found applications in EUV lithography as well.<sup>422</sup>
--[p346]-- A very prominent example of this type of resist is a copolymer of 4- hydroxystyrene with tert-butyl ester-protected 4-hydroxystyrene (TBEST) (LII) (see Scheme 4.55), developed at IBM and sold by Shipley Company under the brand name of APEX-E™. The dissolution properties of this resist system are presented in Section 3.8 of this book.
--[p347]-- The poly(hydoxystyrene-co-tert-butyl acrylate) copolymer can be readily prepared by direct radical copolymerization of 4-hydroxystyrene with tertbutyl acrylate or alternatively via radical copolymerization of 4-acetoxystyrene with the t-butyl acrylate, followed by selective hydrolysis of the acetate group with ammonium hydroxide (see Scheme 4.57).<sup>421</sup>

===== [p423-424] Chapter 5 Theory of Block Copolymer Self-assembly Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 5.2.2.2 Block copolymers via stable free-radical polymerization (SFRP) (7块) =====
--[p424]-- Here, BCPs are prepared by nitroxidemediated polymerization of the first monomer, yielding the starting block, which is either isolated or used in situ.<sup>183</sup> The addition of the second monomer to the reaction mixture, with or without the presence of a solvent to aid solubility, and heating the latter, yields the desired BCP in a manner that is similar to the ATRP process, but with one interesting exception that unlike ATRP, the first block can be characterized and stored before the controlled radical polymerization of the second monomer. --[p423]-- 5.2.2.2 Block copolymers via stable free-radical polymerization (SFRP)
Stable free-radical polymerization comprises polymerization techniques mediated by nitroxide radicals (structures VII to XI). These nitroxide radicals mediate reversible deactivation of the growing chains through covalent bond formation.
--[p423]-- It must be mentioned that the use of TEMPO in radical polymerization presents some problems, chief among which, include the necessity to carry out the reaction at high temperature (125–145°C) for a long reaction time (24–72 h) and incompatibility with many important monomer families.<sup>179</sup> Some of these problems are obviated with the use of alicyclic nitroxides such as structures IX to XI.<sup>180,181,182</sup> Unlike TEMPO, which possesses two quaternary a-carbons, these nitroxides possess a hydrogen atom on one of the a-carbons, making them more tolerant than TEMPO to a much wider selection of monomers, including acrylates, arylamides, 1,3-dienes, and acrylonitrile-based monomers.

===== [p238-239] Theory of Photochemical and Radiochemical Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 4.2.5 Spectral sensitization (6块) =====
--[p239]-- As a practical matter, spectral sensitization always extends the absorption range of the system to longer wavelengths, corresponding to lower excitation energies. 51
--[p238]-- This spectral mismatch between the emission lines of the mercury arc lamp and the poly(vinyl cinnamate) absorption is the principal cause of the low sensitivity of unsensitized poly(vinyl cinnamate) resist.<sup>50</sup>
45. N. Kim and S. E. Webber, “Effect of molecular weight on triplet exciton processes. 4. Delayed emission of solid poly(2-vinylnaphthalene),” Macromolecules 13, 1233–1236 (1980).
46. A.
--[p239]-- It is possible to improve the light-collecting ability of the system through energy transfer by incorporating into the system (such as a resist) a component that absorbs the available energy efficiently and transmits it to the reactants. This process, which extends the action spectrum of the system, is referred to as spectral sensitization or photosensitization. The effect of sensitizers on the performance of a system can be quite dramatic.
--[p238]-- 4.2.5 Spectral sensitization
Spectral sensitization of a resist system provides a means of utilizing radiative energy that is not directly absorbed by the reactants. Given that the most common lithographic exposure sources emit within rather narrow wavebands, resists, in particular, photoresists, which do not absorb in one of these emission regions, will not respond to the radiation.
--[p238]-- A very good example of a resist system whose absorption spectrum is mismatched with the emission spectra of the exposure source is illustrated by poly(vinyl cinnamate) under UV exposure from a medium-pressure mercury arc lamp. The strongest absorption peak of the poly(vinyl cinnamate) spectrum occurs around the DUV region (around 250 nm), missing most of the strong emission lines of the mercury arc lamp, which occur around 360 nm.

===== [p26-26] MOLECULAR THEORY OF LITHOGRAPHY > 1.3 Advanced Lithographic Patterning Techniques and Imaging Mechanisms (2块) =====
--[p26]-- 1.3 Advanced Lithographic Patterning Techniques and Imaging Mechanisms
Shown in Fig. 1.2 are various advanced lithographic patterning techniques that are currently being used to fabricate integrated circuit devices. We will briefly review their main attributes in this section as a way of providing necessary background information that will be required in our analysis of their chemistries in subsequent chapters.
Shown in Fig.
--[p26]-- 1.3 are lithographic imaging mechanisms underlying the lithographic techniques shown in Fig. 1.2. There are three main categories of lithographic imaging mechanisms: (1) photo- and radiochemical imaging mechanisms, (2) block copolymer self-assembly imaging mechanisms, and (3) imprint imaging mechanisms. We provide the theoretical basis of these imaging mechanisms in Chapters 4, 5 and 6, respectively.

--[p103]-- In reality, diffusivity depends on temperature and is intimately related to the extent of amplification. The connection between diffusivity and the extent of chemical amplification stems from the fact that as the amplification reaction proceeds in the specific case of positive resists based on protection group chemistry, the deprotection events of polymers generate volatile species that leave the film, resulting in a decrease in film thickness and an increase in free volume.

--[p105]-- Acid losses occurring between exposure and PEB lead to delay time effects, exemplified by the diffusion of atmospheric base contaminants into the top surface of the resist, and resulting in neutralization of the acid there, accompanied by a reduced amplification reaction for positive resists. In the severest case, an insoluble skin referred to as “T-top” forms during development.
--[p105]-- As mentioned above, acid loss from the resist film negatively impacts the chemical amplification reaction in the sense that such lost acid does not contribute to the desired reaction. Two basic acid-loss processes have been identified: those that occur between exposure and PEB and those that occur during the PEB.

===== [p255-257] Theory of Photochemical and Radiochemical Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 4.3.1 Radiation-induced crosslinking imaging mechanisms (13块) =====
--[p255]-- 4.3.1 Radiation-induced crosslinking imaging mechanisms
--[p257]-- Although charged-particle radiation-induced polymerization has been demonstrated primarily for curing applications, the applications of polymerization-mediated crosslinking in lithographic imaging have been weighted primarily in the direction of photoradiation. For this reason, the discussion in this section is devoted primarily to photoinduced polymerization crosslinking processes used in lithographic imaging applications.
Resier has provided an excellent overview of the photochemistry of these processes.<sup>102</sup>
--[p256]-- Bitumen of Judea is a tar-like petroleum substance that has been recovered in chunks from the Dead Sea since Egyptian times and has been used for embalming mummies, as a building material, and as a black varnish material. It has the peculiar property of softening when heated but hardening when exposed to light— essential properties of a negative resist.
--[p257]-- As alluded to above and described below, in crosslinking resists, radiation-induced changes in solubility are brought about by the formation of a three-dimensional network from an ensemble of linear polymeric chains. A similar result can be achieved by radiation-induced polymerization of monomers in the presence of polyfunctional components.
--[p256]-- Okoroanyanwu, Chemistry and Lithography, SPIE Press, Bellingham, Washington, Chapter 2 (2010).
99. ibid.
100. M. S. Barger and W. B. White, The Daguerreotype: Nineteenth Century Technology and Modern Science, Johns Hopkins University Press, Baltimore, pp. 19–20 (1991).
101. C. G. Willson, R. A. Dammel, and A. Reiser, “Photoresist materials: A historical perspective,” Proc. SPIE 3050, 38–51 (1997).
--[p256]-- It is soluble in lavender oil, and highquality films of it on a variety of substrates such as polished pewter and glass can be coated from lavender solution, as Nicéphore Niépce, the inventor of photography and photolithography, discovered.<sup>100</sup> He coated it on a polished pewter plate and projected onto it an image of his courtyard in Chalon-sur-Saône on a bright sunny day, with the aid of a camera obscura.
--[p256]-- Next, he developed the image by immersing the exposed bitumen- of-Judea-coated pewter plate in lavender oil, which washed away the unexposed part of the bitumen film, revealing to varying degrees the surface of the pewter, while leaving intact the hardened (crosslinked) exposed parts of the bitumen of Judea resist. In this way, Niepce was able to capture and record the image of his courtyard.
--[p255]-- In general, the reactions that generate crosslinks in radiation-sensitive resist materials made of organic polymers, complexes of organic polymers and inorganic metal oxides, complexes of organic polymers and fullerenes, and metal oxides, are classified into two types: (1) those where crosslinks are formed by the direct reaction of an excited molecule or group, and (2) those where crosslinks are formed through the action of a radiation-generated reactive species in the ground state.<sup>97</sup> Below we discuss representative resist systems utilizing the radiation-induced crosslinking imaging mechanism. But first, we present a few preliminary remarks on the history of the development of these mechanisms.

--[p256]-- It is fully well accepted that very few photochemical and radiochemical reactions have led to such important technical applications as the insolubilization of radiation-sensitive coatings by photochemically or radiochemically induced crosslinking. A review of such materials must perforce start in the ancient Egyptian era, and leap forward after many thousands of years to arrive at the work of Joseph Nicéphore Niépce around 1824, when he introduced this application to lithography.
--[p256]-- The photoinsolubilization of a bitumen layer afforded him the possibility of etching the unprotected parts of a support, a discovery that opened the way to modern lithographic techniques,<sup>98</sup> as briefly described below. Using bitumen of Judea, he succeeded in making the first permanent photograph of nature<sup>99</sup> using photolithographic techniques.
--[p257]-- Such results have found application in the field of lithographic imaging, especially with the aid of image amplification based on crosslinking, which results from the immobilization of large molecules by a small number of crosslinks. In radiation-induced polymerization processes, the source of amplification is the chain reaction of the polymerization process.

===== [p117-118] Chapter 2 Theory of the Lithographic Process > 2.6.6 Stochastic modeling of latent image formation in resists (5块) =====
--[p117]-- This quantized nature of light, atoms, and molecules lends itself to a probabilistic description of the nature of lithography and involves the use of random variables and probability density functions and distributions, which we can characterize in terms of moments such as mean and variance to describe the expected statistical fluctuations or most probable outcome of a lithographic event.<sup>186</sup> This approach becomes all the more relevant in lithography in regimes where the length scales are within nanoscale dimensions (≤10 nm) and where the number of exposure photons or charged particles, including electrons and ions, is extremely low.
--[p117]-- 2.6.6 Stochastic modeling of latent image formation in resists
The premise of the analysis in this section is the recognition and usage of the fact that light is quantized into discrete photons, and matter and chemical concentrations are quantized into spatially distributed discrete molecules and atoms.
--[p117]-- An excellent treatment of stochastic modeling of resist chemistry has been provided by Mack;<sup>187</sup> here, we highlight the most relevant results on photon shot noise, photon absorption and exposure, acid diffusion, acid-catalyzed reaction– diffusion, acid-catalyzed deprotection, and acid–base quenching reactions in resist exposure.

===== [p451-452] Chapter 5 Theory of Block Copolymer Self-assembly Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 5.4.3 Topographical patterning with grapho-epitaxy (5块) =====
--[p452]-- Alignment of perpendicular cylinders of PS in poly(styrene-b-isoprene-bstyrene) (PS-b-PI-b-PS) diblock has been demonstrated in silicon substrates patterned with 60-nm deep and 166- to 433-nm wide channels.<sup>274</sup> Facetted sapphire wafer surfaces have also been demonstrated to template the orientation of cylinders in PS-b-PEO, PS-b-P2VP, or PS-b-P4VP diblocks with a PS matrix.<sup>275</sup> Additionally, grapho-epitaxy of spherical domains in a monolayer of PS-b-P2VP diblock has been shown to be induced by the presence of lithographically channel-patterned silicon substrate.<sup>276,277</sup>
--[p451]-- Perpendicularly aligned lamellae were also observed by Rockford et al.<sup>272</sup> on topographically patterned Si (1 1 3) surfaces with 60-nm periodicity. Alignment of the stripes was observed when the BCP domain was commensurate with that of the substrate, but not otherwise.
--[p452]-- Alignment of perpendicular lamellae formed by a symmetric PS-b-PMMA diblock on a lithographically patterned polystyrene brush has been investigated, and it has been shown that the diblock lamellae was able to follow the patterned circular features despite the distortion caused by the bending of the lamellae.<sup>273</sup>
--[p451]-- 5.4.3 Topographical patterning with grapho-epitaxy
Patterned substrate topography is another method for manipulating BCP film morphology. Through the use of substrate topography, diverse BCP film morphological patterns with a range of length scales can be created.
--[p451]-- The ordering of symmetric poly(styrene-b-n-butyl methacrylate) (PS-b-PnBMA) diblocks on corrugated substrates has been investigated using the faceted (1 1 3) surface of silicon,<sup>271</sup> exhibiting sawtooth profile corrugations of 2-nm amplitude and periods in the 100-nm range, where it was observed that islands of PnBMA were in registry with the peaks in the substrate, in contrast to the random arrangement of such islands on flat substrates.

--[p71]-- The combination of the source and the condenser lens is called the illumination system; its purpose is to deliver light to the mask and subsequently to the objective lens with sufficient intensity, proper directionality and spectral characteristics, and adequate uniformity across the field. One can define an ideal imaging lens as one that produces an image that is identical to the Fourier transform of the light distribution entering the lens.

--[p458]-- 5.5 Lithographic Patterning with Block Copolymers
The main applications of BCPs in lithography include their use as lithographic etch masks, as templates for patterning inorganic and biological materials, and as templates for inorganic materials synthesis. Next, we review these three applications of BCPs in lithography.<sup>298</sup>

===== [p205-206] Chapter 3 Theory of Molecular Interactions in Lithography > 3.6.1.3 Free energy of mixing resist polymeric solute with developer solvent (13块) =====
--[p205]-- It thus follows that the dissolution of the resist polymer in nonpolar solvents is driven more by the enthalpic term.
By definition, the chemical potential of a solvent in a solution relative to that in the pure solvent is expressed as
$$
--[p206]-- \ln a _ { 1 } = \ln ( 1 - \Phi _ { 2 } ) + \left( 1 - \frac { 1 } { x } \right) \Phi _ { 2 } + \chi _ { 1 2 } \Phi _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } .\tag{3.164}
$$
Similarly, we determine the activity of the resist polymeric solute from Eq. (3.156) as
$$
\ln a _ { 2 } = \ln ( \Phi _ { 2 } ) + ( 1 - x ) ( 1 - \Phi _ { 2 } ) + \chi _ { 1 2 } \Phi _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } .\tag{3.165}
$$
--[p206]-- Recall that the change in the chemical potential for a nonideal solution such as that of resist polymer in an aqueous solvent is defined in terms of activity a (instead of concentration) as
$$
\mu _ { 1 } - \mu _ { 1 } ^ { \circ } = R T \mathrm { ~ l n ~ } a _ { 1 } .\tag{3.163}
$$
Comparing Eq. (3.163) with Eq. (3.162), we can thus determine that the activity of the developer solvent in a solution of the resist polymers is given by
$$
--[p205]-- \Delta G _ { \mathrm { m i x } } = R T ( \chi _ { 1 } n _ { 1 } \Phi _ { 2 } + n _ { 1 } \ln \Phi _ { 1 } + n _ { 2 } \ln \Phi _ { 2 } ) .\tag{3.156}
$$
Equation (3.156) describes two aspects of the dissolution process, shown schematically in Fig. 3.15, and involving both entropic and enthalpic contributions as stated above. The entropic terms are the first two terms on the right-hand side of the equation, while the last term on the right-hand side is the enthalpic term.
--[p205]-- 3.6.1.3 Free energy of mixing resist polymeric solute with developer solvent
To determine the Gibbs free energy change $\Delta G _ { \mathrm { m i x } }$ for the dissolution of a polymeric resist solute in the developer solvent, we use the standard thermodynamic equation
$$
\Delta G = \Delta H - T \Delta S ,\tag{3.155}
$$
where $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$ stand for enthalpy and entropy change, respectively. Substituting Eqs. (3.144) and (3.150) into Eq. (3.155), we obtain
$$
--[p205]-- \mu _ { 1 } - \mu _ { 1 } ^ { \circ } = R T \left[ \frac { n _ { 1 } } { \phi _ { 1 } } \left( \frac { \partial \phi _ { 1 } } { \partial n _ { 1 } } \right) _ { n _ { 2 } } + l n \ \phi _ { 1 } + \frac { n _ { 2 } } { \phi _ { 2 } } \left( \frac { \partial \phi _ { 2 } } { \partial n _ { 1 } } \right) _ { n _ { 2 } } + \chi _ { 1 2 } \phi _ { 2 } + \chi _ { 1 2 } n _ { 1 } \left( \frac { \partial \phi _ { 2 } } { \partial n _ { 1 } } \right) _ { n _ { 2 } } \right] .\tag{3.158}
$$
--[p206]-- \partial \ln \Phi _ { 1 } = { \frac { \partial \Phi _ { 1 } } { \Phi _ { 1 } } } ,\tag{3.161}
$$
we can rewrite Eq. (3.158) to obtain
$$
\pmb { \mu } _ { 1 } - \pmb { \mu } _ { 1 } ^ { \circ } = R T \bigg [ \ln ( 1 - \Phi _ { 2 } ) + \bigg ( 1 - \frac { 1 } { x } \bigg ) \Phi _ { 2 } + \chi _ { 1 2 } \Phi _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } \bigg ] .\tag{3.162}
$$
--[p205]-- The partial derivatives of Eq. (3.156) can be evaluated from the definition of volume fraction. Recalling that volume fractions can be written in terms of the molar volume ratio $x ,$ defined in Eq. (3.125), such that
$$
\Phi _ { 1 } = \frac { n _ { 1 } } { n _ { 1 } + x n _ { 2 } } ,\tag{3.159}
$$
$$
\Phi _ { 2 } = \frac { x n _ { 2 } } { n _ { 1 } + x n _ { 2 } } ,\tag{3.160}
$$
and making use of the relation
$$
--[p205]-- \mu _ { 1 } - \mu _ { 1 } ^ { \circ } = \left( \frac { \partial [ G _ { \mathrm { s o l n } } - G _ { 1 } ^ { \circ } ] } { \partial n _ { 1 } } \right) _ { T , P , n _ { 2 } } = \left( \frac { \partial \Delta G _ { \mathrm { m i x } } } { \partial n _ { 1 } } \right) _ { T , P , n _ { 2 } } .\tag{3.157}
$$

$$
--[p205]-- From the entropic terms, it can be seen that there is very little driving force for the mixing of polymer with solvent if the chain is large because its contribution is reduced by the degree of polymerization of the chain. It is this weak entropic contribution to the mixing process that is responsible for the extreme difficulty in mixing different polymer types in polymer blends, and also that reduces the entropic driving force for the formation of polymer solution.
--[p206]-- Negative values of $\chi _ { 1 2 }$ are typical of systems in which either the resist polymer or the developer solvent is polar, which increases the attractive interactions between the polymer and solvent molecules on mixing.<sup>106</sup> This is indeed the case with many positive resist polymers whose functional groups (typically esters and carbonates) are, upon exposure and baking, converted from nonpolar to polar groups (typically carboxylic acid and hydroxyl) that are readily attracted by their corresponding counterions of polar TMAH solution in water.
Resist dissolution in the developer solvent will only be favored thermodynamically (i.e., $\Delta G < 0 )$ at those temperatures and compositions for which the negative terms in the free energy expression, Eq.
--[p206]-- (3.156), are numerically greater than the entropy of mixing. Therefore, the condition that favors thermodynamic or equilibrium dissolution of the resist polymer in the developer solvent is given by
$$
- ( n _ { 1 } \ln \Phi _ { 1 } + n _ { 2 } \ln \Phi _ { 2 } ) > \chi _ { 1 } n _ { 1 } \Phi _ { 2 } .\tag{3.166}
$$

===== [p444-446] Chapter 5 Theory of Block Copolymer Self-assembly Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 5.4.1 Neutral brushes for perpendicular alignment (10块) =====
--[p444]-- When they incorporated short PTFE segments into the diblock poly(styrene-b-methyl methacrylate) film, these random copolymers self-assembled to the free surface due to their lower-surface-energy chain ends, and thereby became anchored to the polymer–air interface, creating a neutrality condition. Samples with the neutral brush at only one of the interfaces did not show defined perpendicular lamellar orientation.
--[p446]-- Controlling the surface tension at the top surface of a BCP has been shown to be effective in driving perpendicular orientation of BCP domain nanostructures. Exploiting this effect, Ryu et al.<sup>252</sup> used the surfactant oleic acid, which segregates to the air interface and interacts preferentially with PMMA, to drive the perpendicular orientation of lamellar or cylindrical domains in PS-b-PMMA diblocks.
--[p444]-- At the silicon–substrate interface, poly(styrene-r-methyl methacrylate) random copolymer chains of appropriate composition were end-grafted to the surface, forming a dense “brush” that could not diffuse into the cast diblock film. They end-functionalized additional poly(styrene-r-methyl methacrylate) random copolymer chains of the same composition with short poly(tetrafluoroethylene) (PTFE) segments.
--[p444]-- 5.4.1 Neutral brushes for perpendicular alignment
As discussed above, the orientation of domains in BCP thin films is highly dependent on the surface energy boundary conditions imposed on the system. In general, the orientation of diblock copolymer domains in thin films is parallel to the surface because of the preferential segregation of one of the components to the interface.
--[p446]-- Another approach commonly used for tuning the surface energy of the substrate involves the use of methyl silesequioxane, an organosilicate polymer, which, upon high temperature bake during the thermal curing step, undergoes complete condensation of the silicate cage and an accompanying increase in the hydrophobicity of the substrate.<sup>253</sup>
It should be mentioned that aligning all of the lamella to be vertical is only the first part of the problem.
The other equally important part of the problem is to direct the self-assembly with guide patterns.
--[p444]-- Removing these preferential interactions, for example, by the use of surface fields that are neutral with respect to each of the blocks, causes the copolymer domains to orient perpendicular to the surface and the substrate interfaces.<sup>233,234,235</sup> This perpendicular alignment of the microdomains is favored over the parallel arrangement because of configurational restrictions that force the diblock copolymer molecules to orient parallel to nonpreferential interfaces.<sup>236</sup> This effect has been exploited by Huang et al.<sup>237,238,239</sup> to realize a surface-perpendicular orientation in both lamellar and cylindrical poly(styrene-b-methyl methacrylate) systems.
--[p444]-- They accomplished this by fabricating double neutral surfaces from random copolymers of poly(styrene-r-methyl methacrylate) of carefully tuned composition of monomers identical to the diblock copolymer,<sup>240,241,242</sup> and localizing them at the film substrate–air interfaces through the following means.
--[p445]-- Subsequent research in this area has exploited the use of third monomers to crosslink polymer thin films and hence modify wetting properties,<sup>243</sup> or to attach the random copolymers to the surface through multiple graft points using various covalent chemistries,<sup>244,245,246</sup> including photopatternable ones.<sup>247,248</sup> These approaches have been very thoroughly examined for end hydroxy-functionalized poly(styrene-r-methyl methacrylate) (HO-PS-r-PMMA) or random copolymers poly(styrene-r-methyl methacrylate-r-2-hydroxyethyl methacrylate) (PS-r-PMMA-r-PHEMA) and poly(styrene-r-methyl methacrylate-r-glycidyl methacrylate) (PS-r-PMMA-r-PGMA).<sup>249</sup>
--[p445]-- Investigations using small-angle neutron scattering and cross-sectional transmission electron microscopy of the alignment of PS-b-PMMA lamellae in thin films on substrates with varying surface energy, controlled by the composition of a PS-r-PMMA copolymer, revealed the existence of a mixed lamellar orientation when the difference in the interfacial energies between each block and the substrate was not strong enough to force parallel lamellae throughout the film.<sup>250</sup>
--[p446]-- Nealey and co-workers<sup>251</sup> have synthesized random copolymers poly (styrene-r-2-vinyl pyridine-2-hydroxyethyl methacrylate) (PS-r-P2VP-r-PHEMA) and systematically investigated their utility in controlling the orientation of the BCP poly(styrene-b-2-vinyl pyridine). Neutral surfaces have also been reported with blends of hydroxyl-functionalized homopolymers and the corresponding diblock to ensure compatibility of BCPs of PS-b-PMMA and PS-b-P2VP lamellae.

--[p143]-- 2.8.3.2 Effects of electron beam curing
--[p143]-- Electron-beam-induced crosslinking of the resist polymer increases the bulk modulus and bulk toughness of the feature pattern, as well as the interfacial toughness of the substrate–resist polymer bond, thereby ensuring that patterned resist features will be better able to withstand bending, breaking, collapse, and mechanical deformation of the features during etch processing.<sup>284</sup> In addition, crosslinking and decomposing the functional groups in the resist polymer make the patterned features more impervious to etchant species, thereby improving the etch stability of the cured resist. ===== [p399-400] Chapter 5 Theory of Block Copolymer Self-assembly Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 5.2.1.1.1 Initiation (6块) =====
--[p400]-- The choice of an appropriate anionic initiator for the polymerization of a particular type of vinyl monomer is a judicious affair because the characteristics of carbanions differ significantly by their nucleophilicity and depend on the solvent polarity. The rate of initiation is a strong function of the aggregation state of the anion and the intermolecular interactions of ion pairs that are formed through opening of the vinyl bond of the monomer and the formation of new propagating species.
--[p400]-- A major requirement for the initiator is that it must react rapidly with the monomer at the initiation step of the polymerization and, specifically, must have a faster reaction rate than the propagation step. This ensures the formation of polymers with narrow molecular weight distribution since all of the active sites start polymerizing the monomer almost simultaneously. We will explore this idea in Section 5.2.1.2 on anionic polymerization kinetics.
--[p399]-- It should be pointed out that in undergoing addition across the double bond of the monomer, the ion pair adds in such a manner that the anion from the initiator gets attached to the carbon atom farthest from the electronwithdrawing group (R<sup>0</sup>), i.e., the carbon atom that possesses the lower electron density. It should also be noted that during initiation and subsequent steps, the active site at the end of the chain is accompanied by a counterion.
--[p400]-- The initiation reaction is generally fast and is not reflected in the overall rate of the polymerization for well-controlled anionic vinyl polymerization reactions. The propagation step predominantly controls the kinetics of the polymerization.
--[p400]-- However, some initiators initiate vinyl monomer slowly over a period of time or with an induction period and have significant influence on the overall reaction rate; they can also affect the molecular weight distribution of the polymers formed.<sup>100</sup>
--[p399]-- 5.2.1.1.1 Initiation
Initiation occurs by the dissociation or heterolytic cleavage of the initiator into metallic cation and corresponding radical anion, resulting from the donation of electron from the metal to the monomer, followed by the addition of the initiator across the double bond of the monomer. In polymerizations initiated by pure metals such as sodium, the initiation occurs when an electron is transferred from the sodium atom to the monomer, generating a radical anion.

--[p422]-- To produce well-defined BCPs with the ATRP technique, two fundamental criteria must be fulfilled: (1) the chain end of the first block must be fully functionalized with the appropriate halogen atom, such that each chain must be able to initiate polymerization of the second monomer; and (2) initiation of the second monomer must be faster than its propagation.
--[p422]-- 5.2.2.1 Block copolymers via atom transfer polymerization (ATRP)
In ATRP, radicals are generated through a reversible redox process, catalyzed by transition metal complexes of Cu, Ru, Fe, Ni, Rh, and Pd, such as, for example, CuX/bipyridine, that undergo a one-electron oxidation with the abstraction of a halogen atom from the dormant species. The transition metal compound acts as a halogen atom carrier.

The most widely used development rate models are: the kinetic development rate model,<sup>247</sup> the enhanced kinetic development rate model,<sup>248</sup> and the lumped parameter model<sup>249</sup> proposed by Mack. We briefly outline their derivation here.<sup>250</sup>
--[p132]-- 2.7.5.2 Development rate models
Development rate models seek to determine the dissolution rate as a function of the PAC or photoacid concentration within the resist after PEB. Many development rate models have been proposed over the years;<sup>245</sup> a few of them are reviewed here. The first development rate model was proposed by Dill and his co-workers and is of the form<sup>246</sup>
$$
R = e ^ { E _ { 1 } + E _ { 2 } m + E _ { 3 } m ^ { 2 } } ,\tag{2.173}
$$
--[p133]-- It is assumed that the solvent development of a conventional positive resist occurs in three steps: (1) diffusion of developer from the bulk solution to the surface of the resist, (2) reaction of the developer with the resist, and (3) diffusion of the product back into the solution. It is also assumed that the last step, diffusion of the dissolved resist into solution, occurs very rapidly and therefore can be ignored.<sup>251</sup>

===== [p322-322] Theory of Photochemical and Radiochemical Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 4.4.1 Photolysis and radiolysis imaging mechanisms (5块) =====
--[p322]-- Each imaging process that is based on photolysis proceeds via two essential steps: (1) a photochemical or radiochemical reaction whereby the PACs, PAGs, and sensitizers absorb the exposure photons or interact with the secondary electrons generated from the resist matrix resin and become excited (as in UV lithography) and are photolyzed or radiolyzed; and (2) a stabilization and/or development step.
--[p322]-- Two main distinct reaction mechanisms that underlie photolysis in resists include: dissolution inhibition and deprotection. Resists based on these two photolytic reaction mechanisms can be divided into two broad categories: non–chemical amplification photolytic resists, and chemical amplification photolytic resists. Presented next are illustrative examples of resists in these two categories.

--[p322]-- 4.4.1 Photolysis and radiolysis imaging mechanisms
Lithographic imaging mechanisms based on photolysis and radiolysis involves the photo- and radiation-induced decomposition of PACs, PAGs, sensitizers, etc., leading to the generation of acids and radicals, which catalyze the photolysis of specific functional groups in the resist polymers or nanoparticles.

--[p271]-- 4.3.1.2.2.1 Condensation/intermolecular dehydration imaging mechanisms

--[p272]-- Note that in step 1 photolysis of the acid generator produces a latent image of acid, while in step 2, acid-catalyzed thermolysis of the acetate produces a carbocation. --[p129]-- 2.7.5 Kinetics and mechanism of resist polymer dissolution
Given the fact that the matrix resins of resists are comprised largely of polymers, it is expected that the dissolution of resists will generally follow the same patterns as polymers with fairly high molecular weight. During the 1960s, Ueberreiter and Asmussen<sup>216</sup> investigated the dissolution of high-molecularweight polymers. They found that polymer dissolution occurs in two stages.
--[p129]-- Ueberreiter found that in the polymer systems he studied, the diffusion of the solvent across the gel layer is the rate-determining step (i.e., it is the slowest of all of the involved steps),<sup>218</sup> and in those cases solvent uptake and the inward movement of the glass–gel interface depend on the square root of time, as is characteristic of Fickian diffusion.
--[p129]-- In other systems, the processes in the glass–gel interface are rate determining, and solvent uptake and interface movement are linear functions of time. Alfrey et al.<sup>220</sup> termed this Case II diffusion or polymer-relaxation-controlled mass transfer.<sup>221</sup> A third type of diffusion in polymers is called Super Case II and shows a power-law dependence on time. Figure 2.19 shows a schematic of diffusant timeconcentration profiles for the three diffusion modes.

--[p129]-- In the first stage, solvent penetrates into the glassy polymer, forming a gel layer that separates the polymer matrix from the pure solvent. In the second stage, the polymer coils disentangle from the gel, eventually diffusing into the liquid. Three distinct phases in the steady state dissolution process are<sup>217</sup>
Glassy polymer | Swollen gel | Solvent or solution.

--[p246]-- 4.2.8.1 Backbone scission and crosslinking
The radiation chemistry of resist polymers is governed by two main processes: backbone scission and crosslinking. Whether the polymer will act as a positive or negative resist resin under lithographic imaging through radiation chemistry depends on whether backbone scissioning or a crosslinking process is dominant.<sup>66</sup>
Backbone scission leads to polymer degradation and to a decrease of the molecular weight of the polymer.

===== [p469-469] Chapter 6 Theory of Imprint Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 6.3.2 Photoimprint lithographic imaging mechanism (3块) =====
--[p469]-- In principle, the imprinted features are true replicas of the master/template/stamp, and any-sized pattern can be made.
30. S. Franssila, Introduction to Microfabrication, John Wiley & Sons, New York, Chapter 18 (2010).
--[p469]-- 6.3.2 Photoimprint lithographic imaging mechanism
The photoimprint lithographic imaging mechanism is based on a pressuredriven flow of photocurable monomers, oligomers, crosslinking agents and additives that is induced by pressing a template/master/stamp containing the features to be printed against the liquid resist mixture composition, such that the latter fill the cavities in the master, forming an inverse replica of the master once the resist liquid solution is polymerized and crosslinked.
--[p469]-- The imprinting or embossing temperature is typically at room temperature, and the required pressure is very minimal, given the low viscosity of the resist solution. The imprint time can be on the order of one second or less. Demolding or de-embossing takes place after photocuring. The photocurable layer must be exposed and cured through the template, unless the substrate is transmissive to UV light.<sup>32</sup> A schematic for the PIL process is shown in Chapter 1 [Fig. 1.11(b)].

--[p333]-- 4.4.1.2 Chemical amplification mechanism

===== [p130-130] Chapter 2 Theory of the Lithographic Process > 2.7.5.1 Dissolution mechanism of phenolic resists (4块) =====
--[p130]-- And lastly, Choi and Cho adopted and extended the gel layer concept of Ueberreiter–Asmussen to the dissolution of phenolic resist polymers, whereby the assumption is made that the diffusion of the base and deprotonation of the phenolic group of the polymer take place simultaneously in the gel layer, following which are the rapid rearrangement and transfer of polymer chain into solution when deprotonation at the front edge of the gel zone reaches a critical degree.<sup>243,244</sup> Although the above models have been successful in explaining different aspects of phenolic resist polymer dissolution, we will focus in the next section on the most popular development rate models used in lithographic simulations.
--[p130]-- This deprotonation of the phenolic groups continues until the solubility limit of the phenolate in the polymer matrix is exceeded, at which point a new phase, called the penetration zone, is formed from which the polymer is dissolved.
--[p130]-- 2.7.5.1 Dissolution mechanism of phenolic resists
The mechanism of phenolic polymer resist dissolution has been a hotly contested and debated concept. Most researchers, however, agree that the dissolution mechanism of phenolic polymers depends on a number of variables, including polymer molecular weight,<sup>222,223,224,225</sup> developer base concentration<sup>226,227,228,229,230</sup> and composition ,<sup>231,232,233,234</sup> base cation size,<sup>235,236,237,238</sup> etc.
Many models have been proposed to explain how this process plays out. We briefly recount the main features of each of the important models.
--[p130]-- Peppas and co-workers proposed the chain disentanglement model based on reptation theory, whereby the polymers disentangle and slither out of their matrix in some type of reptation movement in the developer at regimes well below their entanglement chain lengths.<sup>239,240</sup> Willson and co-workers proposed the critical ionization model based on the idea that a critical fraction of acidic sites on the polymer chain must ionize through equilibration of the base–acid reaction for the chain to dissolve in the aqueous developer.<sup>241,242</sup> Reiser and co-workers proposed the percolation model based on the idea that at the onset of dissolution, the base diffuses into the polymer film and converts some of the phenols into phenolates by the deprotonation of the hydroxyl groups.

--[p187]-- Hydrogen bonding is considered to be a subset of acid–base interactions since its enthalpy can be accurately described by the Drago equation.<sup>70,71</sup>
Hydrogen bonding plays a significant role in the interaction between resist polymer surfaces bearing hydroxyl, carboxyl, and amino and similar functional groups, while pure hydrocarbon polymers without the above functional groups cannot interact via hydrogen bonding.
--[p186]-- 3.4.8 Hydrogen bonding interactions
A necessary condition for the existence of hydrogen bonding<sup>68</sup> interaction within the developer solvent or within resist polymers or between resist polymers and the developer solvent and its constituents is the presence of a hydrogen atom covalently bonded to a highly electronegative element such as O, N, F, or Cl (see Fig. 3.12).
--[p186]-- These bonds are unique in that they only involve hydrogen atoms, which, because of their tendency to become positively polarized and their uniquely small size, can interact strongly with nearby electronegative atoms. The result is an effective H-mediated bond between two electronegative atoms.<sup>69</sup>
Hydrogen bonding is believed to be predominantly an electrostatic interaction.
--[p187]-- Often, solubility switching action of resists derives from the exposure- and baking-induced reactions that convert lyophilic polymers such as polyolefins, polystyrene protected with labile acidic functional groups, to hydrophilic polymers with acidic functional groups.
--[p187]-- Upon dissolution in the developer, the hydrophilic polymers with acidic functional groups are able to interact with the water and TMAH molecules of the developer via hydrogen bonding interaction, helping to maintain the solubilization of the polymers in the resist developer. As the starting and unexposed part of the resin cannot interact via hydrogen bonding with the developer and its electrolytes, it is not dissolved in the developer solution.
In this way, this difference between the starting and unexposed part of the resin with the exposed part underlies the contrast between the two areas.

--[p85]-- Resists with an imaging mechanism based only on exponential attenuation of radiation (i.e., with no mechanism for photobleaching or chemical amplification, for example) are limited to a certain maximum of allowable contrast, sidewall angle, and ultimate resolution due to the inherent absorption trade-off required when imaging into the resist film.
--[p85]-- 2.6.5 Continuum modeling of latent image formation in the resist
In the analysis in this section, we shall employ continuous mathematical functions, averaged over a sufficient number of participating entities or species in the system to describe the most likely state of the system.
--[p87]-- It should be pointed out that the basis of the resist contrast in semiconductor lithographic imaging of any resist occurs in two phases: the light (or radiation) phase and the dark phase. The light phase comprises the chemical and physical transformations taking place during the exposure processes, while the dark phase comprises the changes taking place during the post-exposure and development stages, as will be explained in the following sections.
The kinetics of the light reactions are described by the Dill model, which is discussed next.
--[p85]-- Concepts such as aerial image, latent image, chemical concentration, diffusion, reactivity, etc., are all fairly accurately described by this so-called continuum approximation, at least down to micrometer-length scales, but start to become inaccurate at nanometer-length scale.
Being radiation-sensitive, the resist film can be selectively exposed in some areas and not others, depending on the mask pattern, thus, effectively transferring the image of the mask patterns onto the resist.
--[p85]-- The transformation of the sinusoidal aerial image into the latent image by the resist and subsequently into a fairly straight-edged developed image is a highly nonlinear process, one that lies at the heart of semiconductor lithographic imaging phenomena. How effective a particular resist is in performing this transformation determines its resolution as well as its process capabilities, both of which depend on many factors, chief among which is its radiation absorption characteristics.
--[p86]-- The dimensionless product A 5 εcz is called the absorbance (formerly called the optical density) of the resist sample, and the ratio $I / I _ { 0 }$ is the transmittance T. These two quantities are related as follows:
$$
\log T = - A .\tag{2.73}
$$

===== [p96-97] Chapter 2 Theory of the Lithographic Process > 2.6.5.2.1 Post-exposure bake of DNQ resists (8块) =====
--[p96]-- The most important effects of PEB are in smoothing out standing waves in the resist through thermal-induced diffusion of photoacid in DNQ/ novolac resists and chemical amplification in chemically amplified resists.<sup>125</sup> As presented in Section 3.63, standing waves result from the interference of the incident and reflected waves from a reflective substrate, which creates a nonuniform distribution of the radiation intensity and, thus, a latent image within the resist film.
--[p97]-- The consequences of these processes manifest as resolution loss on account of uncontrolled diffusion, line edge roughness, heightened propensity to environmental poisoning (as in PEB delay stability issues), and temperature variation (measured in terms of PEB sensitivity). In the following section we examine some of these dark-phase processes and reactions that are associated with PEB.

Reaction [4.28] represents the many possible termination steps that end the reaction and set a limit to chain growth.

===== [p400-402] Chapter 5 Theory of Block Copolymer Self-assembly Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 5.2.1.1.1.1 Initiators (8块) =====
--[p400]-- 5.2.1.1.1.1 Initiators
Initiators<sup>101</sup> for the anionic polymerization of vinyl monomers can be generally categorized into three main groups: radical anions, carbanions, and oxyanions.
Table 5.2 shows the different classes of initiators that are known to initiate anionic polymerization. Organic radical anions such as sodium naphthalenide are prepared by electron exchange reaction between sodium and naphthalene.
--[p400]-- As already described above, the direct use of radical anions such as sodium naphthalenide in polar solvent for the polymerization of styrene forms dimerized bifunctional anionic propagating species during propagation.<sup>102</sup> Many aromatic hydrocarbons and a-olefins containing aromatic substitution can react with alkali metals to form radical anions.
--[p400]-- A good example is the reaction of sodium metal and 1,1-diphenylethylene (DPE), which generates a radical anion in polar solvent and, as such, is used as an initiator for anionic polymerization.<sup>104</sup>
100. D. Baskaran and A. H. E. Mueller, “Anionic Vinyl Polymerization,” in Controlled and Living Polymerizations, A. H. E. Mueller and K. Matyjaszewski, Eds., Wiley-VCH Verlag GmbH & Co. KGaA, Weinheim, pp. 1–56 (2009).
101.
--[p402]-- They are particularly efficient in nonpolar solvents in the polymerization of hydrocarbon monomers.<sup>110</sup>
Alkali metal suspensions are synthesized by dispersion of a molten alkali metal in an inert organic solvent. Grignard reagents are prepared by the reaction of magnesium turnings with an organic halide.
--[p401]-- The structure and reactivity of a carbanion also depends on the size of its countercation, as this determines the interionic distance in a contact ion pair and the extent of solvation and intermolecular association. Alkyllithiums are highly reactive and unstable in polar solvents, requiring the initiation step involving them to be carried out at low temperature $( - 7 8 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$ 109

--[p401]-- Another category of initiators for anionic polymerization is simple carbanions, especially alkyllithiums, derived directly from the reaction of alkylhalide and lithium.<sup>105,106,107,108</sup> Alkyllithiums exist mainly in aggregated form in hydrocarbons. The behavior of carbanions and their ion pairs is controlled by their solvation with solvent molecules. As such, the reactivity of carbanions differs significantly depending on the solvent polarity.
--[p400 [表]]-- The terms initiator and catalyst are often erroneously used interchangeably in polymer chemistry. In reality, the initiating species is usually not recoverable at the end of the reaction, while a catalyst is recoverable. In this book, we will strive not to propagate this error.

===== [p373-374] Theory of Photochemical and Radiochemical Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 4.4.2.2 Poly(methyl isopropenyl ketone) resists (3块) =====
--[p373]-- 4.4.2.2 Poly(methyl isopropenyl ketone) resists
Another group of positive UV resists operating on the principle of radiationinduced main-chain scission utilizes the efficient photochemistry of polymeric ketones, exemplified by poly(methyl isopropenyl ketone) (PMIPK), to effect image discrimination. Scheme 4.72 shows the photolysis of this resist.<sup>492</sup>
PMIPK is reported to be five times more sensitive than PMMA under the same exposure conditions.
--[p374]-- A major drawback of the PMIPK resist system is its relatively low plasma resistance, which is even lower than that of PMMA. An approach that has been employed to improve its etch resistance is to blend it with more resistant aromatic polymers, but this is at the expense of decreased sensitivity.<sup>495</sup>
--[p374]-- In addition, it has been reported that PMIPK can be chemically sensitized with substituted benzoic acids to yield exposure speeds that are 25 times faster than those of PMMA, depending on the exposure wavelength.<sup>493</sup> The enhanced sensitivity of PMIPK resists has been attributed to a Norrish type II process, where internal hydrogen abstraction is the primary reaction step (see Scheme 4.73).<sup>494</sup>

--[p360]-- 4.4.1.2.1.4 Acetal- and ketal-protected poly(hydroxy styrene)-based resist systems
A number of acetal- and ketal-protected poly(hydroxy styrene) resists designed for 248-nm and 193-nm imaging have been demonstrated. Characteristically, these resists deprotect at much lower temperatures than their high-temperature t-BOC-protected and tert-butyl ester-protected analogs.
--[p360]-- SPIE 3333, 73 (1998).
449. H. Ito, “Chemical Amplification Resists for Microlithography,” Adv. Polym. Sci. 173, Springer-Verlag, Berlin, p. 106 (2005).
Examples of a ketal-protected resist polymer are the ketal resist systems (KRSs) from IBM, comprising two main resists: the first is formulated with a partially 2-methoxypropyl-protected poly(p-hydroxystyrene) (MOP) (LXIV), and the second is formulated with a partially 2-benzyloxy-protected poly(phydroxystyrene) (BOP) (LXV).
These resists have been largely used in electron beam lithographic applications.
--[p360]-- Acid diffusion in the resist matrix is, after all, a thermally driven process, implying that few, if any, generated acid will be available at the resist film surface to be neutralized by airborne bases, as occurs in T-topping (or environmental poisoning). As a result, acetal- and ketal-protected polymers have greater PEB delay stability or environmental stability (less susceptibility to airborne base contamination) than their highactivation-energy counterparts.
--[p361]-- Ketal resists based on the structure in (LXIV) have been reported to have excellent resolution (,100 nm), high sensitivity ( 12 mC/cm<sup>2</sup> at 50 kV), and high contrast (.10) without the need of PEB.<sup>450</sup> However, this resist was found to have low thermal stability, excessive outgassing during exposure, and insufficient dissolution inhibition during development in the standard aqueous base developer, 0.26 N tetramethylammonium hydroxide (TMAH).<sup>451</sup> The ketal resist based on structure LXV was designed to address the above shortcomings of the resist based on LXIV, and met with somewhat reasonable success.<sup>452</sup>
450. U. Kumar, A. Pandya, R. Sinta, W.-S. Huang, R. Bantu, and A. Katnani, “Probing the environmental stability and bake latitudes of acetal vs.
--[p360]-- While the majority of chemical amplification resists require PEB to accelerate the acid-catalyzed reactions, deprotection of acetal- and ketalprotected resist polymers proceeds at room temperature as soon as acid is generated during irradiation. At such a low temperature, the diffusion of the radiation-induced acid is limited to a rather short diffusion length, much shorter in fact than that of the high-activation-energy t-BOC and tert-butyl ester-protected resist polymers.
--[p360]-- Acetal- and ketal-protected resist polymers, however, tend to have poor hydrolytic and storage stability. They also tend to outgas more than their high-deprotection-temperature counterparts. In addition, they tend to suffer from excessive standing-wave problems given their rather low deprotection temperature; thus, little or no thermally driven diffusion of the photoacids occurs to smooth out the standing waves.

===== [p302-303] Theory of Photochemical and Radiochemical Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 4.3.3 Radiation-initiated polymerization imaging mechanisms (4块) =====
--[p303]-- Plambeck<sup>242</sup> invented the photopolymer printing plate most likely sometime in the early 1950s but was granted the patent in 1956. This was followed in rapid succession by the patents of Leekely and Sorenson<sup>243</sup> in 1956 and by Hoerner and Olsen<sup>244</sup> in 1958. All of the early work and almost all of the systems currently in use are based on free-radical polymerization.
Recently, cationic ring-opening polymerization has been developed to the point where it offers some distinct advantages.<sup>245</sup>
--[p302]-- Radiation- or photoinitiated polymerization may be considered to proceed in four distinct steps: (1) the production of the primary initiating species, (2) the initiation of the chain reaction, (3) the propagation of the chain, and (4) the removal of the reaction species.
The earliest reports on the use of photoinitiated polymerization for the purpose of imaging were by Eggert et al.<sup>239</sup> in 1938, Morton<sup>240</sup> in 1949, and
Oster et al.<sup>241</sup> in 1957.
--[p302]-- 4.3.3 Radiation-initiated polymerization imaging mechanisms
The polymerization of unsaturated resist monomers can be radiation- or photoinitiated by free radicals, ionic species, or radical ions. The vast majority of commercialized systems are based on photoinitiated free radicals.
--[p302]-- Due to the chain character of the polymerization process, the quantum yields, defined as monomer molecules converted per absorbed photons, can reach very high values, and high sensitivities are possible with these processes in the absence of inhibition reactions.<sup>238</sup>

===== [p304-304] Theory of Photochemical and Radiochemical Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 4.3.3.1.1 Photogeneration of radicals (2块) =====
--[p304]-- 4.3.3.1.1 Photogeneration of radicals
Photoinitiation is the first step in the formation of free radicals from photoinitiators (molecules capable of forming radicals on irradiation). Most photoinitiators in use today are based on one of two mechanisms: photofragmentation and photoinduced hydrogen abstraction.<sup>248</sup>
In photofragmentation, radicals are formed by breaking a covalent bond in the initiator I (Reaction [4.24]):
$$
--[p304]-- I \stackrel { h \nu } { \longrightarrow } R _ { 1 } ^ { \bullet } + R _ { 2 } ^ { \bullet } .
$$
In photoinduced hydrogen abstraction, the excited initiator I<sup>\*</sup> reacts with a hydrogen donor (coinitiator) to produce free radicals (Reactions [4.24] and [4.25]):
$$
I { \stackrel { h \nu } { \longrightarrow } } I ^ { * } ,\tag{[4.29]}
$$
$$
I ^ { * } + H D  I H ^ { \bullet } + D ^ { \bullet } .\tag{[4.30]}
$$

===== [p305-305] Theory of Photochemical and Radiochemical Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > C. Benzoin derivatives (2块) =====
--[p305]-- C. Benzoin derivatives
Benzoin (XXIV) and its alkyl ether derivatives are known to undergo photoinitiated cleavage of the C—C bond adjacent to the carbonyl group, leading to the simultaneous formation of the benzoyl radical and alkoxybenzyl radical (Scheme 4.31).
Photoscission is particularly efficient in the alkyl ethers of benzoin, which are among the most widely used photoinitiators in the UV curing industry.
--[p305]-- The benzoyl alkyl ethers absorb between 330 and 350 nm.<sup>253</sup> Both the benzoyl radical and the alkoxyblenzyl radicals take part in the initiation process.<sup>254</sup> It should be mentioned that generic benzoin ethers suffer from poor shelf life, which is linked to the presence of a labile hydrogen on the ether carbon.<sup>255</sup> The substitution of this labile hydrogen with benzyl ketals, such as 2,20-dimethoxy-2- phenylacetophenone (DMPA) (XXV) eliminates this problem (Scheme 4.32).<sup>256</sup>

--[p39]-- 1.3.5.1 Thermal imprint lithography
Based on the original invention of Chou and co-workers,<sup>41</sup> thermal imprint lithography (TIL) involves coating a thin layer of a thermoplastic resist polymer on an appropriate substrate, followed by the application of heat to raise the temperature of the resist above its glass temperature and taking it to a viscoelastic stage, then pressing a rigid mold with predefined patterns onto the glassy, rubbery resist polymer fluid.
--[p39]-- After cooling the imprinted polymer fluid to room temperature so as to solidify it, the mold is separated from the imprinted resist film. This technique has shown resolution down to 20 nm with good fidelity.<sup>42</sup> Subsequent pattern transfer processing, including reaction ion etching, is used to transfer the pattern in the resist to the underlying substrate.

===== [p129-129] Chapter 2 Theory of the Lithographic Process > 2.7.4.2 Physical development in resist processing (3块) =====
--[p129]-- 2.7.4.2 Physical development in resist processing
In physical development, no chemical reaction is involved in the dissolution process. Instead, the resin dissolves in a solvent (typically organic) with similar solubility parameters through mixing and solvation.
--[p129]-- Examples of resists that employ physical development include negative resists based on cyclized polyisoprene and aromatic bisazide, or positive chain scission resists such as polymethyl methacrylates, which are developed in xylene and similar organic solvents. In the cyclized polyisroprene resists, the resist film in the exposed areas has been insolubilized by crosslinking reactions and, therefore, does not dissolve in the developing solvent.
--[p129]-- In the case of the PMMA, the exposed film has lower molecular weight than the unexposed film and is, therefore, soluble in the organic solvent, whereas the unexposed film is not. The insolubilized resist film, however, swells in the developing solvent. This swelling decreases the resolution capability of the resist.<sup>214</sup>
In instances where a chemical amplification resist is developed in a nonpolar solvent to give a negative pattern, the resist is physically developed.<sup>215</sup>

===== [p453-453] Chapter 5 Theory of Block Copolymer Self-assembly Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 5.4.5 Other methods used in aligning the orientation of self-assembling block copolymers (1块) =====
--[p453]-- 5.4.5 Other methods used in aligning the orientation of self-assembling block copolymers
Other methods used in aligning the orientation of self-assembling BCPs include application of electric field, contact line pinning, directional crystallization, shear alignment, and soft lithography.
