===== [p413-413] Chapter 5 Theory of Block Copolymer Self-assembly Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 5.2.1.3.1.3 Diblock copolymers containing 2- or 4-vinylpyridine and styrene or diene blocks (2块) =====
--[p413]-- 5.2.1.3.1.3 Diblock copolymers containing 2- or 4-vinylpyridine and styrene or diene blocks
Diblock copolymers containing 2- or 4-vinylpyridine and styrenic or dienic blocks are prepared after the method of Matsushita et al.<sup>142</sup> by sequential monomer addition in polar solvents and low temperatures, so as to prevent the attack of the reactive anionic centers on the pyridine ring, activated due to the presence of a nitrogen atom on the ring.
--[p413]-- The presence of nitrogen on the pyridine ring lowers the reactivity of the vinylpyridine anion. As such, vinylpyridine monomer is added as the second monomer in copolymerization between it and styrene or dienic monomers (see Scheme 5.6).

===== [p391-391] Chapter 5 Theory of Block Copolymer Self-assembly Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 5.2 Block Copolymer Synthesis (3块) =====
--[p391]-- Hillmyer<sup>50</sup> and Hadjichristidis et al.<sup>51</sup> have written excellent books on BCP synthetic techniques.
Modern BCP molecular design strategy is driven and often dictated by the intended applications. We provide in this section general BCP synthetic methods that have been successfully adapted by research groups working in the area of BCP lithography. Table 5.1 shows some BCPs used in lithography.
--[p391]-- 5.2 Block Copolymer Synthesis
Block copolymer synthesis has witnessed considerable evolution since the introduction and development of living anionic polymerization by Szwarc et al.<sup>47</sup> more than 60 years ago.
--[p391]-- In addition to anionic polymerization, the other principal methods currently used in the synthesis of BCPs include controlled radical, ring-opening, and cationic polymerizations, often in combination with highly selective and efficient functional-group transformation techniques.<sup>48,49</sup> Sequential addition of monomers, as well as use of coupling agents and of di- or multifunctional initiators to link two or more polymer chains are some of the strategies used.

===== [p421-421] Chapter 5 Theory of Block Copolymer Self-assembly Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 5.2.2 Block copolymers via controlled radical polymerization (6块) =====
--[p421]-- 5.2.2 Block copolymers via controlled radical polymerization
--[p421]-- Because the living radical polymerization mechanism involves propagation through radicals, considerations involving monomer purity and reactivity in conjunction with relative rates of crossover and propagation reactions for the second monomer are factored into the overall sequential monomer addition synthetic strategy. The intermediate product formed after the polymerization of the first monomer must be able to initiate the polymerization of the second monomer.
--[p421]-- The strategy underlying controlled radical polymerization is to establish a dynamic equilibrium between a small fraction of growing free radicals and a large majority of dormant species, while eliminating or suppressing undesired termination and chain transfer reactions.<sup>168</sup> Such a dynamic and rapid equilibrium permits an equal opportunity for all growing or dormant chains to propagate via the frequent interconversion between the active and dormant species, leading to nearly uniform chains with narrow molecular weight distribution. This technique reduces the rate of radical recombination by lowering the effective concentration of radicals.
--[p421]-- The two main types of controlled radical polymerization techniques currently in use are: (1) stable free-radical polymerization (SFRP), involving the use of stable free radicals such as nitroxides as reversible terminating agents to control the polymerization proces s,<sup>169,170</sup> and (2) atom transfer polymerization (ATRP).
--[p421]-- The polymerization mechanism in controlled radical polymerization comprises: (1) the initiation step, where the initiating radicals are formed via homolytic or heterolytic cleavage of the initiator into radicals, followed by addition of the radical across the double bond of the monomer; (2) the propagation step, in which the monomers successively insert into the bond between the growing chain end and the radical; and (3) the chain termination, where radicals combine with each other to form stable species. The propagation and termination of the generated free radicals are as in conventional radical polymerization, although the presence of a small fraction of radicals prevents premature termination.
--[p421]-- Often, this may require the purification of the intermediate product to eliminate all traces of the first monomer. Furthermore, if purification of the intermediate product is not performed, statistical copolymerization of the second block may occur.

===== [p402-402] Chapter 5 Theory of Block Copolymer Self-assembly Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 5.2.1.1.3 Termination (2块) =====
--[p402]-- In practice, it impossible to sustain the reaction indefinitely, as residual water molecules within the reactor or Si—OH groups on the inside surfaces of glass reactors can function as termination agents.
--[p402]-- 5.2.1.1.3 Termination
Termination can be brought about by intentionally using a suitable electrophile that is useful for end group modification. Chain growth can be terminated when the growing chain end reacts with a molecule of carbon dioxide or with water, alcohols, or other protonic reagents. If termination reagents are absent, the growing chain end could remain active indefinitely, giving rise to what are called “living” polymers.

--[p43]-- 1.3.5.3 Roll-to-roll photoimprint lithography (R2R-PIL)
A major limitation with conventional imprint lithography is that it does not meet throughput requirements for patterning large-area products on a costeffective basis, largely because it is not a continuous process. To overcome this limitation, R2R-PIL was developed and is fast becoming a potential method for industrial scale manufacturing, using imprint lithography.
--[p43]-- In this technique, a photocurable and imprintable resist material, comprising monomers, oligomers, additives, initiators, and possibly a small amount of polymer, is coated on flexible substrate [such as poly(ethylene terephthalate), PET] film, which is then transported by means of a conveyor system integrated with rollers to a station where the resist is imprinted with transparent template containing the negative images of the desired patterns, then onto a station where it is irradiated with UV light and cured, and then onto a station where the mold is released from the resist, leaving only the patterned resist on the substrate [see Fig. 1.14(a) for the schematic of the process steps].<sup>53</sup> The use of two types of molds [roller and flat/plate molds, Figs.

===== [p33-34] MOLECULAR THEORY OF LITHOGRAPHY > 1.3.3 Electron beam lithography (7块) =====
--[p33]-- It is also employed in low-volume fabrication of exploratory IC device layers with extremely small features. EBL has also found application in nanotechnology research.
--[p33]-- Like photons, electrons exhibit particle and wavelike properties, but their wavelength (0.012 to 0.024 nm, corresponding to 50- to 100-keV energy electrons used in EBL) is 4 orders of magnitude shorter than the wavelength of UV radiation used in optical lithographic exposure tools; hence their resolution is not limited by diffraction.<sup>18</sup> Only features with atomic scale dimensions are able to diffract electron beams.<sup>19</sup> Electron beam lithography therefore has the potential for extremely high resolution. In fact, features as small as 2.5 nm have been successfully fabricated with EBL.<sup>20</sup> In addition, electron beams image with extremely large depth of focus, providing relief from one of the most challenging problems of optical lithography.<sup>21</sup>
--[p34]-- The final resist patterns on the wafer represent either a positive tone (same as the image of the electron beam pattern from the electron beam writer) or a negative tone (reverse of the image of the electron beam pattern from the electron beam writer), depending on the chemistry of the resist.<sup>22</sup>
Given that electrons can be focused to a few nanometers in diameter, resolution approaching the diameter of the electron beam might, in principle, be expected to be possible.
--[p34]-- Unfortunately, many factors other than the size of the electron beam determine the extent of the exposed volume in the resist and, consequently, the developed profile of the resist.
--[p34]-- The conventional technique for fabricating IC circuits with EBL uses electron beams with relatively high acceleration voltages in the range of 50–100 kV, as well as thick resists; these are conditions that favor electron scattering and make it the dominant factor in limiting resolution in this lithographic technique.<sup>23</sup>
--[p33]-- 1.3.3 Electron beam lithography
Electron beam lithography (EBL) refers to a lithographic patterning technique in which a focused beam of electrons is used to expose and pattern resist-coated semiconductor substrates as part of a number of steps employed in the fabrication of IC devices. Today, EBL is used primarily in fabrication of masks employed in optical lithography and EUV lithography.
--[p34]-- Irradiation of resist coatings with electron beams produces in the polymeric resin microstructural changes such as chain scissioning, or crosslinking, or selective bond-breaking that with the aid of post-exposure bake, where necessary, results in some sort of polarity change in the exposed region of the resist relative to the unexposed region during development.

===== [p245-246] Theory of Photochemical and Radiochemical Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 4.2.7 Radiation chemical yield and dosimetry (3块) =====
--[p245]-- For a process leading to a certain number of reaction products, the G-value of each is defined as the number of moles of that product resulting from 100 eV of energy deposited into the system. In a system of unit volume (1 L), the molarity of the product [P] produced by a dose D is expressed as
63. ibid., p. 303
64. ibid.
$$
[ P ] = G ( P ) \times \frac { D } { 1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { e V } } ,\tag{4.30}
$$
--[p245]-- 4.2.7 Radiation chemical yield and dosimetry
Because the energy of ionizing particles or radiation is not absorbed at a specific site or within a particular molecule, the quantum yield of a reaction involving such a particle or a unit of radiation can be fairly well defined. The inherent efficiency of a radiation chemical process during resist exposure is measured in terms of a radiation chemical yield or G-value.
--[p246]-- where $G ( P )$ is defined as the number of product species produced per 100 eV of energy loss by the charged particle and its secondary electrons. In practice, the determination of the G-value requires the measurement of a product quantity and dose or dose rate.<sup>65</sup>

===== [p277-277] Theory of Photochemical and Radiochemical Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 4.3.1.3 Resist systems based on crosslinking by radicals (2块) =====
--[p277]-- 4.3.1.3 Resist systems based on crosslinking by radicals
A substantial proportion of negative resists are based on radiation-induced crosslink formation initiated by radicals. Polymers such as polyethylene, various rubbers, polystyrene, and poly(vinyl chloride) are known to crosslink on irradiation; however, from a lithographic standpoint their radiation sensitivity is too low.
--[p277]-- The crosslinking efficiency of these materials can be significantly enhanced by introducing specific radiation-sensitive (labile) groups (e.g., epoxy groups) or bonds.<sup>159</sup> In this section we briefly discuss a few important examples of negative resists whose imaging action is due to radicalinitiated crosslinking of polymeric resins.

===== [p57-57] Chapter 2 Theory of the Lithographic Process > 2.3 Resist Coating (1块) =====
--[p57]-- 2.3 Resist Coating
After priming, the wafer is coated with a liquid solution of BARC (in the case of spin-on BARCs), baked, and cooled, before it is coated with a liquid solution of resist. Wafers with chemical vapor deposition (CVD) inorganic BARCs are coated with resists immediately after priming. There are several methods of coating resists on wafers, including spin coating, spray coating, and dip coating.
The most widely used methods for coating resist in the semiconductor industry are spin-coating methods.

===== [p264-264] Theory of Photochemical and Radiochemical Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 4.3.1.2.1.2 Condensation imaging mechanism ofmetal oxide sulfate resists based on hafnium and zirconium oxide sulfates (3块) =====
--[p264]-- 4.3.1.2.1.2 Condensation imaging mechanism ofmetal oxide sulfate resists based on hafnium and zirconium oxide sulfates
These resists are metal oxide sulfates such as $\mathrm { H f S O } _ { x }$ and $Z \mathrm { r } { \bf S } { \bf O } _ { x } ,$ which are complexed with a peroxo complexing agent that caps the inorganic clusters and inhibits crosslinking or network formation during spin coating and postapplied bake processing steps of the resist.
--[p264]-- Upon exposure, the interaction of this resist complex with EUV photons or an electron beam leads to the generation of secondary electrons that decompose the polymerization inhibitor, leading to the formation of active metal sites. --[p264]-- These three-dimensional network structures produce the differential solubility between unexposed and exposed regions of the resist.<sup>125</sup>
It should be pointed out that this resist does not contain organic components, either as ligands, or as photoinitiators, or as solvents. The resist is developed in 25% w/w tetramethyl ammonium hydroxide. The resists form atomically smooth, dense and pin-hole free amorphous films.<sup>126</sup>

--[p135]-- 2.7.5.2.2 Enhanced kinetic development model or enhanced Mack model
To explicitly account for the dissolution inhibitory effect of the PAC and the dissolution enhancement of the photogenerated acid from the PAC, Mack proposed an enhanced kinetic model (now called the enhanced Mack model) in 1992:<sup>256</sup>
$$
R = R _ { \mathrm { r e s i n } } \biggl [ \frac { 1 + k _ { \mathrm { e n h } } ( 1 - m ) ^ { n } } { 1 + k _ { \mathrm { i n h } } m ^ { l } } \biggr ] ,\tag{2.187}
$$
--[p136]-- R _ { \mathrm { m i n } } = \frac { R _ { \mathrm { r e s i n } } } { 1 + k _ { \mathrm { i n h } } } .\tag{2.188}
$$
When $m = 0$ , corresponding to complete exposure, the development rate is at its maximum:
$$
R _ { \mathrm { m a x } } = R _ { \mathrm { r e s i n } } ( 1 + k _ { \mathrm { e n h } } ) .\tag{2.189}
$$
--[p136]-- where $k _ { \mathrm { e n h } }$ is the rate constant for the enhancement mechanism, n is the enhancement reaction order, $k _ { \mathrm { i n h } }$ is the rate constant for the inhibition mechanism, l is the inhibition reaction order, and $R _ { \mathrm { r e s i n } }$ is the development rate of the resin alone.
For no exposure, $m = 1$ , the development rate is at its minimum, and Eq. (2.187) reduces to
$$
--[p136]-- where $r _ { \mathbf { B } }$ is the bulk development rate, $r _ { 0 }$ is the development rate at the surface of the resist relative to $r _ { \mathbf { B } } .$ , and d is the depth of the surface inhibition layer.
--[p136]-- Thus, the application of the enhanced Mack model of development rate in lithographic simulators calls for the specification of the following five parameters: $R _ { \mathrm { m a x } } , R _ { \mathrm { m i n } } , R _ { \mathrm { r e s i n } } , n .$ and l.

--[p42]-- 1.3.5.2.2 Hard PIL—Jet and Flash Imprint Lithography
The Jet and Flash Imprint Lithography (J-FIL™) process, formerly called Step and Flash Imprint Lithography (S-FIL ), a technique developed by Willson and co-workers<sup>49,50</sup> (see Fig.

--[p76]-- 2.6.2.1 Aerial image formation models
Aerial image formation models of varying complexity have been derived over the years to account for a range of physical phenomena involved in image formation. ===== [p26-26] MOLECULAR THEORY OF LITHOGRAPHY > 1.3.1 Optical lithography (5块) =====
--[p26]-- The term “optical lithography” as used in this book encompasses all lithographic patterning techniques where photons are used in such a manner that the imaging action obeys the laws of geometric optics—the simple laws of reflection and refraction, to mention but a few.
--[p26]-- The technology was adopted during the early days of planar transistor development and is still the dominant technology of choice.<sup>11,12</sup> Spanning a period of over 50 years and many generations of device technology nodes that have witnessed critical dimension reduction of over three orders of magnitude, and up to now comprising largely photons with wavelengths from the visible (436 nm) through the mid-UV (365 nm), DUV (248 nm and 193 nm), and vacuum UV (157 nm) regions of the spectrum, optical lithography has demonstrated remarkable longevity that is expected to continue into the foreseeable future. Since its introduction, photolithography has undergone many innovations and evolutions.
10.
--[p26]-- With this usage, the terms photolithography and optical lithography are interchangeable, denoting the fact that photons are the primary agents that initiate the chemical transformations of the resists, resulting in the contrast between the exposed and unexposed regions, and ultimately leading to the effective transfer of the mask image to the semiconducting substrate.
11. W. S. DeForest, Photoresist Materials and Processes, McGraw-Hill, New York (1975).
12. U.
--[p26]-- Okoroanyanwu, Chemistry and Lithography, SPIE Press, Bellingham, Washington, Chapter 1 (2010).
--[p26]-- 1.3.1 Optical lithography
Lithography using photons,<sup>10</sup> otherwise called photolithography or optical lithography, has been and continues to be the preeminent lithographic technique used in the fabrication of integrated circuit devices in the semiconductor industry since the invention of the transistor and the integrated circuit.

===== [p322-322] Theory of Photochemical and Radiochemical Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 4.4 Positive-Resist Imaging Mechanisms (2块) =====
--[p322]-- 4.4 Positive-Resist Imaging Mechanisms
Figure 4.1 shows the imaging mechanisms used to generate images in positive working resist systems. The dissolution rate of a polymer increases as the molecular weight decreases and/or as the solubility parameter of the polymer approaches that of the developer solution.
--[p322]-- Because the imaging action in positive resists is based on the enhanced solubility of the exposed part relative to the unexposed part in the developer solution, common approaches for designing positive resists rely on radiation- and photoinduced reduction of the molecular weight of the resin through photolysis, depolymerization, and radiation-induced polarity change, including photo-Fries rearrangement, deprotection, and Claisen rearrangement (in both non–chemical amplification and chemical amplification modes). These techniques have been fairly well reviewed.<sup>320</sup> In the following sections, different classes of positive-resist platforms, their components and chemical properties, as well as lithographic regimes of their applications, are considered individually.

===== [p365-365] Theory of Photochemical and Radiochemical Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 4.4.2 Photo- and radiation-induced main-chain scissioning imaging mechanisms (3块) =====
--[p365]-- 4.4.2 Photo- and radiation-induced main-chain scissioning imaging mechanisms
Short-wavelength radiations emanating from the DUV region (,250 nm) to the x-ray region (0.1–10 nm) of the electromagnetic spectrum, as well as charged particles such as electron and ion beams, possess energy in excess of the binding energy of common C─C bonds<sup>459</sup> in resists (3.6 eV).
--[p365]-- In particular, lithographic exposures utilizing DUV radiations (248 and 193 nm), VUV radiation (157 nm), EUV radiation (13.4 nm), x rays, electron beams, and ion beams can lead to the degradation of the resist polymer backbone and bring about a change in solubility by lowering the molecular weight. In this section we review resists based on main-chain scission events.
--[p365]-- Consequently, the interaction of these short-wavelength radiations and charged particles can lead directly to the scission of C─C bonds and to the formation of carbon-centered radicals, which is a characteristic of radiation chemistry.

===== [p221-221] Theory of Photochemical and Radiochemical Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 4.1 Introduction (7块) =====
--[p221]-- Relative to the starting unexposed resist material, the positive-tone imaging mechanisms lead to either a significant decrease in molecular weight (as in main-chain scissioning or depolymerization imaging mechanisms) or polarity switching (as in photolysis and radiolysis imaging mechanisms). Before we delve into the specifics of the above imaging mechanisms, we provide preliminary remarks on the photochemistry and photophysics associated with the interaction of radiation and resist materials.
--[p221]-- For positive resists, the exposed part of the resist film is dissolved away during development, reproducing a positive image of the mask; in negative resists, the unexposed part of the resist is dissolved away during development, leaving the exposed part, and reproducing a negative image of the mask.
--[p221]-- 4.1 Introduction
The interaction of organic and inorganic resist materials with photons of wavelengths between the x-ray region of the spectrum (0.2 and 2 nm) through the EUV (13.5 nm), DUV (193 and 248 nm), mid-UV (365 nm), and visible region of the spectrum (405, 436, and 700 nm), and with charged particles such as electrons have been exploited in lithographic imaging.
--[p221]-- This chapter attempts to describe the most important organic and inorganic photochemical and radiochemical imaging mechanisms that underlie these lithographies.
Listed in Fig. 4.1 are the main photochemical and radiochemical imaging mechanisms that underlie advanced lithography. As discussed in Chapter 1 and shown in Fig. 1.1, resists are in two tones: negative and positive.
--[p221]-- Relative to the starting unexposed resist material, the negative-tone imaging mechanisms either lead to significant increase in molecular weight of the exposed resist material (as in polymerization and crosslinking imaging mechanisms), or polarity switching (as in condensation, pinacol rearrangement, esterification, and ligand exchange imaging mechanisms).
--[p221]-- In contrast, the photochemical and radiochemical reactions that engender positive-tone resist imaging mechanisms include photolysis and radiolysis, as well as radiation-induced main-chain scissioning, and depolymerization. The photolysis and radiolysis imaging mechanisms include dissolution inhibition, deprotection, and Claisen and photo-Fries rearrangement reactions.
--[p221]-- The photochemical and radiochemical reactions that engender negative-tone resist imaging mechanisms include photo- and radiation-initiated polymerization, crosslinking, and polarity switching reactions such as condensation, pinacol rearrangement, esterification, and ligand exchange.

===== [p186-186] Chapter 3 Theory of Molecular Interactions in Lithography > 3.4.7 Acid–base interactions (2块) =====
--[p186]-- On the other hand, halogenated hydrocarbons, nitro groups, and, in general, all electrophilic sites are electron acceptors, and thus are Lewis acids. --[p186]-- 3.4.7 Acid–base interactions
It is a given that all polymers, except those that are saturated hydrocarbons, have acidic or basic sites in the sense of the Lewis acid–base theory.<sup>67</sup> According to the Lewis acid–base theory, electrons, oxygen, nitrogen, sulfur, and similar elements as well as p-electrons of polystyrene and polymercontaining aromatic groups are electron donors, and thus are basic.

--[p429]-- 5.2.3.1.3 Chain transfer
Chain transfer occurs via the donation of a proton from a terminal side group to a monomer molecule (Scheme 5.21). The monomer molecules thus initiated can continue to grow, generating a new chain. If more chains are initiated in this way, the average chain length of the polymer will, of course, be reduced. Chain transfer is important at temperatures near room temperature.

===== [p463-463] Chapter 6 Theory of Imprint Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 6.1 Introduction (1块) =====
--[p463]-- 6.1 Introduction
As discussed in Chapter 1, imprint lithography involves a mechanical replication process where surface reliefs from the template/stamp are embossed into a thin layer of polymeric fluid or liquid monomer with crosslinking agents on the substrate. Two versions of imprint lithography are currently practiced. One version is based on the thermal embossing of a thermoplastic polymer and is called thermal imprint lithography (TIL).
The other version is based on embossing of photocurable monomers and oligomers with crosslinking agents and is called photoimprint lithography (PIL).

===== [p207-207] Chapter 3 Theory of Molecular Interactions in Lithography > 3.7 Molecular Interactions Operating in Thermally Driven Diffusion of Photoacids During PEB of Resist Films (2块) =====
--[p207]-- 3.7 Molecular Interactions Operating in Thermally Driven Diffusion of Photoacids During PEB of Resist Films
--[p207]-- Three main phenomena associated with the PEB protocol of photoresists, especially chemical amplification resists without quencher or base contaminants are: (1) the creation of an immiscible polymer–polymer interface defined by the spatial extent of the distribution of the photoacid within the exposed part of the film, (2) photoacid diffusion with its counterion and, (3) possible acid evaporation at the resist–air interface.
We consider the molecular interactions that underpin each of these three phenomena in the next sections.

===== [p432-433] Chapter 5 Theory of Block Copolymer Self-assembly Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 5.2.4 Improving chemical and thermal stability of block copolymers (4块) =====
--[p432]-- 5.2.4 Improving chemical and thermal stability of block copolymers
Unsaturation marked by double bonds in polymers, including copolymers, is often a site of enhanced chemical reactivity. As such, hydrogenation designed to saturate the double bonds in polymers is often used to improve the chemical and thermal stability of polymers.
--[p432]-- Similarly, hydrogenation of poly(styrene-b-butadiene) is selectively hydrogenated (using the Wilkinson catalyst) on the poly(butadiene) block to yield poly(styrene-b-ethylene) diblock copolymer, after the method of Schulz<sup>193</sup> (Scheme 5.28).
193. D. N. Schulz, in Encyclopedia of Polymer Science and Engineering 7, H. F. Mark, Ed., Wiley-Interscience, New York, p. 807 (1987).
Hydrogenation is typically performed under hydrogen pressure with either homogenous (soluble) or heterogeneous (insoluble) catalysts.
--[p432]-- For instance, hydrogenation of poly (isoprene-b-styrene) saturates the double bonds in the polyisoprene (PI) block of the copolymer, converting it to a poly(ethylene propylene) PEP block, which is chemically distinct from PI and has different properties (Scheme 5.27). In contrast to PI, PEP is much less sensitive to oxidation and thus may be heated in the presence of oxygen with no significant degradation.
--[p433]-- Typical heterogeneous catalysts include the $\mathrm { P d } / \mathrm { C a C O } _ { 3 }$ system<sup>194,195</sup> and show very low selectivity but are efficient for the hydrogenation of aliphatic double bonds of polydienes<sup>196</sup> and the hydrogenation of aromatic rings under severe conditions (Scheme 5.27).<sup>197</sup> Diene blocks in copolymers containing diene, and polar blocks containing ester groups such as, for example, alkylmethacrylates are selectively hydrogenated with Cr- or Ni-based catalysts, following the method of Yu et al.<sup>198</sup> Selective hydrogenation of diene blocks in BCPs can also be accomplished with the tosylhydrazide method (a noncatalytic hydrogenation method), after the manner of Hahn.<sup>199</sup>

===== [p461-461] Chapter 5 Theory of Block Copolymer Self-assembly Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 5.5.3 Block copolymers as templates for biomolecular patterning (1块) =====
--[p461]-- 5.5.3 Block copolymers as templates for biomolecular patterning
Diblock copolymers comprising domains with differential hydrophobicity have been demonstrated to pattern proteins that selectively adsorb onto the more hydrophobic component, for instance PS in the case of PS-b-PMMA diblock.<sup>308</sup> It was observed that catalytic activity of adsorbed enzymes was retained in these structures.<sup>309</sup>

===== [p456-456] Chapter 5 Theory of Block Copolymer Self-assembly Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 5.4.5.5 Soft lithography (1块) =====
--[p456]-- 5.4.5.5 Soft lithography
In soft lithography, resist is imprinted with a PDMS stamp to create grating patterns, following which, BCP film is spin coated onto the space between the gratings to template the location of copolymer domains. The BCPs, in turn,
self-assemble and align parallel to the gratings in a perpendicular orientation to the substrate.<sup>297</sup>

The two main modes of spectral sensitization involving energy transfer include triplet sensitization and electron transfer.

===== [p378-378] Theory of Photochemical and Radiochemical Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > 4.4.3 Photo- and radiation-induced depolymerization imaging mechanisms (1块) =====
--[p378]-- 4.4.3 Photo- and radiation-induced depolymerization imaging mechanisms
During exposure, resists based on the photo- and radiation-induced depolymerization imaging mechanism literally depolymerize and revert back to the monomer. The depolymerization can be directly initiated by the radiation in non–chemical amplification mode, or indirectly via photo- or radiation-generated acids from onium salts, which go on to catalyze the depolymerization in chemical amplification mode.
Poly(phthaldehyde) resists are a prime example of this class of resists.

===== [p307-307] Theory of Photochemical and Radiochemical Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > E. Ketoxime esters of benzoin (1块) =====
--[p307]-- E. Ketoxime esters of benzoin
Ketoxime esters of benzoin, exemplified by 1-phenyl-1,2-propanedione-2-Obenzoyloxime (PPO) (XXVII), upon photolysis, eliminate two volatile fragments after the primary scission of the N—O bond (Scheme 4.34). The radical yield of PPO decomposition is very high $( \Phi = 0 . 9 )$ . The phenyl radical, the final product of fragmentation, is an aggressive polymerization initiating species. 259

--[p398]-- 5.2.1.1 General mechanism of anionic polymerization
Anionic polymerization proceeds via organometallic sites, carbanions (or oxanions) with metallic counterions. ===== [p71-71] Chapter 2 Theory of the Lithographic Process > 2.6 Exposure (1块) =====
--[p71]-- 2.6 Exposure
The exposure of the resist-coated wafer immediately follows the alignment of the wafer to the mask (containing the circuit patterns). Performed in the lithographic exposure tool, using mostly projection scanners and steppers, it involves illuminating the mask with the exposure radiation and projecting the transmitted/reflected image of the mask (called the aerial image) onto the resist film.

===== [p309-309] Theory of Photochemical and Radiochemical Lithographic Imaging Mechanisms > B. Michler’s ketone (1块) =====
--[p309]-- B. Michler’s ketone
Michler’s ketone, also called 4,40-bis(dimethylamino)benzophenone (XXXII) is an aromatic ketone as well as a tertiary amine and is by itself a complete initiating system. It undergoes hydrogen abstraction on irradiation and is a useful photoinitiator.<sup>266</sup> Its absorption at 365 nm is stronger than that of benzophenone. It is often used as a coinitiator together with benzophenone, in which case it acts as the hydrogen donor.<sup>267</sup>
